  guard `resolve_allows_a_run_whose_forward_inputs_are_plain_objects`. The
  cross-crate coupling is guarded from the other side too: the core suite already
  pins the envelope's exact shape with an `assert_eq!`, so changing it fails there
  loudly rather than silently blinding this detector.

  ### P1 — the retry endpoint must inflate history before classifying an unwind

  The compensation envelope lives in `ActivityScheduled.input`, and `input` is a
  **payload-bearing field**. With payload offloading (issue #524) enabled, an
  oversized envelope is replaced wholesale by an `_harvest_offload_envelope`
  reference before it reaches `harvest_events`; a codec-encrypting deployment
  (issue #608) wraps it likewise. The retry endpoint loaded history with plain
  `store::load_history`, so the structural predicate never saw the three
  compensation keys.

  On its own that is only a missed signal, but combined with the other two failure
  modes it reopens the exact hole the previous fix closed: an unwind at a drained
  signal frontier records **no marker** (signal 1 blind), a since-renamed
  compensator defeats the name check (signal 3 blind), and an offloaded envelope
  defeats the shape check (signal 2 blind) — so a fully rolled-back run becomes
  retryable and resumes onto rolled-back state. Unlike the codec case, which fails
  CLOSED (`load_history` hard-errors `UnknownPayloadCodec`), the offload case fails
  **open** and silently.

  Fixed at the call site, which is where the information exists:
  `retry_dag_run_inner` now loads via `store::load_history_inflated` with the
  runtime's real codecs and payload offloader.

  This is deliberately **not** fixed in `resolve_retry_plan`. An offloaded input is
  indistinguishable from a large ordinary forward input, so treating one as a
  compensation signal would reject every legitimate retry of a big-payload
  compensating DAG. The resolver's contract is therefore "you must hand me
  inflated history", pinned by
  `an_offloaded_compensation_envelope_is_invisible_and_must_be_inflated_by_the_caller`,
  which asserts both halves: fed the offloaded form the rolled-back run wrongly
  resolves `Ok` (the fail-open the endpoint prevents), and fed the inflated form it
  correctly resolves `Err(CompensatedRun)`.

  With no `PayloadStore` registered `load_history_inflated` delegates verbatim to
  the inline path, so the default deployment is byte-for-byte unchanged; only
  oversized payloads cost a blob fetch, on a low-frequency operator endpoint.
  Passing the runtime's real codecs (rather than the identity default
  `load_history` uses) additionally makes the endpoint work at all on a
  codec-encrypting deployment, where it previously returned an error. No payload is
  surfaced to the caller — the plan carries only node names and an event id.

  ### P2 — the envelope signal must corroborate against the dispatch name

  `is_compensation_envelope` matched on shape alone (exactly the three keys
  `dag_compensate`/`input`/`output`, with a string `dag_compensate`). That shape is
  reachable by accident: a mapped cell or an `input_from` binding hands a node the
  **raw upstream output**, which is arbitrary user data. A forward activity whose
  input happened to carry those keys was therefore classified as a compensation
  dispatch — 409-ing a perfectly retryable run, and doing so even for a DAG that
  declares **no compensators at all** and so cannot possibly have unwound.

  RED evidence (a non-compensating `a → b → c → d` DAG whose `a` input is
  `{"dag_compensate": "looks_like_a_node", "input": 1, "output": 2}`):

  ```
  a_forward_dispatch_mimicking_the_envelope_is_not_an_unwind
  panicked: a non-compensating DAG must stay retryable: CompensatedRun
  ```

  Signal 2 now corroborates against the dispatch's **name**: an envelope-shaped
  input counts only when the dispatch is *not* named after a declared node. Every
  forward dispatch is named after a node, and
  `DagBuildError::CompensatorNameCollidesWithNode` guarantees at build time that no
  compensator shares a node's name — so the corroboration rejects every forward
  dispatch while costing nothing.

  Crucially it preserves the rename-resilience signal 2 exists for: a compensator
  that was renamed, or **removed outright**, is still absent from the node set and
  still detected. Pinned by
  `a_genuine_unwind_is_detected_even_after_all_compensators_were_removed` (the
  definition declares zero compensators, yet the marker-less unwind is still
  rejected) alongside the existing rename test.

  The envelope's `dag_compensate` *value* is deliberately left unchecked. It names
  a forward node, so validating it against the definition would reintroduce exactly
  the registry dependence signal 2 was introduced to escape.

  ### P1 — the envelope corroboration must be historical, not definition-based

  The previous round corroborated the envelope signal against the **current node
  set**: an envelope-shaped input counted only when the dispatch was not named
  after a declared node. That closed the user-payload false positive, but
  introduced a new blindness — `CompensatorNameCollidesWithNode` is a
  *per-definition-version* guarantee. It stops a compensator from sharing a node's
  name in the build that declared it; nothing stops a **later** build from
  introducing a forward node named after a compensator that has since been renamed
  away. The current-definition check then suppressed a genuine envelope.

  RED evidence (current definition `a → undo_a → c` with `undo_a` now a forward
  node and no compensator declared; history carries a marker-less unwind that
  dispatched `undo_a`):

  ```
  a_genuine_unwind_is_detected_even_when_a_later_node_reuses_the_compensator_name
  left:  Ok(DagRetryPlan { reset_to_event_id: 2,
          nodes_to_re_execute: ["c", "undo_a"], nodes_carried_over: ["a"] })
  right: Err(CompensatedRun)
  ```

  `nodes_carried_over: ["a"]` is the double-spend — `undo_a` had already rolled
  `a` back.

  The corroboration is now drawn from **history only**: the envelope's
  `dag_compensate` value must name an activity that actually **succeeded in this
  run** (correlated `ActivityScheduled` → `ActivityCompleted` by `activity_id`,
  since the completion event carries no name). The unwind only ever compensates
  succeeded nodes, so a genuine envelope always satisfies it.

  Signal 2 therefore has **no registry dependence at all**, and survives every way
  the definition can drift from the run that produced the history — compensator
  renamed, removed outright, or its name later reused as a forward node. All three
  are pinned:

  - `resolve_rejects_a_marker_less_unwind_whose_compensator_was_since_renamed`
  - `a_genuine_unwind_is_detected_even_after_all_compensators_were_removed`
  - `a_genuine_unwind_is_detected_even_when_a_later_node_reuses_the_compensator_name`

  The user-payload false positive stays closed
  (`a_forward_dispatch_mimicking_the_envelope_is_not_an_unwind`: the mimic's
  `dag_compensate` names nothing that succeeded).

  Residual, documented and safe-direction: a forward dispatch whose input is
  exactly the three envelope keys *and* whose `dag_compensate` happens to name a
  node that succeeded in the same run is still a false positive — which marks a
  retryable run non-retryable (start a fresh run), never the double-spend.

  ### P2 — the FailFast policy table described cancellation it never performed

  `docs/getting-started/08-dags-and-schedules.md` promised `FailFast` would "stop
  execution and cancel in-flight instances on first failure". The cancellation half
  was **never** true: a mapped cell is a durable `harvest_task_queue` row, so
  abandoning the workflow's future never cancelled it. The stop-execution half
  became inaccurate with this PR's P1-B fix, which drains the instance stream so
  the replay cursor stays clean for the unwind.

  The table now describes what actually happens — the first cell failure decides
  the node's outcome and stops **downstream** work, while already-dispatched cells
  are drained to completion — with a paragraph stating that `FailFast` is an
  outcome policy, not a cancellation policy, and is not a tool for bounded failure
  latency.

  ### P1 — an old forward node named like a *current* compensator faked an unwind

  The name-only signal 3 (a dispatch whose *name* is a currently-declared
  compensator) was the mirror of the name-reuse hole fixed above, in the other
  direction: a run produced by an **older** definition, where `undo_a` was an
  ordinary forward node, is resolved against a **current** definition that has
  since introduced `undo_a` as a compensator. Signal 3 then reported
  `CompensatedRun` for a run that never unwound at all, blocking a legitimate
  retry with a permanent `409`.

  Root cause is the same per-definition-version scope of
  `DagBuildError::CompensatorNameCollidesWithNode`: it guarantees no compensator
  shadows a node *within one build*, and constrains nothing across versions. Two
  consecutive review rounds hit that boundary from opposite sides, so rather than
  add a third name-keyed patch, **signal 3 was removed entirely**. Detection is
  now two signals, both purely historical:

  1. a `saga_compensat*` marker, or
  2. a compensation envelope whose `dag_compensate` names a node that **succeeded
   in the same run**.

  Signal 3 was redundant with signal 2 by construction — every unwind this engine
  produces writes the envelope, and only succeeded nodes are ever compensated — so
  dropping it loses no detection while removing the only remaining cross-version
  false-positive vector. No name-keyed check against the current definition
  survives in either direction.

  Pinned by `an_old_forward_node_named_like_a_current_compensator_is_not_an_unwind`
  (RED before the change: `CompensatedRun`); the marker-less regression test was
  also rewritten onto a realistic envelope-bearing fixture via a new
  `compensator_dispatch` helper, since the old one asserted on a history the
  engine cannot actually produce (a `Value::Null` input on a compensator dispatch).

  ### P1 — dispatch rejections have no history footprint (documented, not fixed)

  A `PayloadTooLarge` rejection is routed to the unwind as an ordinary node
  failure (that is the earlier P1-A fix, which stops it from `?`-escaping past the
  terminal check and stranding a succeeded compensable upstream). It leaves **no**
  history footprint by design — no activity id, no command, no event — which is
  precisely what makes that routing safe, and is also its one limitation: the
  decision is re-evaluated on every replay against **live** configuration.

  Raise the activity-input cap while a compensating DAG is mid-unwind and the
  previously-rejected node now dispatches, colliding with the recorded
  compensator's `ScheduleActivity`.

  Assessed and **documented rather than fixed**, for three reasons:

  1. The consequence is a #603 **nd-block** — the run stays `RUNNING`, retries with
   backoff, and recovers when the cap is reverted. Never a silent partial
   rollback.
  2. It needs a four-way conjunction: `PayloadTooLarge` + a compensating DAG + a
   cap change + that change landing inside the unwind's decision-cycle window.
  3. It is the same class as the pre-existing engine-wide
   `known_limitation_early_config_dependent_failure_does_not_replay_cleanly` (renamed `early_config_dependent_failure_replays_cleanly` and CLOSED by issue #952)
   (issue #601), pinned there with a plain non-DAG `spawn_child_workflow_raw`
   call. Issue #780 **enlarges** the surface rather than creating it: before the
   unwind existed a rejection sealed the run `FAILED` with no compensation
   events, so nothing could collide.

  The durable fix is out of scope by construction: it means giving the *engine's*
  activity-dispatch path a history footprint for deterministic pre-dispatch
  rejections, so replay reads the decision back instead of re-deciding it. It
  cannot be done inside the DAG runtime — a level dispatches concurrently through
  `join_all`, so a marker pushed from inside a task future has no deterministic
  position, and one pushed after the join is read too late to gate the dispatch.
  That is an engine-wide change affecting every workflow.

  Pinned by `dag_compensation_tests::known_limitation_raising_the_cap_mid_unwind_diverges`
  (asserts the divergence surfaces as nd details, i.e. a recoverable block) and
  documented in `docs/saga.md` plus the `is_deterministic_dispatch_rejection` doc
  comment, with the operational guidance: do not change payload caps while
  compensating DAG runs are in flight.

  ### P2 — the DAG run-graph read compensation dispatches as forward nodes

  Issue #780 introduced a **new class** of `ActivityScheduled` event — the
  compensator dispatch — that every name-keyed history reader now sees for the
  first time. The retry resolver was hardened against name reuse across
  definition versions in the previous rounds; the run-graph view (#690) was not,
  and it shares the same readers.

  Within one definition version `CompensatorNameCollidesWithNode` keeps a
  compensator distinguishable from a forward node. Across versions it does not: a
  later definition may introduce a **forward node** named after an older
  definition's compensator. `GET /dags/{name}/runs/{id}` would then report that
  never-executed node as succeeded/failed, with the compensation's timestamps.

  Both name-keyed readers now skip a compensation dispatch, using the same
  history-only corroboration the retry guard uses (an envelope whose
  `dag_compensate` names a node that succeeded in the same run), so neither can
  drift across versions:

  - `dag_retry::node_outcome` — node status (feeds the run-graph view too);
  - `dag_graph::latest_scheduled` — node timing, attempts, and error.

  Fixing **both** is load-bearing: they are separate readers of the same
  authoritative attempt, so excluding in only one would leave a name-reused node
  reporting `pending` alongside the old compensation's timestamps. The shared
  predicate is exported as `dag_retry::is_compensation_dispatch`.

  RED first, at both levels:

  - `node_outcome_ignores_a_compensation_dispatch_named_like_a_forward_node`
  - `a_compensation_dispatch_is_not_read_as_a_same_named_forward_node`
  (run-graph level; asserts `status`, `started_at`, and `attempts` together)

  The user-payload false positive stays closed by the same corroboration
  (`node_outcome_still_reads_a_forward_node_whose_input_mimics_the_envelope`: the
  mimic's `dag_compensate` names nothing that succeeded, so a genuine forward
  dispatch is never swallowed).

  ### P1 — a `CollectAll` node whose cells all failed was not detected as compensated

  The corroboration for signal 2 (and for the run-graph exclusion above) required
  the envelope's `dag_compensate` to name a node that **completed**. That was too
  strict, on a case the DAG's own status model creates:

  a `CollectAll` mapped node folds each cell failure into the cells array and
  never flips the node's `TaskStatus` — only a deterministic dispatch rejection
  does. So a node whose cells **all** failed still settles `Succeeded` at the DAG
  level and is genuinely compensated, while recording **no** `ActivityCompleted`
  under its name. Both guards missed it: retry-from-node stayed available on a
  rolled-back run (the double-spend, when the marker was also absent), and the
  run-graph exclusion failed to skip the compensation dispatch.

  Fixed by moving the bar from **completion** to **dispatch** —
  `dispatched_activity_names` / `compensates_a_dispatched_node`. That is precisely
  the unwind's own guard (`dispatched_forward`): a node is compensated only if it
  dispatched forward work, and dispatching records an `ActivityScheduled` under
  the node's activity name. So the corroboration now matches the invariant it was
  always meant to encode, rather than a proxy for it. An empty mapped fan-out is
  excluded for free — it dispatches nothing and is never compensated.

  Still purely historical, so every cross-version drift mode stays closed.

  Pinned by `a_collect_all_node_whose_cells_all_failed_is_still_detected_as_compensated`
  (RED before the change: `Ok(DagRetryPlan { .. })`). The false-positive guards
  still hold — their mimic envelopes name activities that were never dispatched.

  Accepted widening, documented: a forward dispatch whose user input is exactly
  the three envelope keys *and* whose `dag_compensate` names a node that was
  dispatched-but-failed is now a false positive where it previously was not. Same
  safe direction as before — it marks a retryable run non-retryable, never the
  double-spend.

  ### Review round 5 — the run-graph readers must decode before they filter, and no reader may hold a pool slot across blob I/O

  Two independent P2s on the same root: the compensation filter reads
  `ActivityScheduled.input`, a **payload-bearing** field, and the surfaces that
  consume it were not set up to see through a stored envelope.

  **(1) Codec/offload deployments silently lost the run-graph exclusion.** Both
  run-graph readers — the #690 API handler and the Vantage DAG detail page — load
  raw history (`store::load_history_with_timestamps` explicitly leaves payload
  fields undecoded). On a codec-encrypting (#608) or payload-offloading (#524)
  deployment the filter was handed an opaque envelope, returned `false`, and a
  never-executed forward node was reported with an older definition's compensation
  status, timings, and attempts — exactly the defect the round-4 exclusion exists
  to close, reopened for those deployments.

  Fixed with one shared pass (`api::decode_graph_history`) used by both readers, so
  they can never disagree about whether the filter is looking at real payloads:

  - **Gated on a cheap structural scan** (`graph_history_needs_inflation`) of only
  the two fields the derivation reads — `ActivityScheduled.input` and
  `MarkerRecorded.details`. The identity codec's `encode_payload` is a
  pass-through, so a default deployment stores no envelope, the scan answers
  `false`, and the pre-#780 read path runs byte-for-byte unchanged.
  - **Degrades rather than errors**: the run graph is read-only observability, so
  an inflate/decode failure logs and renders from the raw history instead of
  failing the page. The retry endpoint keeps the opposite posture — fail closed,
  because there a hidden envelope permits the double-spend.
  - Surfaces no payload (node names, statuses, timings, attempts, and a truncated
  `error`, which is not payload-bearing), so it needs no #608 read-decode opt-in
  or audit row — the same rationale the awaitables endpoint's replay drive uses.

  New core predicate `payload_codec::is_codec_envelope`, delegating to the existing
  authoritative `codec_envelope_parts` shape check so a caller's "is this opaque?"
  question cannot drift from what the decoder recognises. Its offload sibling
  (`payload_store::extract_offload_ref`) was already public.

  **(2) The retry endpoint held a DB connection across sequential blob fetches.**
  `store::load_history_inflated` loads the rows and then fetches every offloaded
  blob while still holding the connection it loaded them with, so a slow or
  unavailable payload store — or a few concurrent retries over large histories —
  could pin pool slots and stall unrelated API and worker work. The endpoint now
  loads raw, releases the pool slot, inflates/decodes in memory, and reacquires a
  connection for the preview/reset — the discipline the awaitables endpoint
  already established. It still fails closed on any inflate/decode error.

  Pinned by `a_codec_encoded_compensation_dispatch_is_only_recognised_after_decoding`
  (asserts the predicate is blind on the raw stored history and correct after the
  pass), `graph_history_needs_inflation_detects_opaque_payload_fields`, and two
  end-to-end run-graph tests — a codec-encoded compensator named like a current
  forward node is excluded (status `pending`, no timing, zero attempts) while an
  ordinary codec-encoded forward dispatch still reads normally.

  ### Post-review hardening (round 6) — a bare unwind marker is not proof of rollback

  An automated review found a **P1** in the compensated-run retry guard: signal 1
  accepted a `saga_compensat*` marker on its own, but the marker is recorded
  *before* anything is rolled back.

  `Saga::run_compensations` calls `observe_saga_unwind_start` — which records
  `saga_compensated:{seq}` — and only then enters the compensation loop. A
  compensator can be rejected *pre-dispatch*: `execute_activity_raw` returns
  `PayloadTooLarge` before `push_command(ScheduleActivity)` when the
  `{dag_compensate, input, output}` envelope exceeds the activity-input cap and no
  payload offloading is configured. A run whose sole compensator is rejected that
  way therefore ends as `[…, saga_compensated:1, saga_compensation_failed:1,
  WorkflowFailed]` — a marker, zero `ActivityScheduled` events, and the upstream
  side effect still live.

  The guard read that marker as "already rolled back" and returned `409
  CompensatedRun`, telling the operator to start a fresh DAG run — which **repeats**
  the still-live upstream side effect. The rejection was in the dangerous direction:
  it refused the safe recovery and recommended the unsafe one.

  Signal 1 now requires a `saga_compensat*` marker **followed by at least one
  activity dispatch**. The check is positional (any `ActivityScheduled` after the
  marker's index), never name- or payload-keyed, which is why signal 1 is *refined*
  rather than dropped: an issue #495 payload erasure tombstones the envelope's
  contents so signal 2 goes blind, and only signal 1 keeps a genuinely rolled-back
  run non-retryable. Because a DAG compensator is always dispatched as an activity,
  the marker always precedes it, and no forward dispatch can follow it (the unwind
  runs only after the level walk returns), the refinement introduces no false
  negative.

  Pinned by `a_marker_only_unwind_that_dispatched_nothing_stays_retryable` (a
  marker pair with zero dispatches resolves `Ok`) and by
  `resolve_rejects_a_run_whose_compensation_failed_after_dispatching`, which was
  strengthened to dispatch its compensator so it proves the rejection path for a
  real rollback rather than for a bare marker.

  **Final detection contract** (supersedes the two-signal lists in the earlier
  rounds above, which record what each round found rather than the end state). A
  run is treated as compensated iff **either**:

  1. a `saga_compensat*` marker is followed by at least one `ActivityScheduled`, or
  2. an `ActivityScheduled` carries a `{dag_compensate, input, output}` envelope
   whose `dag_compensate` names an activity **dispatched** in the same run.

  Both read only the run's own recorded history — never the registered definition.
  A partial unwind still trips signal 1: if any compensator dispatched, the `409`
  stands even when a later one is rejected. Only an unwind that dispatched
  *nothing* stays retryable, which is precisely the case where nothing was rolled
  back.

  ### Post-review hardening (round 7) — a PII-erased run is refused outright

  An automated review found a **P1** at the intersection of two features neither
  round had considered together: **issue #495 payload erasure** and the
  **drained-signal-frontier** unwind (issue #801).

  Erasure tombstones every payload field, so on an erased history
  `ActivityScheduled.input` is `{"_harvest_erased": true}` and **signal 2 is
  blind**. Signal 1 normally still holds — a marker's *name* is not a payload
  field, and the round-6 positional "dispatch after the marker" check reads no
  payload — but a run that unwound at a drained signal frontier recorded **no
  marker at all**, leaving signal 1 nothing to anchor on. On that intersection a
  fully rolled-back run looked retryable, and the retry would carry over upstream
  nodes whose side effects had already been undone. Erasure is irreversible, so no
  amount of inflating or decoding recovers the evidence.

  The round-6 changelog and docs claimed the positional check "survives payload
  erasure" without qualifying it — accurate only when a marker exists. Corrected in
  `docs/saga.md`.

  `retry_dag_run_inner` now refuses an erased source run before it resolves
  anything, with a `409` naming erasure as the blocker. The check is
  `erase::execution_input_is_erased(&execution.input)` — O(1), and the same guard
  the issue #612 terminal-query path uses (erasure always tombstones the execution
  row's own `input` column first).

  **The refusal is correct independently of compensation.** The issue #148 fork
  carries over the upstream events, whose `output` fields are now tombstones, so a
  re-executing downstream node with an `input_from` binding (issue #702) would be
  handed `{"_harvest_erased": true}` as its input. Retry-from-node on an erased run
  produces garbage whether or not it ever compensated.

  The cost is a safe-direction false positive: an erased run of a DAG that declares
  no compensators is refused too. Deliberate — "the current definition declares no
  compensators" is exactly the cross-version registry signal earlier rounds removed,
  since the definition that produced the history may have declared them.

  Pinned by `retry_erased_run_is_conflict` (erases a seeded FAILED run through the
  real `erase_workflow_payloads`, asserts the `409` names erasure and a fresh run,
  and asserts no fork was created) and by the characterization test
  `an_erased_marker_less_unwind_is_invisible_and_must_be_refused_by_the_caller`,
  which proves the resolver genuinely cannot see an erased unwind — so the guard
  must live in the caller, which holds the execution row.

  ### Post-review hardening (round 8) — a scheduled compensator is not a started one

  An automated review found a **P1** one level deeper than round 6: both signals
  treated an `ActivityScheduled` as proof that a compensator ran.

  An operator cancel landing mid-unwind fails every open task row
  (`queue::fail_open_tasks_for_execution`) **without appending any event**, so a
  compensator that was dispatched but never claimed sits in history as a bare
  `ActivityScheduled` having rolled back nothing. Both signals fired on it,
  returned `409 CompensatedRun`, and sent the operator to a fresh run — re-running
  an upstream node whose side effect is still live. Same failure direction as round
  6: refusing the safe recovery and recommending the unsafe one.

  Both signals now require the dispatch to have **started**. New
  `started_activity_ids` collects every `ActivityStarted`; signal 1 requires a
  *started* dispatch after the marker, and signal 2 requires the envelope-carrying
  dispatch to have started.

  **Why `ActivityStarted` is the right bar** (verified in `worker.rs`): the worker
  appends it in a setup phase *before* invoking the handler, and a failed append
  aborts the dispatch — so *body executed ⇒ `ActivityStarted` exists*. Its absence
  therefore proves the body never ran. Deliberately **not** keyed on a terminal
  event: a worker that started and then crashed mid-body may or may not have landed
  the rollback, and that ambiguity must resolve to "compensated" (refuse the retry),
  not to "safe". Neither `activity_id` nor `worker_id` is a payload field, so the
  signal also survives issue #495 erasure.

  The shared `compensates_a_dispatched_node` predicate is **unchanged**, because it
  is also the forward-dispatch exclusion used by `node_outcome` and
  `dag_graph::latest_scheduled` — a compensator dispatch must be excluded from
  name-keyed node reads whether or not it started. The start requirement is applied
  only in `ran_compensation_unwind`.

  Pinned by `a_scheduled_but_never_started_compensator_stays_retryable` (RED before
  the change) and its mirror `a_started_compensator_with_no_terminal_still_blocks_retry`
  (a started-then-crashed compensator still refuses the retry). Seven existing
  fixtures were made realistic — a compensator that reaches a terminal event always
  carried an `ActivityStarted` in a real history; they had omitted it only because
  nothing read it.

  ### Round 9 — the erasure guard's TOCTOU window, and offload references that outlive their store

  Two P1 review findings, both the same shape as rounds 6–8: a way for the
  compensated-run guard to be reading something other than what it believes.

  **(a) Recheck erasure under the fork's own row lock.** The round-7 guard reads
  the execution row *without* a lock, and the handler then deliberately releases
  its database connection to inflate blobs off the pool before opening the reset
  transaction. `POST /workflows/{id}/erase-payloads` takes its own `FOR UPDATE`
  lock, so it can commit tombstones anywhere in that window — the pre-flight
  having already passed on the intact row. The fork would then copy tombstoned
  events, and the compensation decision would have been made on evidence that no
  longer existed.

  `WorkflowResetRequest` gains `refuse_erased_source: bool` (`#[serde(skip)]`,
  mirroring `allow_terminal_source`), and `reset_workflow_execution` rechecks
  erasure immediately after `load_source_execution(.., lock = true)` and **before
  `load_event_rows`** — under the lock, before copying a single event — returning
  the new `WorkflowResetError::ErasedSource`. That serialises the two operations:
  erasure either committed before the lock (the fork sees it and refuses) or
  queues behind it (the fork completes on intact events). There is no interleaving
  that forks a tombstoned run.

  The DAG retry handler sets the flag; the batch-reset endpoint deliberately does
  not (refusing an erased source there would be an unrelated behavior change), and
  the public reset endpoint cannot set it from the wire, so it is byte-for-byte
  unchanged. The round-7 pre-flight check is kept as the fast path — it answers
  without paying for the history load and blob I/O — and both refusals surface the
  same `409`, so a caller cannot tell which one caught it.

  Pinned by `refuse_erased_source_is_not_settable_from_the_wire` (pure; RED as a
  compile error before the field existed), and by two DB tests that stage the race
  outcome deterministically: `reset_refuses_an_erased_source_under_its_own_row_lock`
  drives `reset_workflow_execution` directly against an already-erased run — the
  exact state the race leaves behind, with the pre-flight guard bypassed by
  construction, so the refusal can only come from the locked recheck — and
  `reset_without_the_flag_still_forks_an_erased_source` pins the unchanged
  behavior with the flag off.

  **(b) Fail closed on an offload reference with no store configured.** A payload
  store is optional, so `offloader` is `None` both on the default deployment and on
  one that *removed* its store. In the latter case the stored history still carries
  `_harvest_offload_envelope` references, `inflate_and_decode_events` skips the
  inflate pass entirely, and `decode_event` returns the reference verbatim — it is
  not a codec envelope, so nothing rejects it. Signal 2 would then look for
  `dag_compensate` inside a blob pointer and find nothing, leaving a marker-less
  rolled-back run retryable.

  Any reference surviving the pass is now an error naming the blob key and store
  id. Placing the check inside `inflate_and_decode_events` gives both callers the
  right posture for free: the retry endpoint propagates it (fails closed), and the
  run-graph reader catches it and degrades to the raw history with a warning, as it
  already does for a decode failure. When a store *is* configured the check is
  unreachable — inflation either resolves the reference or rejects a foreign
  `store_id` — so it only fires on the configuration-removal case and otherwise
  costs a few key lookups per event.

  Pinned by `a_residual_offload_reference_fails_closed_when_no_store_is_configured`
  (RED before the change) with `a_plain_history_still_passes_with_no_store_configured`
  as the control that the default deployment is untouched.
- **Phase 3.52** (implemented): Activity run metadata and deadline via `ctx.info()` — see issue #783. The activity-side mirror of the workflow-side `ctx.info()` (issue #698). **Before:** an `#[activity]` body could read its `attempt()`, `max_attempts()`, and `previous_failure()`, but not *which run it belonged to* — so a log line from an activity could not be correlated back to the owning workflow without threading the ids through the activity's own input, and an activity had no way to ask how much of its `start_to_close` budget was left. A long activity therefore had exactly two options: finish, or be killed mid-item by the timeout scanner and lose everything it had done. **After:** one read-only, zero-footprint accessor `ActivityContext::info() -> ActivityExecutionInfo` bundles the attempt's owning-run and dispatch metadata — `execution_id`, `workflow_id`, `workflow_type`, `activity_type`, `activity_id`, `attempt`, `max_attempts`, `is_local`, `queue_name`, `task_id` — plus three deadline accessors: `deadline() -> Option<DateTime<Utc>>`, `time_remaining() -> Option<Duration>`, and the guard `is_expiring_within(reserve) -> bool`. Each `info()` field also has a standalone accessor (`ctx.execution_id()`, `ctx.workflow_id()`, …). **One-hop correlation (AC3):** the reported `execution_id` is exactly the `{exec_id}` segment of `GET /api/harvest/workflows/{exec_id}` — it renders as the bare UUID and round-trips through `FromStr` — so an on-call engineer paging from a log line opens the run with zero directory lookups. Alongside it, `task_id` is the `harvest_task_queue` row PK the operator `retry-now` (#516) / `fail-now` (#765) routes address, so the pair is directly actionable (`None` for a local activity, which has no queue row). **Retry-stable identity (AC4):** the new `ActivityIdentity` struct (`execution_id`/`workflow_id`/`workflow_type`/`activity_type`/`activity_id`, returned by `ActivityExecutionInfo::identity()`) is byte-identical on every attempt of one logical invocation; only `attempt` and the deadline advance. Asserting on the struct rather than a hand-written field list keeps a stability test honest as fields are added. Deriving an idempotency key from `identity()` therefore reuses one key across retries. **Deadline is the minimum of two clocks (a deliberate extension of the issue's literal scope, flagged for spec-owner review):** `deadline()` returns the earliest of the attempt's `start_to_close` budget (`started_at + start_to_close`) and the activity's cross-retry `schedule_to_close` deadline (#378). The issue names only `start_to_close`, but `schedule_to_close` enforcement kills a `RUNNING` row too, so reporting only the per-attempt budget would over-report the time available and let an activity work right up to a kill that discards everything — the destructive direction. `time_remaining()` saturates at zero (never negative). `is_expiring_within(reserve)` is **always `false` when unbounded**, closing an `Option`-ordering trap: `None < Some(_)`, so a naive `ctx.time_remaining() < Some(reserve)` checkpoints *immediately* on an unbounded activity. **Zero mid-timeout progress loss (the success metric):** an activity can now resume from `ctx.heartbeat_details()`, check `is_expiring_within(reserve)` before each unit of work, and yield with a retryable error while there is still time to flush — so the retry resumes from the checkpoint and re-executes **nothing**. **Threading (no new queries):** `append_activity_started_if_pending` already loaded the full `WorkflowExecution` row under its `FOR UPDATE` lock and discarded it; it now returns a `StartedActivity { activity_id, workflow_id, workflow_name }`, so the regular dispatch path gets the owning identity for free. The local path takes the same pair from the caller's already-loaded `prepared.execution`. Local activities report `is_local: true`, `task_id: None`, the owning workflow's `queue_name`, and a deadline drawn from `WorkerConfig::max_local_activity_start_to_close` (the same clamped `per_attempt_timeout` the inline `tokio::time::timeout` enforces), so an unset — or above-cap — `start_to_close` reports the cap (AC5). **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no replay-determinism impact** (AC6): activities are never replayed, so every field is plain already-resolved dispatch state and no value crosses the event log. New `#[must_use]` builders (`with_execution_id`, `with_workflow_id`, `with_workflow_type`, `with_activity_type`, `with_activity_id`, `with_queue_name`, `with_task_id`, `with_deadline`) make each field settable on a test-constructed context (AC7), joined by two testing-gated constructors: `ActivityContext::new_test_with_heartbeat(tx)` (exercise the checkpoint pattern without a worker or database) and `new_test_with_identity(identity)`. `ActivityIdentity` and `ActivityExecutionInfo` are re-exported from `lib.rs` and the prelude. **Refactor:** the metrics/WASM-anchor `let started_at = Instant::now()` in `process_activity_task` was renamed `attempt_clock_start` — that name belongs to `task.started_at`, the wall-clock `TIMESTAMPTZ` both the start-to-close scanner and `deadline()` are anchored to, and conflating the two would silently disagree with the mechanism that kills the attempt. Docs: "Activity run metadata and deadline" in CLAUDE.md (with two new rows on the local-vs-regular decision matrix and a cross-reference from the #698 section); example `autumn-harvest/examples/activity_ctx_info.rs` (operator correlation + deadline-aware checkpointing, 5 embedded tests). Tests, TDD red→green→refactor: 13 pure unit tests for the extracted helpers `attempt_deadline` / `time_remaining_from` / `should_checkpoint` (incl. the min-of-two-clocks rule in both directions, the "never fall back to `scheduled_at`" trap, overflow → `None`, saturate-at-zero, and the `Option`-ordering trap made explicit); 11 pure unit tests for the accessor surface; 6 DB/worker integration tests in `tests/integration/activity_info_tests.rs` — AC1+AC3 (every field describes the real run, `execution_id` round-trips and selects the seeded row, `task_id` addresses the real queue row), AC2 (the reported deadline is exactly `started_at + start_to_close` read off the row the scanner reads, *and* the real `find_timed_out_tasks` reclaims a probe row positioned just past that arithmetic while sparing one just short of it), min-of-two-clocks, AC4 (identity byte-identical across a real worker-driven retry while attempt and deadline advance), AC5 (local `is_local`/`task_id: None`/cap-derived deadline/above-cap clamp), and the success metric (12 items across a forced retry, ledger asserts every item ran **exactly once**, with a negative control proving an unguarded activity is killed by the start-to-close scanner and its work discarded). Both worker-threading mutants (deadline → `None`, identity → synthetic) were verified to fail the suite. **Post-review hardening (four review agents: correctness/threading, API design/semver, test quality/falsifiability, replay safety/invariants — no P1 correctness or replay defect found; every finding below addressed):** (1) **`with_heartbeat_details` doc was false and the example was red** — the builder seeds the resume snapshot and the auto-heartbeat re-send cell but does not attach a flusher, so `heartbeat_details()` still rejects on a bare `new_test()` context. Corrected the doc (rather than clearing `heartbeat_unsupported_reason`, which would make `ctx.heartbeat(..)` silently `Ok(())` into a dropped payload — a worse footgun) and switched the example's attempt-2 context to `new_test_with_heartbeat`, matching a real retry; pinned by a new unit test asserting both directions. (2) **AC5's cap assertion was one-sided and passed a mutant** that ignored the cap entirely (`deadline >= before` is vacuous); replaced with a two-sided `before + cap ..= after + cap` sandwich on both the unset and above-cap halves — **verified to fail** a hardcoded-1s-deadline worker mutant. (3) **AC2's "`None` when unbounded" was only covered by the pure helper**; TEST A now dispatches a second, genuinely unbounded activity and asserts `deadline() == None` through the real worker — **verified to fail** a `.or(Some(now + 1h))` mutant. (4) **`queue_name` was unfalsifiable** (workflow queue, activity queue and asserted value were all `"default"`); the worker now polls a second queue and the sibling activity is dispatched on it, so a hardcoded `"default"` fails. (5) **The negative control asserted the wrong thing** — the start-to-close scanner reclaims the task *row* while the in-flight future keeps running in memory, so the control's in-process ledger legitimately shows every item; the "work was discarded" claim is now asserted on the durable record (no `ActivityCompleted` ever appended) plus a non-empty ledger, and the misleading comment corrected. (6) **The heartbeat clock is a third `RUNNING`-matching scanner predicate** not folded into `deadline()`; documented on the public accessor (not only on the `pub(crate)` helper) with the reasoning — it is dynamic, and freezing the worst case would make a correctly-heartbeating activity with a short `heartbeat_timeout` believe it is permanently out of budget and yield on every attempt — plus the practical rule (`heartbeat_timeout < start_to_close` must actually heartbeat) and a corrected doc example that no longer demonstrates the trap. (7) **The claimed local-activity over-report was refuted, and the real residual documented**: the enclosing workflow-task budget is `max(workflow_task_timeout, max_local_activity_start_to_close)`, so on stock defaults it is 60s, not 10s — extracted as the pure `worker::effective_workflow_task_timeout` and pinned by a unit test, since the `max` is load-bearing for this feature; the genuine residual (cycle time consumed *before* a local attempt is charged to the enclosing budget, not to the reported deadline) is documented on `deadline()` and the over-claiming inline comment corrected. (8) `ActivityIdentity::for_test()` gated behind `testing`, matching its only consumer. (9) `ActivityContext::identity()` added — the docs recommend asserting on `identity()`, and `ctx.info().identity()` cloned the shared strings twice. (10) `ActivityContext::new_test_local()` added: `is_local` is constructor-set, so downstream code previously had no way to unit-test an activity that branches on it. (11) The local path's `owner: (&str, &str)` tuple replaced with a named `OwningRun` struct — two adjacent same-typed `&str`s where a transposition type-checks silently and would mislabel every local activity's owning run. (12) Two gratuitous `String` clones dropped from the regular dispatch path. (13) `with_task_id` gained a debug-assert against the `is_local` + `Some(task_id)` state the worker never produces. (14) Documented divergences from the workflow-side `ctx.info()` sibling (nominal-vs-enforced deadline, `chrono::Duration` negative vs saturating `std::time::Duration`, and how to recover overrun magnitude), reciprocally on both sides; plus the claim-time-snapshot/pause-shift caveat, the Postgres-vs-host clock-domain note, `queue_name`'s empty-in-bare-test-contexts case, `task_id`'s `None` ⇏ local biconditional, the raw-`uuid::Uuid` rationale, and `ActivityIdentity`'s `Hash`/`new()`-is-the-downstream-path notes. (15) Test hygiene: TEST C's vacuous `Utc::now()`-relative sanity assertion replaced with a comparison against the actual un-shortened clock; AC4 extended to pin `task_id`/`queue_name`/`is_local` across a real retry; `identity()`'s projection pinned field-by-field; `checkpoint_start` now fails loudly instead of silently resuming from 0; the `FLUSH_WAIT`/`RESERVE` margins re-derived and widened; the TEST B module doc corrected to describe what part 2 actually drives; and the probe rows' orphan `PENDING` workflow tasks retired so a shared `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` database cannot leak them into a later suite. **AC3 gap closed:** the core-crate suite could only prove the reported id round-trips through `FromStr` and selects the right `harvest_workflow_executions` row — the management-API route lives in `autumn-harvest-plugin`, so AC3's literal "`GET /api/harvest/workflows/{id}` → 200" clause was unproven. New plugin suite `autumn-harvest-plugin/tests/activity_info_api_integration.rs` closes it end-to-end and self-reporting: the activity itself returns `ctx.info().execution_id.to_string()` as its output, a real worker drives the run to `COMPLETED`, and that *activity-observed* string — never a value the test knew up front — is spliced straight into the request URI against the real `harvest_api_router`, asserting `200` plus `body["execution"]["id"] == reported`, with a fresh-id `404` control proving the `200` is attributable to that id. Dual-mode DB (`HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` or testcontainers) and registered in `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt`; verified to fail a mutant activity that reports a different id. **Post-review hardening, round 2 (Codex on PR #1154, two findings, both real and both fixed):** (P1) **the local-activity deadline is now clamped to the enclosing workflow-task budget.** The earlier pass documented this as an accepted residual — "cycle time spent BEFORE this attempt is charged to the enclosing budget and not to us" — but it is the destructive direction and reachable on stock defaults: the enclosing `effective_workflow_task_timeout` (issue #494) starts at the top of the decision cycle, and with `max(10s, 60s) == 60s` against a 60s local cap even a *first* attempt drifts, while a second attempt can claim nearly a full budget moments before the outer timeout cancels it — precisely defeating the deadline-aware checkpointing this feature exists to enable. The dispatch that arms that timeout now captures its absolute cut-off and threads it (`process_task` → `process_workflow_task` → `run_local_activity_inline`, one new `Option<DateTime<Utc>>` param on each; `None` on the untimed arm), and the new pure `worker::local_attempt_deadline` reports the **minimum** of the two clocks — the same min-of-two-clocks rule the regular path already applied to `schedule_to_close`. Pinned by `local_attempt_deadline_clamps_to_the_enclosing_workflow_task_budget` (the 30s-into-a-60s-cycle case, the equal-budgets first-attempt drift, a genuinely shorter per-attempt budget still winning, the timeout-disabled path, and both overflow arms) — **verified to fail** an unclamped mutant. AC5's DB test is undisturbed (its 7s local cap under a 30s task timeout never makes the enclosing clock the earlier one), and the `deadline()` / `effective_workflow_task_timeout` docs that described the residual were corrected. (P2) **`with_activity_id` re-derives the idempotency key.** `new_test` deliberately mints both from one id so `info().activity_id` and `idempotency_key()` cannot disagree, but the builder moved only the identity — handing tests a context production dispatch never produces, in which an activity keying an external call off `idempotency_key()` looks correct in a test and collides in production. The builder now re-derives the key from the new id **when one is attached**, and never manufactures one on a keyless context (so `new_local_activity`'s documented `Config` error is preserved); an explicit `with_idempotency_key` *after* the id remains the escape hatch. Three unit tests pin all three behaviours. Also fixed in this round: a `clippy::duration_suboptimal_units` failure on `Duration::from_millis(2_000)` (CI runs clippy 1.97, which carries a lint the local 1.94 toolchain does not).
- **Tooling** — Task-claim / enqueue throughput benchmark and CI-gated performance contract — see issue #786. Harvest published a CPU-path budget for replay (10k events < 200 ms, #135) but **nothing at all** for `queue::claim_task`, the single most scalability-critical query in the engine and the one that has accreted roughly a `WHERE` predicate per phase since 3.7 (build-id routing #171, per-key concurrency #247, rate-limit gate #332/#699, circuit-breaker tracked set #369, `schedule_to_close` #378, PAUSED skip #383, worker sessions #606, queue pauses #619, capability labels #382, sticky routing #235). Each was added for correctness; none was measured. **Zero engine impact (AC6): no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no schema change, no public API change, and the claim query is byte-for-byte unchanged** — `git diff --name-only 301c70a..HEAD | grep -E "^autumn-harvest/src/|migrations/"` is empty. This slice measures; tuning is separate work, and tuning without a published baseline is how you get an unfalsifiable "optimisation". **Three artifacts sharing one harness.** `autumn-harvest/tests/integration/claim_bench_support.rs` is the harness; `benches/claim_bench.rs` is the exploratory report; `tests/integration/claim_budget_tests.rs` is the CI gate. The bench reaches across to the harness via `#[path = "../tests/integration/claim_bench_support.rs"]` rather than duplicating it, so the **published numbers and the gated number can never be produced by different code**. **Why not criterion:** `claim_task` is destructive (`PENDING → RUNNING`), so criterion's repeat-the-closure model would drain the seeded backlog and end up timing "claim against an empty queue" — the opposite of the thing under test. Hence `[[bench]] harness = false` with its own `main()`, seeding a backlog of N and performing a bounded number of claims (never more than `N/5`, `measured_claims_for`). **Headline measured findings** (published in the new `docs/performance.md`, framed explicitly as starter reference numbers, not an SLO; all tables from one run on an idle 4-core reference box against Postgres 16): (1) **claim latency scales superlinearly with pending-backlog depth** — 1k → 10k rows costs ~19x latency (10.44 ms → 200.03 ms p50), 10k → 100k a further ~15x (→ 2 919.99 ms), so a queue parked at 100k pending rows collapses fleet throughput to ~3 claims/s regardless of worker count while the *write* side still sustains ~4 600 enqueues/s — **a queue that deep does not drain**; (2) **the cause is structural** — the claim query's `ORDER BY` leads with a non-indexable `CASE` on `sticky_worker_id`/`sticky_until` (#235), so `idx_harvest_tq_poll` cannot serve the ordering and Postgres `Seq Scan`s + `Sort`s all 10 000 eligible rows to satisfy a `Limit 1` on every claim (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` is printed by the bench and excerpted in the doc), with the `harvest_queue_pauses` anti-join (#619) contributing `loops=10000` — 20 000 of 20 223 buffer hits; (3) **per-gate attribution (AC2)**, read off the published table rather than quoted from an earlier run: rate-limit gate +2%, circuit-breaker tracked set +4%, build-id routing +13%, **per-key concurrency +644%**, and all gates together +1797% — the first two are reported as “free” rather than as an ordering, because they have swapped rank with each other between runs; (4) **enqueue is not the problem (AC3)** — ~4 800 rows/s at p50 ~1.5 ms, flat from 1k to 100k backlog (inside run-to-run noise; the *middle* depth measured fastest, which is the tell that the spread is noise rather than depth). **An equal-depth control corrected a published conclusion.** An earlier revision compared the `paused_rows` scenario against `baseline`, measured +1319%, and concluded the PAUSED-execution skip was the most expensive predicate on the claim path. It is not. `paused_rows` seeds its PAUSED ballast *in addition to* the claimable backlog, so it walks a table twice as deep — and claim latency is strongly superlinear in depth, so that delta charged the anti-join for the extra rows. The new `ClaimGate::DoubleBacklog` control seeds the same 20 000 total rows with **no PAUSED population at all** and costs **+1383%**, within a percent of what `paused_rows` costs (`ClaimGate::comparand()` reports `paused_rows` against it, not against baseline). So the operational finding is a *depth-controlled* one: at equal table depth a paused population costs what a live one does — **+1403%** vs baseline, roughly 15x — and the actionable conclusion is **drain the rows**. What that control does **not** establish is the cost of the anti-join predicate in isolation, and this changelog does not claim it: `double_backlog` matches on *total* rows but not on the population that reaches the sort, which is where the claim query spends its time. The anti-join is a `WHERE` predicate, so it is evaluated before the `ORDER BY` — the control feeds 20 000 rows to the sort while `paused_rows` feeds 10 000, and in the control the PAUSED `SubPlan` shows `never executed` (every seeded row is `task_type = 'activity'`, short-circuited by the type test). The residual **+1%** is therefore the probe cost minus the sort saving from ten thousand fewer sorted rows — two effects of opposite sign this measurement cannot separate, which is also why its *sign* flips between runs. `docs/performance.md` carries the full plan comparison and states what a properly matched control would need. **Round 28 retracted the companion claim that used to sit here**, which said the `all_gates` row was the surviving bound on combined predicate cost (+28% against an equal-depth comparand). `all_gates` seeds the PAUSED ballast too, so it carries the identical confound in the identical direction: it *scans* 20 000 rows like `double_backlog` but *sorts* only 10 000, so that comparison charges the row for every predicate while crediting it with half the sort work. **+28% therefore bounds nothing in either direction** — deriving a direction for it would mean adding the unmeasured 10 000-row sort saving back to the difference, which assumes the difference decomposes into predicate cost plus sort cost. It does not: the scenarios also filter to different post-filter populations and can reach different plans, so there is neither a measured term to add back nor an established direction for the bias. What *is* population-matched is the top of the table: `rate_limited`, `circuit_breaker_set`, `build_policy` and `concurrency_key` all seed exactly the 10 000 claimable rows `baseline` does, and they do not support a “predicates are a rounding error” reading either — `concurrency_key` costs **+644%** on an identical population. The defensible statement is narrower than the one this entry used to make: *depth* is the dominant cost (~15x from 10k to 20k rows), *one* predicate is separately expensive at this depth (`concurrency_key`, ~7.4x), and the combined cost of all of them is not something these scenarios can bound in either direction. `the_paused_rows_control_seeds_equal_total_depth` pins the control's equal-depth property and was verified RED by mutation; `the_paused_rows_delta_is_not_attributed_to_the_predicate` pins the narrowed reading. **The CI gate (AC5)** runs the headline scenario (10 000 pending / 8 claimers / 4 queues) via a new `linux` row in `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt` and fails the build when **p50** exceeds **1 500 ms** (~6.4–7.5x the quiet-box reference, which spans **200–234 ms** across runs, and ~2.9x the worst loaded observation at ~516 ms). **It asserts p50 rather than p99, from measurement, not preference:** the scenario deliberately oversubscribes the box (8 claimers on 4 cores), and an oversubscribed *tail* measures the run queue rather than the claim path — across repeated reference runs p50 moved ~2.3x between an idle and a loaded box while p99 moved ~15x (~300 ms → ~4 665 ms), and a p99 gate at this budget failed **2 runs in 6** during review on the same hardware class that produced the published numbers. p99 is still measured, still published, and printed in the failure message, so a genuine tail regression stays visible; it is simply not the assertion. The budget is documented as a **cliff detector, not a drift detector** — it cannot catch a 50%-slower predicate when the reference statistic itself moves 2.3x with machine load, but the two measured predicates that *do* add a per-row subplan to the full scan land at 6.9x and 14.6x, so 6.4x headroom sits below them and above the noise — and the doc says plainly that the number was derived on the reference machine, that the first Linux CI runs are the real calibration, and that the fix for flake there is to re-derive from CI observations rather than widen by guesswork. Overridable with `HARVEST_CLAIM_BUDGET_MS` (deliberately *not* named for a statistic, so the name cannot become a lie). **Four** soundness assertions fail *loudly* rather than reporting a meaningless percentile — ≥100 samples collected, **the run was not truncated by the wall-clock ceiling**, ≥90% of operations actually claimed a task, and the backlog was not drained below 80% (enforced two ways: the planned operation count is capped at `backlog / 5`, and `claims_for_claimer` splits it exactly rather than rounding up, so the claimers between them can never exceed the plan). The truncation assertion earned its place immediately: it fired on the first real run and exposed that the 60 s wall-clock ceiling was *smaller* than a run at the 1 500 ms latency budget would need (`(800/8) × 1.5 s = 150 s`), so truncation would have fired before the latency verdict ever rendered; the default is now 240 s and `wall_clock_budget_admits_a_run_at_the_latency_budget` holds the two constants to a coherent pair. Locally (no Docker, no `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL`) the gate skips with a notice; **under `CI` it fails instead**, because a performance gate that silently no-ops when its dependency is missing is not a gate. A companion test proves the gate is falsifiable *against real measured data* (a budget below the observed p50 must trip it), `each_gate_scenario_actually_seeds_its_trigger_column` censuses the seeded rows so the published cost table cannot silently start lying (verified RED by mutating the build-id seed expression to `NULL`), and `enqueue_throughput_is_measured_against_a_non_empty_queue` now asserts the post-run `PENDING` count equals `backlog + rows` so the harness cannot quietly stop seeding and still pass while measuring the easy case. **Measurement hygiene** (each of these is a defect that was found and fixed during the work, not a precaution): percentiles are **nearest-rank** so a reported p99 is a claim someone actually waited for; **a tenth of each claimer's observations is discarded as warmup, applied post-hoc rather than by planned index** — an earlier revision discarded a flat 3 per claimer and the headline p99 read ~2 900 ms instead of ~300 ms, i.e. the metric had silently become a cold-start measurement, while applying the fraction after collection also stops a wall-clock-truncated scenario from discarding every sample it took; **zero samples render as `n/a`, never `0.00`**, so a scenario that measured nothing cannot publish a number that looks instantaneous, a truncated scenario is marked `⚠` with its sample count shown, and a scenario below the gate's own 100-sample floor is marked `‡` and flagged directional-only; `ANALYZE` runs after every set-based seed; the pool is always sized above the claimer count so no measurement includes pool-checkout queueing; and `explain_claim` asserts its bind count before substituting literals, so the printed plan cannot silently drift from the real query. The report's per-gate table is **streamed row by row** rather than buffered (a full sweep takes tens of minutes), which is sound only because every comparand is measured before its dependent — pinned by `every_gate_is_ordered_after_its_comparand`. The doc is candid about what reproduces: across three independent runs only `build_policy` (+15%, +13%, +15%) and `paused_rows` vs `baseline` (+1319%, +1346%, +1321%) repeat to the point; `rate_limited` and `circuit_breaker_set` have *swapped rank with each other* between runs, so they are reported as "free" rather than as an ordering; and `concurrency_key` (+306%, +283%, +590%) grows as a run progresses, consistent with its `COUNT(*)` subquery counting a `RUNNING` population the benchmark itself is growing. `all_gates` is explicitly **not** a strict upper bound — its circuit-breaker tracked set short-circuits the rate-limit `EXISTS` and the debit CTE via `= ANY($5)`, so a deployment with rate limiting and no breaker executes strictly more work. **AC7 — platform safety:** the bench is `required-features = ["db"]`, and with neither Docker nor `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` it prints a skip notice and exits 0, so `cargo bench` on a laptop without Docker is not a failure and `--no-default-features` / Windows builds are untouched. When `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` **is** set it is treated as an **admin** URL: a freshly-named database is created and migrated per run (so a 100k-row backlog can never leak into a shared database), and stale databases from earlier runs are swept at *setup* — which also reclaims databases orphaned by a run that panicked, something a teardown hook could never do — skipping any whose database still has a backend attached, so concurrent runs cannot delete each other's working set (liveness is read from the server via `pg_stat_activity`, the one authority that sees every client regardless of host or PID namespace; the sweep, `CREATE DATABASE` and the lease are serialised under one advisory lock so a database in its create-to-lease window is not visible to a peer's sweep). `ci_run_coverage.rs` gained a principled `is_db_harness_only` rule so the shared harness module is classified as a harness rather than an uncovered suite, plus three tests pinning that classification; the rule bites the moment that file gains a `#[tokio::test]` or `block_on`. Also verified: profile is not a variable (debug p50 228–256 ms vs release 242–256 ms at the headline scenario — the work is server-side), so gate and bench numbers are directly comparable. Documented known limitations include the degenerate sort-key distribution of the seeded backlog, that queue count is a parameter held at 4 rather than swept, and that four claim-path predicates (capability labels #382, `schedule_to_close` #378, worker sessions #606, sticky routing #235) are present in the query but held constant. Docs cross-linked from `README.md`, `docs/getting-started/README.md` and `docs/sharding.md` (the backlog-depth table is a sharding trigger). **Post-review hardening (PR #1156, Codex bot — four findings, all valid, all fixed, all confined to the harness so AC6 still holds):** (1) **Credential leak into CI logs.** The admin-connect failure path interpolated the whole `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` into its `SkipReason`, which both the bench and the gate print — so a transient connection blip published a password to anyone with read access to the log. New pure `redact_url` replaces the `user:password@` segment while keeping host/port/database so the message stays diagnostic. Probing `diesel`/`tokio-postgres` with a password-bearing URL across connection-refused, DNS-failure and malformed-string cases showed they report only `"error connecting to server"` / `"invalid connection string"` and never echo the URL, so redacting our own interpolation closes the exposure rather than merely narrowing it — confirmed live, the real skip path now prints `connect postgres://***@localhost:5432/postgres`. (2) **`with_db_name` corrupted URLs carrying options.** Splicing at `rfind('/')` silently dropped `?sslmode=require` (making a TLS-requiring server unreachable through the advertised existing-server mode) and, when a parameter value contained a slash, spliced *inside the query*. Rewritten to replace only the path component and carry query/fragment through; RED-verified against the old body, where the three new tests fail with `postgres://h:5432/postgres?sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/bench_1` (database name spliced into the certificate path) and — worse than reported — `postgres://host` collapsing to `postgres://b`, losing the host entirely. Both functions were moved to the **pure** section so they are covered on every OS including the `--no-default-features` leg. (3) **Stale-database sweep could kill a live run on another host.** `process_is_alive` consults the local `/proc`, so when several machines share one admin URL a run elsewhere looks dead and `DROP DATABASE ... WITH (FORCE)` terminates it mid-measurement. Fixed by asking the one party that can see every client — the server — via `pg_stat_activity`; a database with any backend attached is never reclaimed. Deliberately *not* the suggested host/run marker in the name: a marker answers "is it mine", while the actual question is "is it in use", and only the server can answer that. The local pid check was kept **at this point** as a cheap same-host path, and both checks failed toward "in use", so the worst outcome remained a leaked database. (Superseded in round 5 below, which removed the pid veto outright: in a container the recorded pid is usually 1 and pid 1 is always alive, so the veto skipped every stale database a previous container run had left behind. The server check is now the sole liveness authority.) (4) **The wall-clock ceiling was not enforced during a claim.** The deadline was tested only between calls, and `claim_task` is an unbounded await, so one stalled claim would overrun the advertised 240 s cap indefinitely — precisely the stall the cap exists to bound. Each call is now wrapped in a timeout derived from the remaining budget; expiry marks the run truncated, which the gate already treats as measurement-unsound. Abandoning a connection mid-query can leave it unusable, which is fine and terminal here: the claimer breaks immediately, the pool recycles it, and the run is being discarded anyway. **Post-review hardening, round 2 (PR #1156, Codex bot — two further findings against the round-1 commit, both verified against the source before being accepted, both fixed, both still confined to the harness so AC6 holds unchanged):** (1) **P1 — the round-1 `pg_stat_activity` check left a connectionless window it then read as "abandoned".** Round 1 made the stale-database sweep ask the server "does anything hold a backend against this database?" so a run on another host could not be mistaken for dead. But a live run holds no backend of its own between scenarios: each scenario opens a connection, seeds, drops it, builds a pool, and drops that too — and `setup_bench_db` itself dropped its migration connection before returning. A concurrent run on another host therefore saw zero backends for a perfectly live database and could still `DROP DATABASE ... WITH (FORCE)` a working set out from under it — round 1 narrowed the race without closing it. Fixed by retaining the migration connection as an ownership lease on `BenchDb` for the full lifetime of the database (an idle backend still appears in `pg_stat_activity`, so ownership is continuously visible), rather than by adding a host/run marker to the database name — a marker answers "is it mine", while the question gating the DROP is "is it in use", and the lease makes the server's own answer correct at every instant rather than only while a scenario happens to be running. `None` on the testcontainer path: that server is private to the process, so there is nobody to defend against. Verified red→green against a real Postgres 16 with a permanent regression test, `an_idle_bench_database_still_holds_a_visible_lease`: without the lease an idle bench database reports **0** backends (the test fails with "the sweep would treat a live run as abandoned and drop it"); with it, **1**. The test also asserts the lease *ends* on `BenchDb` drop — an ownership marker that outlived its run would defeat the sweep permanently, so it polls until the count returns to 0 rather than assuming it. Scoped to the existing-server mode, which is the only mode where a foreign client can reach the database at all. (2) **P2 — the scenario deadline was created *after* an unbounded pool checkout.** Round 1 bounded each `claim_task` call, but each claimer still computed its own deadline as `Instant::now() + budget` *after* `pool.get().await` returned — so a stalled or exhausted pool parked every claimer indefinitely with no deadline yet in existence, and the advertised ceiling was again a fiction (a different await, the same class of hole). Fixed by establishing **one scenario-wide deadline before any claimer is spawned** (`started + budget`, which also means the cap now bounds the scenario rather than each claimer separately) and bounding the checkout with its remaining duration; a claimer that cannot check out takes no samples and reports truncated, so the gate calls the measurement unsound instead of publishing a percentile from whichever claimers did start. Because `truncated` is only set where the harness *checks* the deadline — and so can never catch an await that never returns to a check — the gate now also asserts the scenario's measured wall clock directly against the ceiling (+30 s slack for task join under an oversubscribed runner), which is the assertion that would actually fail if some future await escaped the deadline again. Re-verified end to end against a real Postgres 16: all 8 gate tests green, headline p50 **215.66 ms** against the 1 500 ms budget (runs 8–11 measured 276.11 / 204.04 / 211.80 / 215.66 ms, while p99 over the same runs swung 3 316.97 / 2 707.88 / 592.61 / 556.88 ms — reconfirming, for the fourth time, why the gate asserts p50 and merely publishes p99); plus fmt, `clippy --all-features --tests --benches -D warnings`, the same clippy under `--no-default-features --features testing`, `cargo check --no-default-features` (AC7), the 1 103-test no-DB integration suite, and the Linux bench compile-check. The engine diff against the merge-base remains empty across `autumn-harvest/src`, `migrations`, `autumn-harvest-macros/src` and `autumn-harvest-plugin/src` (AC6). **CI calibration (AC5, first Docker-backed Linux run):** the gate ran for the first time on a real GitHub Actions `ubuntu-latest` runner against Docker-backed Postgres 16 on 2026-08-10 and **all seven gate tests passed** in 108 s, the headline scenario taking ~78 s of that — inside both the 1 500 ms p50 budget and the 240 s per-scenario ceiling. The budget derived on the reference machine therefore holds on CI hardware **as published**; it has not been widened to accommodate the runner, which was the open risk when it was first committed. `docs/performance.md` records the observation and also now states honestly that the measured stat line is printed only on failure (the manifest runner passes no `--nocapture`, and libtest shows captured output for failing tests only), so CI logs carry no trend data between failures — run the benchmark for that. **Post-review hardening, round 3 (PR #1156, Codex bot — three findings against the round-2 commit, all verified in source first, all fixed, all still harness-only):** (1) **P2 — a definitely-live pid was allowed to VETO the sweep, so on non-Linux hosts nothing was ever reclaimed.** `process_is_alive` returns a conservative `true` off Linux, and it was consulted with `||` *before* the server check — so on macOS and Windows every parseable candidate short-circuited to `continue` and `database_has_connections` was never reached, leaking every completed benchmark's migrated (up to 100k-row) database forever. Round 2 had introduced the server check but left it unreachable on two of three platforms. Fixed by inverting the authority: the **server-visible lease decides**, and a pid may only ever *protect*, never veto — a definitely-live local pid still covers another local run's create-to-lease window (which the server genuinely cannot see yet), while an unanswerable check now falls through to the server instead of being read as "in use". Because the bug is precisely platform-conditional, the decision was extracted into the pure `sweep_step(owner_token, my_token, owner_pid, same_host_pid_alive) -> SweepStep::{Skip, AskServer}` — the `Option<bool>` liveness argument makes `None` ("cannot answer") a distinct, unit-testable state from `Some(false)`, so **both** platform behaviours are pinned on every OS, including the `--no-default-features` leg. Verified end to end against a real Postgres 16: 8 stale databases present (7 from an earlier process plus one hand-seeded with a foreign token and a dead pid), 1 remaining after a run — the sweep reclaimed all 8. (2) **P2 — database names were not unique across hosts.** `harvest_claim_bench_{pid}_{seq}` collides outright when two containerised runs share an admin URL, since PID 1 is the norm: both mint `harvest_claim_bench_1_0` and race at `CREATE DATABASE`, failing one valid benchmark, and a leftover from a dead host re-collides later. Names now carry a per-run token (`harvest_claim_bench_{pid}_{run_token}_{seq}`) derived std-only from `RandomState`'s per-process OS-entropy seed mixed with the clock and pid — no RNG crate is pulled in for a name suffix. The token does double duty: the sweep's self-exemption keys on it rather than the pid, which fixes the *other* direction of the same bug (a pid-keyed exemption would have made one pid-1 run treat a foreign pid-1 run's live database as its own). (3) **P2 — the round-2 lease test reintroduced the last-slash parsing bug in its own body.** It read the database name back with `rsplit('/')`, exactly the parse `with_db_name` had just been rewritten to avoid: against `?sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/root.crt` the last slash sits inside the query, so the name comes back as `root.crt`, the `pg_stat_activity` count returns zero, and the test fails against a perfectly healthy lease. Fixed by adding the proper inverse `db_name_from_url` beside `with_db_name` in the pure section (so it is covered on every OS) and using it; RED confirmed directly — the naive parse yields `"root.crt"`. Round-3 verification: 30 pure harness tests (up from 22 — 5 for `sweep_step`, 3 for `db_name_from_url` including a round-trip against `with_db_name`), 1 111 no-DB integration tests, 8/8 DB gate tests on Postgres 16, fmt, clippy `-D warnings` under `--all-features --tests --benches` and `--no-default-features --features testing`, `cargo check --no-default-features` (AC7), and the Linux bench compile-check. Engine diff against the merge-base still empty (AC6). **Post-review hardening, round 4 (two more Codex P2s on `2118d0e`):** (F) **the create-to-lease window was still a hole.** Round 2's lease defends a database once it has a backend in `pg_stat_activity`, but it cannot have one until it exists — so between `CREATE DATABASE` and the lease connection a foreign sweep sees a real database with zero connections and correctly concludes it is abandoned. No naming scheme closes that; the two operations have to be made mutually exclusive. Fixed with a cluster-wide advisory lock (`SWEEP_LOCK_KEY`, taken on the admin connection) held across sweep + create + lease and released before the migration — the slow part, where holding it would serialize concurrent runs for no benefit. Postgres advisory locks are per-cluster rather than per-database, so the lock is visible to exactly the set of clients that could sweep us, including ones on other hosts, which is the case that motivated it. Every `?` between lock and release drops the admin connection, ending the session and releasing the lock, so an early return cannot strand it; a 60 s `lock_timeout` turns a wedged peer into a diagnosable failure rather than an unbounded hang (and incidentally bounds the sweep's own `DROP`s, whose errors were already ignored). Verified RED→GREEN on Postgres 16 by the new `setup_waits_for_a_peers_sweep_before_creating_its_database`, which holds the lock externally and asserts setup blocks, then releases and asserts it completes: with the `take_sweep_lock` call removed, setup finishes inside the 1.5 s window and the test fails. (G) **`claims/s` understated throughput by the warmup fraction.** `claimed` was populated after `.skip(warmup)` while `wall_secs` runs from the first warmup call, so the numerator and denominator covered different windows — about 10% low, and inconsistent with the enqueue path, which documents dividing *all* rows by the *whole* clock deliberately. Fixed by tracking `total_claimed` (every success, warmup included) for throughput while `claimed`/`empty` stay trimmed for latency and `claim_ratio`. The split moved into a named `ClaimerOutcome::from_observed` in the **pure** section: three of its fields are `usize` over two different windows, so a positional tuple made transposing them a silent regression, and putting it beside `warmup_claims_for` means the window contract is unit-tested on every OS including the `--no-default-features` leg. RED confirmed by restoring the trimmed numerator — both new window tests fail. The `claims/s` column in `docs/performance.md` is re-measured from a fresh benchmark run accordingly; the latency columns are unaffected by construction, since only the throughput numerator changed. **Post-review hardening, round 5 (one Codex P2 on `615d1ba`):** (H) **the pid liveness veto outlived its justification, and leaked every stale database in a container.** Round 3 gave `sweep_step` a third guard — a definitely-live same-host pid short-circuits to `Skip` before the server is consulted — on the reasoning that it protected another *local* run inside its create-to-lease window, which the server genuinely could not see yet. Round 4's advisory lock closed exactly that window, so the guard now protects nothing: the sweep and every create-to-lease window are mutually exclusive, so a sweep can no longer observe one. Meanwhile the guard's cost is severe in the deployment the harness is written for — a containerised run records pid 1, pid 1 is alive on every host, so `process_is_alive` returns `true` for every stale database a previous container run left behind and the server check is never reached. Each run therefore leaks another migrated, potentially 100k-row database that no later run ever reclaims. Fixed by deleting the veto (and `process_is_alive` with it): `sweep_step` keeps exactly two `Skip` cases — the run-token self-exemption, and a name this harness did not mint — and defers everything else to the server-visible lease, the one authority that sees every client regardless of host or PID namespace. This retires the `Option<bool>` tri-state introduced in round 3 to distinguish "answered: dead" from "this platform cannot answer"; with no veto there is nothing for either answer to gate, and the platform-conditional `#[cfg(target_os = ...)]` branch at the call site goes with it. The pure tests that pinned the veto are inverted rather than deleted, so the new contract is the one under test: `sweep_step_never_vetoes_on_a_live_local_pid` asserts `AskServer` for both pid 1 and this process's own live pid — the two pids most likely to be recorded and most certain to be alive. Re-measuring for (G) also sharpened the published budget rationale: the fresh run's headline p50 came in at 208 ms against the previously published 234 ms, which widens the quiet-box reference to 200-234 ms and therefore the budget from a flat ~6.4x to 6.4-7.5x that reference. That range straddles the ~6.9x `concurrency_key`-class regression the gate was described as catching, so `docs/performance.md` now states the limit explicitly rather than leaving the old flat multiple to imply more than it covers: a ~14.6x depth-class regression trips at every observed reference, while a ~6.9x single-subplan-class one trips on a loaded box and at the slow end of the quiet range but can slip through on the fastest quiet runs.
