It is an inherent limit (the reference itself moves 2.3x with load, so no single threshold separates 6.9x from noise on this hardware) and a mild one in practice, since the gate runs in CI and CI is the loaded case, where even the smaller cliff clears the budget by more than 2x. The per-gate attribution table is deliberately *not* republished from the fresh run: it carries no `claims/s` column, so (G) cannot move it, and the page already reports that table as one representative run alongside the spread across runs -- the fourth run's every row fell inside the ranges already quoted, which is the property that matters, so it was folded into that spread instead of swapping one run's numbers for another's. **Post-review hardening, round 6 (one Codex P2 on `10298ba`):** (I) **the run-token self-exemption stopped a process reclaiming its own finished databases.** With the pid veto gone, `sweep_step` still short-circuited on `owner_token == my_token`, and `run_token()` is constant for the life of a process -- so a process that calls `setup_bench_db` more than once could never clean up after itself, leaving one migrated (up to 100k-row) database behind per call until some *other* process happened to sweep. That is the normal shape of both consumers: the gate suite calls setup once per test and the benchmark calls it a dozen times. The exemption's stated purpose -- covering the database we are about to create, whose lease does not exist yet -- turned out to be vacuous: the sweep runs *before* `CREATE DATABASE`, so that database is not a candidate at all, and round 4's advisory lock already serialises the window in question. Meanwhile a prior database that is still in use holds its lease and is skipped by the server check regardless of who owns it. Fixed by removing the exemption and letting the lease decide for same-token candidates too, which also draws the line by *liveness* rather than by *ownership* -- the question that actually gates a `DROP`. `sweep_step` now has exactly one `Skip` case (a name this harness did not mint, checked as both a parseable pid and a token, since ours always carry both) and is `const`. The run token keeps its round-3 job in the database *name*, where it stops two pid-1 containerised runs colliding. Verified RED->GREEN on Postgres 16 by running the whole gate suite in one process: with the exemption restored it leaves **eight** databases behind (`..._0` through `..._7`), without it exactly **one** -- the newest, which has no successor sweep yet and is reclaimed by the next run. Pinned permanently by `a_later_setup_reclaims_this_processes_finished_databases`, which asserts both halves of why dropping the exemption is safe: a *held* prior database survives a later setup (its lease protects it) and a *dropped* one does not. Confirmed falsifiable -- restoring the exemption fails it with `harvest_claim_bench_7848_60454450ef749eae_0 survived a later setup in the same process`. **Post-review hardening, round 7 (three Codex P2s on `b26bd7a`): advisory-lock scoping, a stale doc paragraph, and a PostgreSQL-13-only `DROP`.** **(J) The round-4 sweep lock did not serialize anything across differing admin databases, and the rationale I published for it was factually wrong.** Round 4 closed the create-to-lease window by taking a `pg_advisory_lock` on the admin connection, on the stated grounds that "Postgres advisory locks are cluster-wide rather than per-database, so a lock taken on the admin connection is visible to exactly the set of clients that could sweep us, including ones on other hosts". **That claim is false and is retracted here.** Verified against a live server: with a session on `postgres` holding key `7860786.0786`, `pg_try_advisory_lock` on the *same* key from a session on `template1` returns `t` (acquired, no conflict), while a second attempt from `postgres` itself returns `f`. Advisory locks are scoped to the session's database. So the lock rode whichever database the operator happened to name in `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL`, and two runs reaching one cluster through different admin databases — the exact multi-host case round 4 was written for — never conflicted at all: each swept while the other sat in its unprotected create-to-lease window, so a foreign sweep could `DROP` a live run's database mid-measurement. Fixed by giving the lock its own connection to a **fixed** database (new `SWEEP_LOCK_DB`), so every client agrees on where it lives regardless of its admin URL: `take_sweep_lock` now takes `&str` (the admin URL) and returns the holding `AsyncPgConnection`, which `setup_bench_db` keeps until just before the migration and which any `?` drops — ending the session and releasing the lock, so an early return still cannot strand it. `SWEEP_LOCK_DB` is **`postgres`**, deliberately *not* `template1`: both are universal, but `template1` is the default template for `CREATE DATABASE`, so holding a connection to it would make our own create — the very operation the lock protects — fail with "source database is being accessed by other users". A server whose `postgres` database is unreachable falls back to the admin URL's own database with a `warning:` naming the reduced coordination scope, rather than skipping the run. **(K) `docs/performance.md` still described the sweep rule round 5 deleted.** Round 5 removed the pid-liveness veto from `sweep_step` and made the server the sole authority, but the "two more things worth knowing" bullet still told operators the sweep "skips any database whose owning pid is still alive" and that "a pid is only ever allowed to *protect* … never to veto" — a description of removed logic, on the page an operator reads before pointing a **destructive `DROP DATABASE`** at a server they care about. Rewritten to state what the code now does: the server is the sole liveness authority, a local pid is deliberately not consulted at all (and why — foreign hosts, non-Linux, and pid 1 under containers), and the one window the server cannot see is closed by the advisory lock, including where that lock lives and why. **(L) `DROP DATABASE ... WITH (FORCE)` is PostgreSQL 13+, but the engine supports 12+.** On PostgreSQL 12 the clause is a syntax error; the sweep ignores every failure by design (a leaked database must never fail a benchmark), so on a 12 server the sweep would silently reclaim **nothing** and 100k-row bench databases would accumulate forever — the precise failure the sweep exists to prevent, on a version the README (`Postgres 12+`) claims support for. Replaced with a version-neutral `pg_terminate_backend(...) WHERE datname = $1 AND pid <> pg_backend_pid()` followed by a plain `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS`. Equivalent in effect: the sweep only reaches that line for a database it has just observed to have zero connections, so the terminate is belt-and-braces against a backend arriving between the check and the drop — exactly what `WITH (FORCE)` was doing. Tests: the new `the_sweep_lock_is_taken_in_a_fixed_database_not_the_admin_url_s` proves J falsifiably and independently of how the suite is configured — a peer holds the lock in `SWEEP_LOCK_DB` while the lock is requested through an admin URL naming a *different* (scratch) database, and setup must block; with the pre-fix code restored it returns immediately and the test fails naming both databases. The pre-existing `setup_waits_for_a_peers_sweep_before_creating_its_database` was also corrected to hold the lock in `SWEEP_LOCK_DB` rather than the admin URL's database, where it would only have conflicted when the two happened to coincide. Both the probe's helper and its scratch database are structured so **no panic can occur between `CREATE DATABASE` and the matching `DROP`** — the scratch is named outside the swept `harvest_claim_bench_%` prefix so a concurrent sweep cannot delete it mid-probe, which also means nothing would ever reclaim it if a panic stranded it on a shared server; the probe therefore reports failures rather than `expect`ing them and every assertion runs after cleanup. (Caught the hard way: the first RED run panicked before its cleanup and left two permanently-orphaned probe databases behind.) L's terminate-then-drop is exercised by `a_later_setup_reclaims_this_processes_finished_databases`, which asserts a finished database is actually gone after a later setup; its version-neutrality is by inspection, since this box runs PostgreSQL 16. **Post-review hardening, round 8 (two Codex P2s on `299ac14`): the sweep-lock fallback and an unbounded write path.** **(M) The round-7 fallback silently reopened the race round 7 had just closed.** When the fixed `SWEEP_LOCK_DB` was unreachable, `take_sweep_lock` fell back to the admin URL's own database with a `warning:`, on the stated grounds that narrower coordination "is worse than nothing only if it is silent". That reasoning is wrong: a warning on a benchmark's stderr protects nobody's data, and the fallback takes a lock scoped to whichever database the operator named — which is precisely the per-database scoping the fixed database exists to escape. Two clients arriving through different admin databases would both enter the supposedly-serialized sweep/create section, and one could `DROP` the other's new database before its lease connects. Fixed by removing the fallback: an unreachable `SWEEP_LOCK_DB` is now terminal, with an error naming the missing grant (`connect postgres for the sweep lock: … Grant the role CONNECT on postgres, or point HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL at a cluster where it is reachable`). Better a run that does not start than a run that silently cannot serialize. The testcontainer path is unaffected — it returns before the lock is taken, since a private container has no foreign client to coordinate with. **(N) The write path had no wall-clock ceiling at all.** `run_enqueue_scenario` carried two unbounded awaits — the pool checkout and `queue::enqueue` itself — and, unlike the claim path (bounded two rounds earlier), never consulted `HARVEST_BENCH_SCENARIO_SECS` and had no `truncated` field. A stalled server would hang the benchmark *and* the CI gate that calls it until the outer workflow timeout, while `docs/performance.md` advertised a per-scenario cap. Fixed symmetrically with the claim path: one scenario-wide deadline fixed before any writer spawns (not inside the task, where a stalled checkout would restart the clock behind an unbounded await), both awaits bounded by its remaining duration, and a new `EnqueueReport::truncated` propagated to the gate — which now asserts it, and asserts the elapsed wall clock against the ceiling directly as the backstop for a *future* unbounded await that `truncated` could never catch. The bench's enqueue rows carry the same `⚠` truncation mark the claim rows already did, so a partial run cannot be transcribed into the published table as a steady-state number. The magic `+30s` slack, now needed by two gates, became the shared `WALL_CLOCK_SLACK`. Tests, both RED→GREEN on Postgres 16: for N, the new `enqueue_stops_at_the_scenario_wall_clock_ceiling` asks for far more rows than a 1 s budget can absorb, so the ceiling *must* bite — it completes in **1.62 s**, and with the deadline neutered the same test was **killed at 180 s** still writing, which is exactly the hang the finding describes. For M, a role deliberately revoked `CONNECT` on `postgres` makes setup refuse with the actionable message; with the fallback restored the identical role proceeds normally and the run completes unprotected — the silent-unsafe behaviour, reproduced. `docs/performance.md` gained both contracts: the no-fallback rule beside the lock's scoping rationale, and a new bullet stating that the ceiling now covers the write path too.

  **(O) The stale sweep validated two fields of a four-field name, so a database it never minted could be destroyed.** The sweep's candidate query is `LIKE 'harvest_claim_bench_%'`, and the shape check behind it required only that the first field parse as a number and that a second field exist. `harvest_claim_bench_123_production` satisfied both — it read as pid `123`, token `production` — so an idle database of the operator's own, sharing nothing but the name prefix, reached `pg_terminate_backend` and `DROP DATABASE`. This is the one destructive thing the harness does to a server it does not own, and it is reachable in exactly the mode the feature advertises for "point it at a server you already have". The structural cause is why it survived four review rounds of scrutiny on this very function: `sweep_step` took an already-parsed `(Option<u32>, Option<&str>)` pair, so the *parse* — the part that decides whether a name is ours at all — sat outside everything the function's unit tests could see. Every test asserted about a decision made from fields; none could assert that `production` is not a token. Fixed by giving `sweep_step` the whole `datname` so the shape check *is* the tested surface, and validating all four components against what is actually minted: literal prefix, decimal `u32` pid, exactly 16 **lowercase** hex digits of run token, decimal `u64` sequence, and no fourth component. `is_decimal` is deliberately stricter than `parse`, which accepts a leading `+`. The `LIKE` prefilter is now explicitly not the authority — `_` is a single-character wildcard, so it over-matches, and every candidate is re-checked against the full shape before anything destructive runs. `BENCH_DB_PREFIX` moved out of `db` to sit beside the validator, so minting and reclaiming cannot disagree about the name shape, and the whole decision stays testable with no server and no `db` feature. The asymmetry is stated in the code as the reason to err strict: failing to reclaim one of ours leaks a database, reclaiming one of theirs destroys data, so every ambiguous case resolves to `Skip`. Verified RED→GREEN on Postgres 16 at both levels. The unit test now names real databases rather than parsed fields and covers fifteen shapes a looser check would have accepted (wrong-width and uppercase hex, a fourth component, empty components, `+1`, an out-of-range pid, a bare prefix, and a name whose prefix only matches under `LIKE`'s wildcard); with the old two-field logic restored it fails on precisely the reported name, `left: AskServer, right: Skip`. The DB test is the one that matters: `a_foreign_database_sharing_our_prefix_is_never_dropped` creates a decoy in the vulnerable class, runs a real setup, and under the old logic the decoy is **gone** — `harvest_claim_bench_123_sweepprobe10306 was dropped by the stale sweep`. It is written defensively for a reason the previous round taught: the decoy must sit *inside* the swept prefix to be a candidate, which after the fix means nothing will ever reclaim it, so no panic may occur between its `CREATE` and its `DROP` — failures are collected into a value, cleanup is unconditional, and every assertion runs after it. The RED run panicked and still left no orphan behind. The sibling `a_later_setup_reclaims_this_processes_finished_databases` passing unchanged is the other half of the evidence: the stricter check did not buy safety by breaking the harness's ability to reclaim its own databases. `docs/performance.md` — the page an operator reads before pointing this at a server they care about — stated only that setup "sweeps stale `harvest_claim_bench_%` databases", which reads as *anything* with that prefix and was, before this fix, true; it now states the full eligibility shape, says outright that sharing the prefix is not enough, and gives `harvest_claim_bench_123_production` as an example of a name that is never a candidate.
  **(P) Two numeric name fields accepted spellings the harness cannot produce.** Round (O)'s whole-name validator checked each numeric component with "non-empty ASCII digits that also `parse`", but `parse` is a strict superset of what `format!("{}")` emits: it accepts a leading `+` and any number of leading zeros. So `harvest_claim_bench_01_0123456789abcdef_0` — and any `007`/`00` spelling of the pid or sequence — still passed a check whose stated contract was "validates every component against what is actually minted", and still reached `pg_terminate_backend` and `DROP DATABASE`. Fixed by replacing the digit-scan-plus-parse with a canonical round-trip, `s.parse::<T>().is_ok_and(|v| v.to_string() == s)`, which is simultaneously stricter and simpler: it rejects every noncanonical spelling without enumerating them, and subsumes the hand-rolled `+1` guard the previous round had written out longhand. The right question at a `DROP DATABASE` gate is not "could this parse to a value we might hold" but "is this byte-for-byte a name we would have written", and only the round-trip asks it. Verified RED→GREEN: the pure test's rejection list grew four leading-zero shapes (pid and sequence, single and multi-zero), and against the pre-fix predicate it fails on precisely the reported name — `harvest_claim_bench_01_0123456789abcdef_0 is not a name this harness mints, so it must never reach DROP DATABASE`. `sweep_step_accepts_a_freshly_minted_name`, which builds its input from the same pieces `setup_bench_db` formats from, stays green, so the stricter check did not narrow past what we actually mint. **(Q) A gate test mutated a process-global to configure itself.** `enqueue_stops_at_the_scenario_wall_clock_ceiling` set `HARVEST_BENCH_SCENARIO_SECS=1` and removed it afterwards, which is safe only under `--test-threads=1`. `cargo test` runs a binary's tests in parallel by default, and the checked CI manifest happens to pass that flag while a plain local `cargo test --features db --test integration claim_budget_tests` does not — so the suite's correctness rested on a harness flag rather than on the code, and a panic before the `remove_var` would have handed every remaining test a one-second budget. Fixed by removing the shared mutable state rather than scheduling around it: `run_claim_scenario_with_budget` and `run_enqueue_scenario_with_budget` take the ceiling as a parameter, the existing entry points delegate with `scenario_time_budget()`, and the environment is read exactly once at the edge by the caller that wants the default. A restore-on-drop guard was considered and rejected — it narrows the window but does not close it, and the window is open for as long as the test runs, which for these is the entire point of them. Both paths gained the injection point together on purpose: the previous two rounds were each a case of the write path missing a property the claim path had, and a helper that exists on only one of them is how that recurs. The natural failure is a latent flake rather than a deterministic one — the long scenario tests read the budget well after the ~1.6 s mutation window closes, and a parallel run of the suite with the old code passed — so it is pinned by the deterministic half instead: running the suite with `HARVEST_BENCH_SCENARIO_SECS=1` in the environment (exactly what a sibling observes if its read lands inside that window) collapses the headline gate to `measurement unsound: only 0 samples collected (need >= 100)`, while `enqueue_stops_at_the_scenario_wall_clock_ceiling` passes unaffected — it no longer reads the variable at all. The whole suite is now green in **parallel** mode as well as serial, so it no longer depends on the manifest's flag.
  **(R) The ownership lease was the one thing on the server that a routine `idle_session_timeout` would kill.** Existing-server mode keeps one connection open for the whole life of its database so a concurrent run can ask "is anyone using this?" and get an answer between scenarios — the lease defends the run by *being* an idle backend, which is precisely what the reaper introduced in Postgres 14 exists to terminate. On a server that sets it, at any level (`postgresql.conf`, `ALTER DATABASE`, `ALTER ROLE`), the lease is dropped mid-run while `BenchDb` still holds the now-dead handle; `database_has_connections` then reports a live run's database as abandoned and a concurrent sweep drops it out from under the benchmark that is still writing to it. Both sides fail silently and both are behaving correctly: nothing tells the victim its lease is gone, and the sweeper is reasoning soundly from the evidence it can see. That makes it the same defect class as (I), (N) and (O) — the sweep destroying something it should not — reached this time by the *defence* evaporating rather than by the check being too weak, and it is specific to the shared-cluster deployment this mode is designed for, since a throwaway testcontainer sets no such default. Fixed with `arm_lease_session`, one session-local `SET idle_session_timeout = 0` applied to the lease connection *under the sweep lock, before the lock is released* — the database must never become visible to a foreign sweep in a state where its only defence has an expiry date. `SET` is session-local and the GUC is `USERSET`, so this overrides any server-, database- or role-level default with no privilege and touches nothing else; a heartbeat was rejected as the alternative because it needs a background task whose lifetime is tied to `BenchDb` and would still leave a window one interval wide, where this closes the hole outright with one statement. The `SET` legitimately fails on Postgres 12/13 where the GUC does not exist, and that tolerance is exactly what could hide a *real* failure on 14+, so the value is read back rather than assumed: `current_setting('idle_session_timeout', true)` returns `NULL` for an unknown GUC, which is what distinguishes "too old to have a reaper" from "the reaper is armed and we failed to disable it". Only the second case warns, and it warns rather than aborting because an unarmed lease degrades a *concurrent* run and this mode is usually a single one — refusing to benchmark would be the larger harm. Pinned by `the_lease_survives_a_server_that_reaps_idle_sessions`, which is falsifiable in both directions: it opens an unarmed control session and an armed one under the same 2 s timeout, sleeps 6 s, and requires the control to be *gone* from `pg_stat_activity` before it will accept the armed session's survival — an armed session that lives proves nothing unless the reaper demonstrably works. The timeout is set per-session rather than with `ALTER ROLE` on purpose: a role-level default is shared mutable state on a server other tests are using concurrently, which is the hazard (Q) was about, and a session-local `SET` reproduces exactly what the lease inherits while reaching nothing else. RED on the pre-fix harness is the assertion `the armed lease was reaped after 6s idle despite a 2s timeout being disabled on its session`. `docs/performance.md` now states the guarantee where the sweep-safety contract is documented, including that the run warns rather than proceeding quietly when it cannot arm the lease on a 14+ server.
  **(S) The gate suite's own probe databases carried pid-only names, so two runs sharing a cluster destroyed each other's probes.** Two tests create real databases of their own on the shared server — `a_foreign_database_sharing_our_prefix_is_never_dropped` mints a decoy the sweep must spare, and `the_sweep_lock_is_taken_in_a_fixed_database_not_the_admin_url_s` mints a scratch database standing in for an operator whose admin URL points somewhere other than `SWEEP_LOCK_DB` — and both named it `…_{pid}` only. That is the *identical* defect (M) fixed for the real bench databases, in the test-support code beside it: PID 1 is the norm for a containerised process, so two runs on different hosts mint the same probe name, and because each probe opens with an unconditional `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS` (there to reclaim a strand from a crashed predecessor) one run deletes the other's *live* probe rather than merely failing to create its own. The decoy case then fails the very assertion it exists to make — that the database survived — which would read as a sweep-safety regression rather than a name collision, and the scratch case can leave a permanent orphan, since it sits outside the swept prefix precisely so nothing reclaims it. The probe names now carry `run_token()`, which is made `pub` rather than duplicated: reusing the one definition means there is a single answer to "which run minted this" and nothing that can drift, and a human debugging a strand can correlate the probe with that run's bench databases. The decoy's name moved into the pure section as `sweep_probe_decoy_name`, because it has to satisfy two properties that pull against each other and neither is visible in a `format!` at the call site — it must be a sweep *candidate* (inside `BENCH_DB_PREFIX`, shaped so an earlier round's two-field check would have accepted it, or the test proves nothing) while never being a name this harness could *mint* (or the test would assert that a real bench database survives the sweep, the exact inverse of the contract). Rejection is over-determined: `sweepprobe` can never be 16 hex digits since it contains `s`, `w`, `p`, `r` and `o`, *and* the extra components put the name past the exactly-three split. `the_sweep_probe_decoy_is_a_candidate_but_never_mintable` pins both halves plus per-run distinctness, and runs on every OS including the `--no-default-features` leg where no database exists. One trade-off taken deliberately: a run-unique scratch name is never reclaimed by a coincidentally same-pid successor, but that was never reliable cleanup — what actually prevents strands is the round-7 structure where nothing between the create and the drop may panic — so trading a coincidence for the removal of a destructive collision is the right direction, and both probe names remain unmistakable to an operator. RED is behavioural rather than a name comparison: against a live server, run A creates `harvest_claim_bench_123_sweepprobe1`, run B's probe opens with the same unconditional drop, and A's decoy count goes `1 → 0` — with the tokens it stays `1`. **(T) The documented CI-gate command claimed to run one test and ran fourteen.** `docs/performance.md` labelled `cargo test … -- claim_budget_tests --test-threads=1` as "the CI gate (the headline scenario only), ~2 minutes". `TESTNAME` is a substring filter, so that command runs the *whole* gate module — the headline budget check plus the eight-scenario coverage sweep, the 250k-row enqueue cutoff, and the sweep/lease probes. The command itself is right and deliberately so: it is byte-for-byte what `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt` runs, so it must stay copy-pasteable and CI-faithful. It was the *label* that was wrong, on the page an operator reads to reproduce a published number — and being wrong about which tests a command runs undermines every timing on it. Rewritten to say what the filter actually selects, with both figures measured on the reference box rather than estimated: ~80 s for the module (68–81 s observed across runs) and ~50 s for the headline check alone, whose narrower `claim_budget_tests::claim_p50_at_headline_scenario_is_within_budget` filter is now given as a second command for anyone who wants only the assertion that fails when a regression lands. The CI figure is flagged as higher, since CI starts a container where the reference box points at a local server.
  **(U) A password supplied as a URL query parameter — or in the libpq keyword/value form — was printed verbatim into CI logs.** The round-2 redactor replaced the `user:password@` userinfo segment and stopped there, but that is one of *three* places a Postgres connection string can carry a credential, and the other two are not exotic. `postgres://host/db?user=u&password=pw` is a fully valid form: `tokio-postgres`'s `UrlParser` feeds every query pair to the same `Config::param` that handles `"password"` (`config.rs:1136` → `:572`), so it authenticates exactly like userinfo does — verified in the vendored source rather than assumed. The keyword/value form `host=h password=pw` is worse still: it contains no `://`, so the redactor's first guard returned it **unchanged**, and `Config::from_str` falls through to that form whenever the URL parser declines, so an operator can legitimately set `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` that way. Both reach a CI log through the `SkipReason` the benchmark and the gate print on a connection failure — the exact exposure the round-2 finding was about, through doors it did not check. Values are now redacted by **allowlist** (`PRINTABLE_CONN_PARAMS`: `sslmode`, `connect_timeout`, `dbname`, `host`, `hostaddr`, `port`, `application_name`, `target_session_attrs`, `load_balance_hosts`) rather than by denying `password`: this gates what reaches a log, so a parameter nobody anticipated must default to hidden — libpq alone carries `password` *and* `sslpassword`, and `options` can carry arbitrary text, so a denylist has to stay ahead of every future addition while an allowlist only has to stay ahead of what is worth printing. `user` is deliberately excluded, since the URL form already replaces the whole `user:password@` segment and printing the username from the query would be inconsistent. Parameter **keys** stay visible — knowing an option was set is diagnostic and a key is not a secret — so a redacted string reads `?sslmode=require&sslpassword=***`. Path/query/fragment are separated in that order, the same discipline `with_db_name` uses, so a slash inside a parameter value cannot be mistaken for the path. RED against the pre-fix redactor is the leak itself: `password survived: postgres://db.internal:5432/harvest?user=alice&password=hunter2`. Four pure tests now cover the query form, the keyword/value form, the fail-closed allowlist (an unknown `sslpassword`/`options` hidden while `sslmode=require` survives), and the pre-existing userinfo cases — all on every OS, including the `--no-default-features` leg. **(V) The page claimed to measure six accreted claim predicates and measured five; the sixth was evaluated against a permanently empty table.** `docs/performance.md` said "queue pauses (#619) *is* exercised but is folded into the baseline, so its cost shows up in the `EXPLAIN` buffer counts" — but `harvest_queue_pauses` appears in the harness exactly once, in the `TRUNCATE`, and nothing ever inserts a row. The predicate runs on every claim against an *empty* relation, which is the cheapest path it has; being in the plan is not being measured. The same is true of four more whose columns the seed leaves null (`schedule_to_close_at`, `sticky_worker_id`, `session_id`, `required_capabilities`), so the real split is **five measured, five not** — the page's "six … remaining four" was off by one in both halves, which is how it survived: neither number was wrong enough alone to look wrong. The root of the over-claim was in the code, not the page: `ClaimGate`'s own doc said the variants "attribute cost to **each** one" of the accreted predicates, which reads as exhaustive and is the sentence a future contributor would trust. Narrowed rather than expanded, which is the honest half of the finding's own "add scenarios or narrow the claim" — each omitted predicate needs a seed variant *and* a report row on a bench that already runs 15-30 minutes, so adding five is a scope expansion to flag rather than take on silently. The enum doc now names the five omissions and says why they are unmeasured; the page's known-limitations bullet ranks them by how much the omission is likely to matter, with capability labels (#382) first — a `NOT EXISTS` + `jsonb_array_elements` subplan, the one whose real cost is least predictable from the query text — and states plainly that the page reports nothing about any of them.
  (W) A `dbname` **query parameter** silently outranked the path `with_db_name` had just rewritten, so every connection the harness derives — the sweep lock, the retained lease, the migration connection — went back to the operator's admin database while the URL still *read* as though it named the new one; the benchmark then ran its migrations and its per-scenario `TRUNCATE` there. `tokio-postgres`'s `UrlParser::parse` runs `parse_path` and *then* `parse_params`, and both assign the same `Config::dbname`, so the query is applied last and wins. This was introduced by the round-3 fix that started carrying the query over to keep `?sslmode=require` alive — the earlier bug was dropping the query, so the correction over-corrected into carrying a parameter that must not be carried. Fixed by dropping any `dbname` key on rewrite so the path is the single selector, and proved against a live server rather than inferred from the parser source: a regression test builds an admin URL carrying `?dbname=<decoy>`, rewrites it the way the harness does, connects, and asserts `current_database()` — pre-fix it lands on the decoy (`left: "harvest_dbname_probe_…", right: "postgres"`), which is the only way to demonstrate a bug whose whole character is that the URL reads correctly while the connection goes elsewhere. The same rewrite was silently broken for the libpq **keyword/value** form, which has no path at all: appending `/{db}` to `host=h dbname=admin` yields a database literally named `admin/b`. Fixed in the same pass rather than left as a known-broken neighbour, since fixing "targets the wrong database" while leaving a sibling path that targets the wrong database would repeat the exact pattern this round is about. (X) The keyword/value redactor added in round 13 split on whitespace, but libpq permits quoted and backslash-escaped values, so `password='hunter two'` was cut in half: the first token redacted and the second — having no `=` — was passed through as though it were a separate parameter, printing the tail of the password into a CI log. Fixed with a real single-pass tokenizer for that grammar (quotes toggle, `\` consumes the next character whatever it is, so `\'` does not close the quote), shared with `with_db_name` above so the two agree on where a value ends. A token with no `=` is still passed through, which is safe *because* the tokenizer is now correct — under the old split it could be the tail of a value, and under this one it cannot be. (Y) The round-14 tokenizer still keyed redaction on an `=` *inside* a token, but libpq allows whitespace around the separator: `password = 'hunter two'` tokenizes as three tokens, none of which contains an embedded `=`, so every one of them was passed through and the complete password reached the `safe_url` printed after a connection failure — the same CI-log leak round 14 was meant to close, one grammar rule further out. The lesson taken was that redaction had been tokenizing when it needed to be *parsing*: fixed by replacing the token pass with a real keyword/value pair parser (`keyword_value_pairs`) that walks keyword, optional whitespace, `=`, optional whitespace, then a quoted-or-bare value, and returns the offset at which it stopped. Redaction is now **fail-closed** on that offset: anything the parser could not consume — an unterminated quote, a keyword with no value — is replaced with `***` rather than printed, so a form nobody anticipated degrades to withholding instead of leaking. The allowlist of printable connection *shape* parameters is unchanged; the change is that a value is only ever printed after it has actually been parsed as one. (Z) `db_name_from_url` — documented as the inverse of `with_db_name` and its literal neighbour — still read only a URL path, so for the keyword/value form that round 14 had just taught `with_db_name` to emit it returned `None` for exactly the strings the harness now produces, and both existing-server tests `.expect()` that value: the documented full gate suite panicked for a supported connection-string form. (Before round 14 the rewrite emitted a stray `/` that this parser happened to read as a path, so the inverse had been working only by accident.) Fixed by giving it a keyword branch — last `dbname` wins, matching `Config::param`, which simply assigns on each occurrence — and, in the same pass, by honouring the *query-over-path* precedence on the URL side that round 14 established for its twin. Leaving that half unfixed would have left two neighbouring functions disagreeing about which parameter names the database for the same input, which is the shape of the next finding rather than the end of this one. (AA) The measurement clock started before the claimer tasks were even spawned, so each claimer began sampling the moment *its own* `pool.get()` returned: claimer 0 could be several operations in while claimer 7 was still connecting. The "8 concurrent claimers" row therefore contained a lower-concurrency ramp-up at the head of its sample — flattering p50 for precisely the scenarios that exist to measure contention — and `wall_secs` counted lazy pool construction as though it were measured work, inflating the throughput denominator. Fixed with a start barrier after checkout and a measurement clock that begins on its release, in both the claim and enqueue runners; the throughput denominator is now the widest per-worker span from that release, which is the real measured phase. The scenario deadline is deliberately **not** re-anchored — it still precedes checkout, because `pool.get()` is an unbounded await and a ceiling that starts after it would not bound it (a round-8 fix this round had to be careful not to undo). Every task arrives at the barrier, including one that failed checkout and is about to return, so a party that is never coming cannot park its peers there; the wait is additionally bounded by the same deadline as every other await in the task, as a backstop for any future path that forgets. The published numbers were re-measured rather than carried over, because a change to the throughput denominator invalidates a throughput column by construction whether or not it moves it. **Round 16 review (BB, CC) — one shared split of the *driver's* URL grammar.** Both findings were the same root cause seen twice: the harness parsed `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` as an RFC 3986 URL, but `tokio-postgres` hand-rolls its own `UrlParser` and that grammar differs in two ways that matter. (BB, P1) `parse_params` runs `self.decode(key)?` *before* dispatching to `Config::param`, so `?db%6Eame=admin` is a `dbname` override — but `with_db_name`'s strip-the-overriding-parameter filter (the round 14 P1 fix) compared the key raw and carried it through untouched. The rewritten string then *read* as though it targeted the isolated bench database while every connection opened from it — sweep lock, lease, migrations, and the benchmark's own `TRUNCATE` — went to the operator's admin database instead: the identical P1 round 14 closed, reached through a spelling that filter could not see. (CC, P2) `parse_params` terminates a value with `take_until(&['&'])` and the parser has no fragment concept at *any* stage (`parse_host` stops at `/` or `?`; `parse_path` runs `take_until(&['?'])` and otherwise takes the rest of the string), so `?password=#hunter2` authenticates with the literal `#hunter2` — but the redactor split the URL at `#` and appended the tail verbatim, printing most of a live password on exactly the connection-failure line operators paste into tickets. Rather than patch the two named call sites — which is the pattern that kept generating these findings — the grammar is now parsed **once**, by `split_driver_url`, into the regions the driver actually sees (`prefix`, `authority`, `path`, `query`, no fragment), and `redact_url`, `with_db_name` and `db_name_from_url` all derive from that single split. Query keys are compared after `percent_decode`, which mirrors `UrlParser::decode` exactly: plain percent-decoding, `+` is *not* a space, and invalid UTF-8 falls back to the raw span rather than being dropped (the driver rejects such a string outright, so there is no live connection for the fallback to disagree with). `db_name_from_url` decodes the value it returns for the same reason `parse_path` does — its result is fed to a `datname` lookup, and `%5F` names a database called `_`, not `%5F` — which changes its return type to an owned `String`. The keyword/value grammar is deliberately left comparing raw keys and *not* decoded: that form has no percent-encoding, so `dbname=%41` names a database literally called `%41`, and decoding it would be a new bug in the opposite direction. Two existing tests asserted the RFC reading (`.../bench_1#frag` → `bench_1`, and a fragment surviving a `dbname` strip) and were inverted to the driver's, with the reason recorded at each: `#frag` is part of the name and part of the value respectively, and reading it any other way has this harness look for a database the driver never asked for.

  **Round 17 review — parse the driver's *order*, not just its grammar; count Unicode whitespace; measure every worker on one clock.** Three findings, two of them further instalments of the same lesson round 16 started: modelling the connection string on the *specification* rather than on `tokio-postgres`' actual code keeps producing credential leaks in the one place they hurt most — the connection-failure line an operator pastes into a ticket. (FF, P2) Round 16 split the URL into regions, but split them the way RFC 3986 defines an authority: stop at the first `/` or `?`, then look for `@` inside what is left. `UrlParser::parse` does not do that. It calls `parse_credentials` **before** `parse_host`, and credentials are `take_until(&['@'])` over the *entire* remaining string, with no `/` or `?` terminator. So `postgres://alice:sec/ret@db:5432/postgres` authenticates as `alice` / `sec/ret` against host `db:5432` — a perfectly ordinary password that happens to contain a slash — while the authority-first split saw `alice:sec`, found no `@` in it, and printed the whole credential verbatim. `split_driver_url` now mirrors the driver's call order (credentials → host → path → query) and reports `credentials` and `host` as separate fields; `redact_url` replaces the whole credential span with `***` and `with_db_name` re-emits it verbatim, because that function rewrites the connection *target* and a truncated credential yields a URL that no longer authenticates. Using the **first** `@` rather than the last is deliberate: it is what the driver does, and for a well-formed URL they are the same character. (DD, P2) The libpq keyword/value tokenizer added in round 15 separated pairs on `u8::is_ascii_whitespace`, but `Parser::skip_ws` is `take_while(char::is_whitespace)` and both value readers break on `c.is_whitespace()` — Unicode, not ASCII. A no-break space genuinely ends a value and starts a new pair for the driver, so `host=db.internal\u{00A0}password=hunter2` is two pairs to it and one to us: the whole tail became the value of the *allowlisted* `host` key and the password was printed in full. The tokenizer is now char-based throughout (`find_from`/`skip_ws`/`simple_value_end`/`quoted_value_end`), which also fixes the byte-arithmetic in the escape handling — `\` is one byte but the char it escapes need not be. (EE, P2) The start barrier added in round 15 removed pool checkout from the measured window, but each worker then timed itself with an `Instant::now()` taken *after* its own `gate.wait()` returned, and the scenario's wall clock was the maximum of those per-worker elapsed times. A worker is not polled the moment the barrier releases — with eight claimers on a four-thread runtime, most are not — so every worker's release-to-resume delay was dropped from the denominator while all of its claims stayed in the numerator, reporting throughput higher than the run achieved. Workers now report a `(resume, finish)` pair and the new pure `measured_window` folds them into one interval on the shared monotonic clock, from the earliest resume (the closest observable stand-in for the release itself) to the last completion. Both the claim and enqueue runners use it, and `docs/performance.md` is republished from a fresh run because the correction moves the denominator up and therefore every claims/s and rows/s figure down. `measured_window` lives in the pure section rather than the `db` module precisely so it is covered by the no-DB suite: its regression test drives two workers that each run for 1 s with the second resuming 2 s late, where the true window is 3 s and the old maximum-per-worker reading was 1 s — a threefold overstatement. **Post-review hardening, round 18 (Codex GG, P2):** the URL/keyword form was chosen by searching for `://` *anywhere*, but `UrlParser::remove_url_prefix` strips `postgres://`/`postgresql://` with `str::strip_prefix` and otherwise hands the whole string to the keyword parser — the form is decided by how a string *begins*, byte-exact. So `host=db password=http://hunter2` was read as a URL, split at a scheme that was really part of a value, and redacted nothing; `with_db_name` corrupted the same string into one that parses as neither form (the surviving `dbname=admin` still selecting the operator's real database while `/bench` was appended to the password). Selection is now `strip_prefix` against the two exact prefixes, which also routes a case variant like `POSTGRES://alice:hunter2@db/x` to the keyword redactor — where it has no `=` at all, and the passthrough that keeps a malformed-string message diagnostic would have printed its userinfo verbatim. That passthrough now drops everything through the last `@` when one is present. The doc's premise for that passthrough ("no `=` ⇒ carries no `key=value` secret") is true of keyword form and false of a scheme-shaped string whose secret is in userinfo; both halves shipped together because the first fix is what makes the second reachable.

  **Post-review hardening, round 19 (Codex HH, P2):** `connect` and `seed` run *before* the measured phase and therefore before its deadline exists, so neither was bounded by anything — a server that accepted the TCP connection and then stopped answering would park the bench, and the CI gate that calls it, until the outer workflow timeout, while the page advertises a per-scenario cap. Every other await in both runners was already bounded; these two were the hole. The new `with_setup_deadline` wraps each step in `tokio::time::timeout` and panics with a message naming the step, and the shared `connect_and_seed` applies it on both the claim and enqueue paths so the bound cannot exist on one and not the other. Setup gets its *own* deadline rather than sharing the measured phase's: a single ceiling spanning both would let a slow seed eat the measurement window and report `truncated`, which says "the claim path is slow" about a run whose claim path was never the problem. Two phases, two ceilings — the worst case is bounded at twice the budget instead of unbounded, and each number means what it says. The same `scenario_time_budget` value is reused so raising `HARVEST_BENCH_SCENARIO_SECS` for a slow machine widens setup with it. The three tests live in `claim_budget_tests.rs` rather than beside the function: a `#[tokio::test]` in the shared harness would reclassify it from harness to suite and trip `ci_run_coverage::claim_bench_support_is_classified_as_a_harness_not_a_suite`, whose own remedy is to put the test in a file that already has a manifest row. They run on a paused clock, so the stalled-server case is decided by the deadline rather than by waiting out four real minutes; with the timeout removed the same test hangs (`cargo test` killed at 40 s against a pre-built binary), which is the bug it pins.
  **Round 20 (Codex II + JJ, both P2):** two holes one level below round 19. **II — provisioning was itself unbounded.** Round 19 bounded `connect` and `seed`, but all eight awaits in `setup_bench_db` — connect to the admin database, take the sweep lock, sweep stale databases, create the benchmark database, connect and arm the ownership lease, release the sweep lock, run migrations — run before any deadline exists, so the same stalled server that round 19 caught after provisioning simply parks the gate before it instead. (`take_sweep_lock` sets `lock_timeout`, but that covers only the advisory-lock *wait*; its own `establish` and `SET` statement were still unbounded.) The new `with_provision_deadline` wraps each step against one deadline fixed before the first await, so the whole provisioning phase is bounded rather than each step getting a fresh budget. It maps a timeout to `SkipReason` rather than panicking, matching `setup_bench_db`'s existing contract that every provisioning failure skips: failing to provision means the benchmark cannot run *here*, which is what skipping is for, whereas a stall after provisioning succeeded is a real fault and still panics. **JJ — the probe cleanup used a `PostgreSQL` 13+ clause.** `claim_budget_tests.rs` dropped its `harvest_dbname_probe_*` decoy with `DROP DATABASE ... WITH (FORCE)`, which is 13+ while the engine supports 12+ (README). On 12 that is a syntax error, the result is discarded — a failed cleanup must not fail the run — and the probe name carries no `BENCH_DB_PREFIX`, so unlike a stale bench database the harness sweep can never reclaim it either: a permanent leak, one database per run. The sweep itself was already version-neutral from round 7; only this site was missed, which is why the fix is a *shared* `db::drop_database_version_neutral` (terminate-then-plain-drop) rather than a second inline copy — the two callers leak in different ways when they disagree, and a helper cannot drift from itself. Its `# Safety` note records why the name is interpolated rather than bound (`PostgreSQL` accepts no parameter there) and what each caller must have done to earn that: minted the name, or cleared it through `sweep_step`. The two JJ tests are deliberately complementary, and the 2×2 was run in full: removing the terminate step leaves the database alive with a backend attached (`left: 1, right: 0` — and the RED runs leaked exactly the two databases the finding predicts) while the source scan still passes; reintroducing the clause trips the scan naming file and line while the behavioural test passes, because `WITH (FORCE)` works perfectly well on the `PostgreSQL` 16 CI runs. Each catches precisely what the other cannot — the behavioural half cannot see a version CI never runs, and a source scan cannot prove terminate-then-drop actually evicts anyone. The scan assembles its needle with `concat!` because it lives inside one of the files it reads; written out, it matched itself and could never have passed, which is how that was found.
  **Round 21 (Codex KK + LL + MM + NN, all P2):** four holes, two of them in the round-20 fix itself. **LL — the provisioning ceiling guarded the wrong branch.** Round 20 bounded the eight existing-server awaits, but the testcontainers branch's three (`start`, `get_host`, `get_host_port_ipv4`) stayed bare — and that is the branch the checked CI manifest runs, since neither `ci.yml` nor `run-suites.sh` ever sets `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL`. A ceiling that protects only the mode CI never exercises is not a ceiling. The deadline is now fixed above the branch and the container path is extracted into `setup_container_bench_db(deadline)` under it, so a daemon that accepts the socket and stops answering mid-pull is bounded too. **NN — the same blind spot in the new test.** `version_neutral_drop_evicts_a_live_backend` gated on `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL`, so the one test proving terminate-then-drop still evicts a live backend never ran in CI at all. Provisioned through `setup_bench_db` instead, it runs in both modes; the mode restriction was convenience, unlike `an_idle_bench_database_still_holds_a_visible_lease`, which is genuinely existing-server-only because a foreign client can only exist there. **KK — the provisioning session sat on the operator's database.** It is held from the first connect until the lease is armed, which spans the whole wait for the sweep lock, so an admin URL naming `template1` turned every *waiting* client into a blocker for whichever client held the lock: `CREATE DATABASE` copies `template1` and Postgres refuses while another session is attached. It now connects through `SWEEP_LOCK_DB`, which costs no reachability — `take_sweep_lock` already refuses to start a run that cannot reach it — and every statement that session issues is cluster-scoped anyway. The choice is extracted into `admin_connection_url` so it is assertable rather than buried in a connect call. **MM — `pg_terminate_backend` signals, it does not wait.** A backend unwinding a transaction can still hold the database when the `DROP` arrives, and that error is discarded, so the outcome is identical to never having terminated anything; the two-argument form that waits is `PostgreSQL` 14+ and version-neutrality is the helper's whole reason to exist, so it polls `pg_stat_activity` instead, bounded at 5 s, and issues the `DROP` either way. Evidence, stated at the strength it actually has: KK is red→green both ways — the pure decision test fails on revert, and the live test fails with Postgres's own `source database "template1" is being accessed by other users` — and NN is verified in the reachable mode locally, with CI the proof for the container mode this sandbox has no Docker to run. LL and MM are structural: neither a stalled Docker daemon nor a slow-unwinding backend is deterministically reproducible here, and MM's poll is strictly no worse than not polling since the `DROP` is attempted regardless. One incident worth recording: during KK's revert the live test first reported a false *pass* because the local server had stopped and it skipped on connect failure — the same "a test that cannot fail" trap as round 18, caught this time before it was reported as evidence. **Round 22 Codex review (`docs/performance.md`, P2) — the analysis was regenerated from the displayed run, and a guard now keeps it that way.** The page's tables are regenerated from a fresh benchmark run whenever the numbers move; the prose around them was not, so it had drifted a full run behind. The reviewer caught the worst pair — the control discussion quoted `+1314%`/`n=240/240` against a table publishing `+1383%`/`n=325/322`, and the enqueue narrative called the deepest backlog the fastest when the table shows the middle one is — but the drift was systematic rather than local: sixteen figures across the TL;DR, the truncation note, the control section, all seven per-gate bullets and the CI-gate cliff table were reading from the previous run. All of them now trace to the published tables (`concurrency_key` +532%→+644%, `double_backlog` +1314%→+1383%, `all_gates` +1665%→+1797%, `all_gates`-vs-control +23%→+28%, `paused_rows`-vs-control −1%→+1%, the 1k→10k multiplier ~24x→~19x, the truncated sweep's 430→583 samples, and the cliff row recomputed from the published 7.44x rather than a stale 6.9x). The multi-run figures that were *already* labelled as spanning runs — the six-run reproducibility paragraph, the "earlier revision" narrative, the quiet-vs-loaded spread table — are deliberately left alone: forbidding them would force the page to hide the run-to-run spread, which is the most operationally honest thing on it. Two substantive corrections beyond arithmetic: the `paused_rows`-vs-control delta *changed sign* between runs, so rather than flip "slightly more" to "slightly less" and let it rot again, the text now states that the sign flips and that the ±1% must not be read as a direction — the sign flip is itself the evidence the predicate is free; and the enqueue claim is restated as "throughput does not order by depth at all", which is what the table actually shows and is robust to which row happens to win next time. **The root cause was that nothing tied the prose to the tables**, which is the same class as the two earlier findings on this PR where a test silently did not run: a stale number renders perfectly. New no-DB guard `tests/integration/performance_docs.rs` parses the published tables out of the Markdown and asserts (a) each table's percentage column is arithmetically consistent with its own latency column — which is what makes the tables trustworthy as the source of truth, and it passed on the first run, confirming the tables were never the problem — and (b) every per-gate bullet quotes the figure the table publishes for it, including that a bullet says "vs the control" exactly when the table measures that row against something other than `baseline`, so a number cannot be silently reattributed to the wrong comparand. Red→green in three directions: re-introducing a stale bullet percentage, corrupting the table's own percentage column, and dropping the "vs the control" qualifier each fail with a message naming the gate and both figures. It needs no CI manifest row — the `allos autumn-harvest integration testing -` row already runs the whole binary unfiltered on all three platforms.

  **Post-review hardening, round 23 (two P2 methodology inaccuracies in `docs/performance.md`, both verified against source before fixing).** (1) **The enqueue throughput denominator does not include task spawn or join.** The caveat under the enqueue table claimed the `rows/s` column "divides all rows by the whole wall clock including warmup and task spawn/join". Warmup is included, but spawn and join are not: `run_enqueue_scenario_with_budget` opens each writer's span at `arrive_at_start_gate(...)` — *after* the task is spawned and its connection checked out — and closes it with an `Instant::now()` captured **inside** the worker closure, *before* the handle is joined; `measured_window` then folds those spans into `min(start)..max(end)`. Calling the result an end-to-end figure therefore misstated the published measurement and contradicted the authoritative Measurement-hygiene bullet a hundred lines below, which correctly describes "earliest resume after the barrier through the last completion — so pool construction is not counted as measured work". The caveat now links to that bullet instead of restating the endpoints in a second voice (restating them is what let the two drift apart), and states the two reasons the column is genuinely a floor: warmup rows are in the numerator, and the window runs to the *slowest* writer so a writer that finishes early still counts toward the denominator. (2) **A published claim number is five client↔server round trips, not one.** "What is actually timed" described `claim_task` as "transaction overhead and one client↔server round trip". It is a multi-statement transaction: `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED` (pinned on the `BEGIN` itself so the pause re-check gets a fresh snapshot), the claim CTE, then — **on a hit only** — `queue_pause::try_lock_queue_for_claim` and `queue_pause::release_claim_if_queue_paused` (a *separate* statement precisely so it takes a snapshot the claim could not have, issue #619), then `COMMIT`. That is five round trips on a hit and three on a miss; the seeded scenarios claim at most a fifth of the backlog they seed, so their samples are overwhelmingly hits. The old text also mislabelled the rate-limit debit and the per-key concurrency advisory-lock re-check as "follow-up work", implying extra statements when both are branches *within* the claim CTE, while omitting the queue-pause statements that genuinely are extra. The section now enumerates the transaction and adds the operational consequence the corrected count implies: against a **remote** database it is the round-trip count, not the query plan, that network latency multiplies — five round trips at 1 ms RTT is a 5 ms per-claim floor no index tuning removes — whereas every number on this page was measured against a loopback server, where that floor is ~0 and the plan dominates. **Anti-drift guards (same class as the round-22 guard, extended to tie prose to *source* rather than to a table in the same file).** `tests/integration/performance_docs.rs` gains two tests. `claim_transaction_statements_are_all_named_in_the_docs` extracts the body of `pub async fn claim_task` from `src/queue.rs`, collects every `crate::queue_pause::` call site in it, and asserts the "What is actually timed" section names each one — matching on whole identifiers, since `release_claim` is a prefix of `release_claim_if_queue_paused` and a substring check would let a doc naming only the longer call appear to name both. Adding or removing a statement in the claim transaction now fails the build instead of silently invalidating a round-trip count a reader is multiplying by their network RTT. `enqueue_throughput_caveat_defers_to_the_authoritative_window_definition` asserts the authoritative hygiene bullet still exists, that the enqueue caveat links to `#measurement-hygiene` rather than restating the endpoints, and that any sentence in the caveat mentioning task spawn also places it *outside* the window — a direction check rather than a keyword ban, so the corrected wording (which mentions spawn precisely to exclude it) passes while the old wording fails. Red→green in three directions, each confirmed by mutating the doc and observing the specific failure: reverting the caveat to the old wording, keeping the link but reversing the spawn claim, and dropping `try_lock_queue_for_claim` from the enumeration. No CI manifest row needed — the existing `allos autumn-harvest integration testing -` row runs the whole binary unfiltered on all three platforms. Verification: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy -p autumn-harvest --all-features --tests -- -D warnings` and the `--no-default-features --features testing` leg both clean; no-DB integration **1147/1147** (up from 1145); DB-backed `claim_budget_tests` **23/23** against a real local Postgres 16, including `claim_p50_at_headline_scenario_is_within_budget`. **No code change** — this round is documentation accuracy plus the guards that keep it accurate. **Round 23 follow-up — the new guards had to survive a CRLF checkout (`Test (windows-latest)` red on `3414dcc`).** The three structural helpers introduced above locate boundaries with `\n`-anchored needles — `"\n}\n"` for a top-level item's closing brace, `"\n\n"` for a paragraph break, `"\n### "` for a section break. `actions/checkout` on the Windows runner checks the tree out with CRLF, so every one of those needles missed and `claim_transaction_statements_are_all_named_in_the_docs` panicked with `queue.rs must define \`pub async fn claim_task(\`` — a message that points at the file's *contents* while the actual fault was its *line endings*. The repository's own `.gitattributes` is the corroborating evidence: it pins `eol=lf` for `*.sh` and the CI manifest precisely because "a CRLF-corrupted `.sh` would fail to parse" on that leg, and deliberately leaves `.rs`/`.md` on Git's default. Fixed by normalising once at read time (`read_normalized`, used by both `read_performance_doc` and the `src/queue.rs` read) rather than by threading `\r?` handling through each helper, and in preference to widening `.gitattributes` to `*.rs`/`*.md` — a repo-wide checkout change that would also not repair an already-checked-out working copy, whereas normalising in the test is correct regardless of anyone's `core.autocrlf`. The regression guard is the point of the fix: `structural_helpers_survive_crlf_line_endings` writes source and Markdown fixtures containing *explicit* CRLF and drives all three helpers through `read_normalized`, so the failure that was previously observable only on Windows CI now reproduces in the ordinary Linux run — confirmed red→green by stripping the `.replace("\r\n", "\n")` and watching it fail locally with the same class of bogus "must define X" panic. It also asserts the helpers still *stop* correctly (the extracted body does not run into the next item; the paragraph stops at the blank line; the section stops at the next `### `), so a future "fix" that normalises by deleting all newlines fails too. Verification: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; both clippy legs `-D warnings` clean; no-DB integration **1148/1148**. **Round 24 — the control does not isolate the predicate it is credited with isolating, and the post-measurement checks were unbounded.** Two findings. **(1) The `paused_rows` attribution was over-claimed.** The page presented `double_backlog` as the control that isolates the PAUSED anti-join's cost, and read the residual **+1%** as "the anti-join is free". `double_backlog` controls for *total rows in the table* — it does not control for the population that reaches the sort, which is where the claim query spends its time. The anti-join is a `WHERE` predicate, so it is evaluated *before* the `ORDER BY`: measured on a real Postgres 16 with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, the control feeds **20 000** rows to the sort while `paused_rows` feeds **10 000** (`Rows Removed by Filter: 10000`). The +1% is therefore the anti-join's probe cost *minus* the sort saving from ten thousand fewer sorted rows — two effects of opposite sign that this measurement cannot separate, which is also the honest explanation for why the figure's *sign* flips between runs. The probe surfaced something stronger than the review stated: in the control the PAUSED `SubPlan` shows **`never executed`** (every seeded row is `task_type = 'activity'`, so the guard short-circuits on the type test — a fact the page already documented two sections away without connecting it to the control), and the two scenarios do not even take the same plan (control: `Seq Scan` + `Hash Anti Join`; `paused_rows`: `Index Scan using idx_harvest_tq_poll` + `Merge Anti Join` + a hashed `SubPlan`). Fixed by narrowing the published claim rather than by re-measuring: the depth-controlled operational finding — a paused population costs ~15x, drain the rows — is untouched and is the actionable one, while the isolated predicate cost is now explicitly **not published**, with a new `#### What that control does *not* establish` subsection showing the sort-input asymmetry in a table and stating what a properly matched control would need (same 20 000 scanned, same 10 000 sorted, excluded by a mechanism cheap enough not to be the thing under test). The TL;DR bullet, the per-gate bullet, the two-questions table and the closing paragraph were all rewritten off the same evidence; the bound that survives is the `all_gates` row — every predicate in the engine *combined* costs +28% against an equal-depth comparand, against ~15x for depth alone. Guarded by `the_paused_rows_delta_is_not_attributed_to_the_predicate`, which requires the subsection and its sort-input table to exist and bans six spellings of the isolated-cost reading (the claim reads so naturally it would come back). **(2) The post-measurement soundness checks were unbounded.** After the measured phase, the gate tests reconnect and count rows to verify the run was sound — the backlog was not drained, the enqueue really did write into a non-empty queue. Those awaits sit *after* the measured phase and therefore after its deadline is already spent, so nothing bounded them: a server that stopped answering between the last claim and the verification parks the CI gate until the outer workflow timeout. This is the same hole `with_setup_deadline` closed at the front of a scenario, at the other end. New `with_verify_deadline` sibling taking a *fresh* `Duration` rather than the measured phase's `Instant` — a scenario is allowed to consume its entire budget, so a shared deadline would have nothing left and every check would "time out" against a healthy server. Applied to all **six** previously-unbounded DB awaits, not only the two flagged: the two gate tests plus the two auxiliary seeding tests, since the hazard is identical and a partial fix invites the same finding again. Three pure tests (`start_paused`, so a never-resolving future is decided by the ceiling rather than by waiting out four real minutes) cover the stall, the pass-through, and — the one that pins *why* the ceiling is fresh — a verification that still succeeds after the measured phase has burned its whole budget. **Round 25 — the doc guards could not fire on a docs-only pull request.** The `changes` job classifies `docs/**` as `code=false`, and every step of the `test` matrix is gated on `code == 'true'`; the ungated `lint` job runs Clippy over these tests, which *compiles* them but never executes them. So for three rounds the `docs/performance.md` prose-vs-table guards were skipped on exactly the change class they exist for — an edit to that file and nothing else. Fixed with an unconditional `cargo test … --test integration performance_docs::` step in the ungated `lint` job. Unconditional rather than `if: code == 'false'` on purpose: "the guards always run" is a stronger property than "the guards run when the other place did not", and does not break silently the day someone edits the matrix's gating. Guarded by `performance_guards_run_on_docs_only_changes`, which parses `ci.yml` and asserts the step exists, filters on this module by name, lives inside the `lint` job rather than the gated `test` matrix, and has not acquired an `if:` — verified red against both failure modes (step deleted; step re-gated). Verification: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; both clippy legs `-D warnings` clean; no-DB integration **1150/1150**; DB-backed `claim_budget_tests` **26/26** against a real local Postgres 16, including `claim_p50_at_headline_scenario_is_within_budget`. The published budget is unchanged. **Round 26 — the release note still published the superseded run, and the harness documented the wrong statistic.** Two findings, both about text that contradicts the code or the tables beside it. **(1) The leading changelog entry was never updated.** This fragment is collated into the public `CHANGELOG.md`, so its opening entry *is* the release note; every round of review appended its correction to the *end* as a development diary. That left the headline quoting an earlier run (`+1357%`, `−2%`) and the attribution retracted in round 24 ("deleting the predicate would buy nothing") roughly ninety thousand characters before the retraction — a reader of the collated changelog meets the superseded claim first and may never reach the fix. Rewritten from the final measurements and the narrowed attribution: the control's published `+1383%`, the depth-controlled `+1403%` operational finding, an explicit statement that the control does *not* establish an isolated predicate cost (differing sort populations; `never executed` `SubPlan` in the control), and the `all_gates` +28% bound that does survive. **(2) The shared harness's module docs said the gate asserts p99.** It asserts **p50** — `claim_p50_at_headline_scenario_is_within_budget` compares `report.stats.p50_ms` against `HEADLINE_P50_BUDGET_MS`, and the p99→p50 switch was deliberate because the headline scenario oversubscribes the box so its tail measures the run queue rather than the claim path. A maintainer reading the harness first would have calibrated or relaxed the budget against a statistic nothing gates. Corrected, with a pointer to the "Why p50 and not p99" derivation and an explicit "do not calibrate against the tail". **Guards.** `changelog_fragment_quotes_the_published_figures` reads the control's multiplier off the published table (never hardcoded) and requires it in the sentence that *introduces* the control, plus bans the assertive spellings of the retracted reading. The scoping is load-bearing and was found by the red check failing to fail: an unscoped `fragment.contains(figure)` passes on a *correct* mention in the appended diary while the leading entry still carries a stale one — precisely the drift under guard — so the first version of this test would have let the bug through. Narrowed to a 400-character window at the introduction, it fails as intended. `harness_docs_name_the_asserted_statistic` parses the harness module doc and requires it to name p50 while rejecting the p99 claim. Both verified red against their specific regression. Both live in `performance_docs.rs` deliberately: `docs/changelog.d/**` is also classified `code=false`, so a changelog-only edit skips the gated matrix, and the ungated lint step added in round 25 runs *this* module. Verification: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; both clippy legs `-D warnings` clean; no-DB integration **1152/1152**. **Post-review hardening, round 27 (one Codex P2 on `ad695f7`, plus a CI outage the round-25 guard could not see).** **(P) The workflow file did not parse, so CI had been running zero jobs for two commits.** The step round 25 added to the ungated `lint` job ended in `--test integration performance_docs::`, and a trailing colon in an *unquoted* YAML scalar is a mapping indicator — so the parser rejected the whole file with "mapping values are not allowed here" at that line. GitHub's response to an unparseable workflow is quiet in exactly the wrong way: it creates a run, names it after the file *path* rather than the workflow's `name:`, loads **zero** jobs, and marks it failed. No leg reports, so no branch-protection context turns red in a way that reads as "this test broke"; the PR simply has a failing run with nothing in it. Commits `5c3f50d` and `ad695f7` both ran that way. Fixed by quoting the value. **The pointed part is that round 25's own guard passed throughout.** `performance_guards_run_on_docs_only_changes` asserts the step exists, is in the `lint` job, and carries no `if:` — all three were true, and all three were meaningless, because the file containing the step could not be loaded. A guard that asserts a CI step exists is worth nothing if it cannot also tell you the file parses. New `ci_yaml_plain_scalars_do_not_contain_a_mapping_colon` closes that: every unquoted `key: value` in `ci.yml` is checked for the two colons YAML reads as mapping separators (a trailing `:` at end of line, and `: ` mid-value), with quoted values and block scalars exempt since those are the correct spellings. It is deliberately a targeted rule rather than a parse — named for what it checks, not for "the workflow is valid" — because a real parse would need a YAML dependency on the core crate, and the only one in the lockfile is both deprecated and reachable solely through `autumn-web`, which this crate does not depend on. The rule is well matched to this file specifically: `ci.yml` is mostly long shell one-liners, and cargo test filters (`module::`), URLs and time expressions are precisely the values that acquire colons. Both branches verified red — the trailing-colon branch against the actual broken line, the colon-space branch against an injected `env: KEY: value`. **(O) The benchmark's generated report still published the attribution retracted in round 24.** Round 24 narrowed the claim in `docs/performance.md` and round 26 caught the changelog's leading entry, but the note `benches/claim_bench.rs` prints under its per-gate table still ended "so the delta is the anti-join's cost rather than the extra depth's". That is the worst of the three surfaces to leave stale: a doc is read once, but the bench output is what someone pastes into a PR when they regenerate the numbers, so the superseded reading propagates into new writing. Rewritten to state the same thing `docs/performance.md` now does — the control matches total table rows but not the population reaching the sort, the anti-join is a `WHERE` predicate and so runs before the `ORDER BY`, `paused_rows` therefore sorts 10 000 rows where the control sorts 20 000, and the delta is probe cost minus that sort saving: two effects of opposite sign the measurement cannot separate. New `the_bench_report_does_not_republish_the_retracted_attribution` guards it, scoped to `println!` content with comment lines stripped so the source may still *explain* the retraction without tripping it — the same explanation-versus-assertion distinction the round-26 changelog guard needed. It also asserts the correction is positively present, so the note cannot be deleted outright and leave the table's `vs` column unqualified, which is how the misreading started. Verification: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; clippy `-D warnings` clean on `--all-features --tests --benches` and on `--no-default-features --features testing --all-targets`; no-DB integration **1154/1154**; `ci.yml` confirmed to parse with all 7 jobs loading and the guard step present, unconditional, in `lint`. **Post-review hardening, round 28 (three Codex P2s on `9aa2887`).** **(Q) The `all_gates` delta was published as a bound on combined predicate cost, and it carries the same confound round 24 retracted for `paused_rows`.** `wants_paused_rows` returns true for `AllGates` as well as `PausedRows`, so `all_gates` seeds the PAUSED ballast too: it *scans* 20 000 rows like `double_backlog` but *sorts* only 10 000, because the anti-join is a `WHERE` predicate and runs before the `ORDER BY`. Comparing the two charges the row for every predicate while crediting it with half the sort. The direction matters and makes the error worse than a wash: a smaller sort is cheaper, so this entry concluded that the +28% that comparison yields was a "floor" on the combined cost rather than a bound. **Round 35 retracted that too** — see the round-35 entry below: naming a direction is itself a bound in that direction, and the 10 000-row sort saving cannot simply be added back, because the scenarios also differ in post-filter population and can reach different plans. Both places the claim appeared are rewritten: the concluding paragraph and the `all_gates` bullet. Fixing it also surfaced a sound result the page already had but had buried — `rate_limited`, `circuit_breaker_set`, `build_policy` and `concurrency_key` all seed exactly the 10 000 claimable rows `baseline` does, so their deltas are population-matched and stand as published, and `concurrency_key` at **+644%** on an identical population contradicts the "predicates are a rounding error" conclusion independently of the `all_gates` confound. The page now says what is defensible: depth dominates (~15x from 10k to 20k rows), one predicate is separately expensive at this depth (`concurrency_key`, ~7.4x), and the combined cost of all of them is not something these scenarios bound in either direction. New `the_all_gates_delta_is_not_published_as_a_predicate_bound` guards the retraction and also requires the *direction* of the bias to be stated, so the claim cannot be deleted while leaving the +28% in the table for a reader to misread the same way. **(R) The benchmark's report-only database awaits had no wall-clock ceiling.** `server_version` (the report header) and `explain_section` connected, seeded and ran `EXPLAIN` with no deadline, so a remote server that accepted provisioning and then stopped answering would hang the process on a path that takes no measurement at all — bypassing the `HARVEST_BENCH_SCENARIO_SECS` ceiling the page advertises. Same class as the scenario-path bounds added in rounds 19-21; these are the corners that produce only prose and so were easy to overlook. Both wrapped in the existing `with_setup_deadline`. New `every_bench_database_await_is_bounded` asserts every `db::connect` / `db::seed` / `db::explain_claim` / `db::server_version` call in the bench sits inside a deadline wrapper, so the next report-only path added cannot quietly reintroduce it. **(S) The overview docs overclaimed predicate coverage.** The harness states plainly that it attributes **five** predicates and names five more (capability labels #382, queue pauses #619, `schedule_to_close` #378, worker sessions #606, sticky routing #235) that are evaluated on every claim but left on their cheapest null/empty path, so they are not measured. `README.md` and `docs/getting-started/README.md` both said the page reports what *each* accreted predicate costs, so a reader evaluating one of the five omitted features could mistake its cheapest path for a measured production cost.
