  (`20260723000000_harvest_retry_chain_index`) adds a partial index on
  `retry_of_exec_id`: routing moves the successor lookup onto the hot path of every
  mutating operator endpoint, and the costly case is the *miss* (proving a `FAILED`
  run has no successor), which without an index is a full sequential scan of the hub
  table — measured ~63 ms parallel seq scan vs ~0.03 ms index scan on 500k rows. It
  mirrors `idx_harvest_wfx_continued_from`, the structurally identical successor-link
  index for the continue-as-new chain (#701). No column added, no data rewritten.

  **Refuted the issue's motivating premise.** The issue worried about a window
  "between attempt 1 sealing `FAILED` and attempt 2 being claimed" with no running
  execution. Verified in `worker.rs` that the successor row is INSERTed in the *same
  transaction* that seals the predecessor `FAILED` and appends
  `WorkflowRetryScheduled`, so an external reader either sees the predecessor still
  live or sees it `FAILED` with its successor already present. **There is no
  row-existence gap** — only a window with no *claimed task*. That collapsed the
  "needs design" concern: signals need no synthetic buffering layer and no rejection
  window, because "deliver on the next attempt" falls out of routing plus the
  engine's existing claim-time signal ingest.

  **Core (`execution.rs`).** New `resolve_live_attempt` / `resolve_live_attempt_id`
  (walk while `FAILED` and a successor exists; a strict no-op for every non-`FAILED`
  row and for a `FAILED` run that is the chain's final outcome, so post-mortem
  operations still target it), `RETRY_CHAIN_MAX_DEPTH` (256) bounding both the walk
  and the re-drive count, the pure `redrive_target` decision helper, and the routed
  `cancel_live_attempt` / `terminate_live_attempt`.

  **Race handling — re-drive only when the act provably did not take effect.**
  A blanket "re-resolve after every op and redo" design was rejected: re-driving a
  *delivered* signal would double-deliver it. So signal/update/cancel re-drive only
  on an `Err` (a rejected insert is rolled back; `admit_update_event` verifies
  `RUNNING` under the same `FOR UPDATE` lock it inserts under, so a re-driven admit
  cannot double-admit); terminate and resume additionally re-drive on an *idempotent
  no-op against a `FAILED` row* — the only available signal that the chain advanced (a
  no-op against any other terminal state is the final answer); and a **keyed** signal
  additionally re-drives on a dedup that reported "not delivered", because a keyed
  insert short-circuits on the unique-index conflict *before* the state check and can
  therefore report success against a row that has since sealed `FAILED`, swallowing a
  re-send the live attempt still needs. Every re-driven shape provably queued nothing,
  so none can double-deliver. Exhausting the walk depth is logged (`tracing::warn!`)
  rather than silently returning a possibly-stale attempt as if it were live, and the
  successor lookup carries a deterministic `ORDER BY` tie-break so the walk is total
  and stable across the two resolutions of a re-drive. The loop terminates
  because each re-drive strictly descends the chain and an unchanged target ends it,
  which is also what stops a genuine error (unknown id, exhausted chain) from being
  retried forever.

  **Signals — "deliver on the next attempt", with the whole mailbox forwarded.** New
  `signal::send_signal_to_live_attempt` (returning `RoutedSignalDelivery { target,
  delivered }`), its already-resolved-target sibling `send_signal_from_resolved`, and
  `signal::forward_signals_to_retry_attempt`. The retry transaction in `worker.rs`
  now moves **every** `harvest_signals` row from the predecessor to the successor and
  resets `consumed` to `false`. Forwarding the *unconsumed* rows is obvious (a signal
  never ingested into any history is not reflected anywhere, so leaving it behind
  strands it against a sealed row forever). Forwarding the **consumed** ones is the
  less obvious half and is required: `consumed = true` means "already ingested into
  *that attempt's* history", and a retry starts from a completely fresh, empty history
  and re-executes every step from zero — so a signal the failed attempt observed is
  one the retry must observe again, or a workflow that replays back to its
  `wait_for_signal` blocks forever on a signal its caller was already told had landed
  (and has no reason to re-send). The failed attempt's own `SignalReceived` events
  stay in its history, so the audit record is unaffected. This deliberately diverges
  from the narrower reassignment `continue_as_new` performs (unconsumed only) — a
  continue-as-new is *voluntary* and carries what it needs in the successor's input,
  whereas a retry carries nothing forward at all. **#521 idempotency keys keep their
  `(workflow_exec_id, idempotency_key)` scope**, and because a forwarded row takes its
  key with it, an at-least-once re-send of an already-delivered key now dedupes
  against the **live attempt** rather than being swallowed by a sealed predecessor.

  **Known limitation — an admitted-but-unresolved update is not carried across a
  retry.** Unlike signals (a table), an update lives in the attempt's *history* as an
  `UpdateAdmitted` event, and a retry starts from an empty history. An update admitted
  onto attempt *N* that *N* fails before resolving is lost; re-submit it against the
  logical handle. Carrying admitted updates across the boundary needs a durable
  pending-update record outside the event log and is tracked separately.

  **Cancel also satisfies "prevent a queued retry from starting"** by two mechanisms
  already in the engine: a retry whose start delay has not elapsed has its
  still-delayed `PENDING` workflow task deleted by the cancel, and a retry whose task
  is already claimable is sealed `CANCELLED` before it can commit any non-cancelled
  terminal (both `update_workflow_execution_completed` and `_failed` filter
  `state = 'RUNNING'`, and the body observes `ctx.is_cancelled()` from line 1).
  Terminate fails **every** open (`PENDING`+`RUNNING`) task row of the attempt it
  seals.

  **`result_snapshot()` follows the chain** — matching what `result_snapshot_with_wait`
  and the HTTP `/result` route already did; the core handle was the outlier and was
  internally incoherent with its own waiting sibling.

  **Pause and resume route too** (`pause_live_attempt` / `resume_live_attempt`).
  Pause is the *reversible* containment lever `docs/runbooks/contain-runaway-execution.md`
  tells operators to reach for first, and `pause_workflow_execution` accepts only a
  `RUNNING`/`PAUSED` row — so unrouted it returned `409 … is already terminal (FAILED)`
  on a retried run, leaving an operator holding the logical handle only the destructive
  levers and inverting the containment ladder. Resume is an idempotent success no-op
  against a non-paused row, so unrouted it would report success while the paused live
  attempt stayed parked.

  **Surfaces.** Applied consistently to the core `WorkflowHandle`
  (`cancel`/`terminate`/ the in-process query and update paths /`result_snapshot`), to
  `TypedWorkflowHandle` — including `result_snapshot`, whose typed
  `error_type`/`error_details`/`non_retryable` are now loaded from the execution the
  snapshot was actually read from (via the new `WorkflowHandle::result_snapshot_resolved`),
  so a routed snapshot can never mix an outer run's `error` with an inner attempt's
  typed metadata — to the `#[signal]`-generated typed client stubs (both
  `signal_{name}` and `signal_{name}_idempotent`), and to the HTTP routes
  `POST /workflows/{id}/signal/{name}` (and its `by-id` sibling), `/cancel`,
  `/terminate`, `/pause`, `/resume`, `GET|POST /workflows/{id}/query/{name}`,
  `POST /workflows/{id}/update/{name}`, and
  `GET /workflows/{id}/update/{update_id}/result` — the paired read for a
  `wait=admitted` admission, whose `202` carries only the `update_id`, so an unrouted
  read would 404 forever against the addressed predecessor.
  `hydrate_ctx_for_query` and `admit_update` resolve the live attempt before
  replaying / admitting; the plugin's duplicated chain walker
  (`load_execution_following_retries`) was consolidated onto the core resolver.

  **Deliberately NOT routed, and documented as such:** reset (#148), erase-payloads
  (#495), legal-hold (#747), triage (#814), the per-activity `retry-now`/`fail-now`
  (#516/#765), and the DLQ replay/redrive routes each act on the **recorded artifact**
  of one attempt rather than steering the live run. `POST /workflows/{id}/rerun` (#777)
  takes the opposite policy and *rejects* a chain predecessor outright, which is
  deliberate — re-run mints a brand-new logical run from an attempt's inputs, so
  silently re-aiming it would change which inputs the new run gets. An erase /
  legal-hold spanning a whole retry chain is a genuine (GDPR-relevant) gap, tracked
  separately rather than smuggled into this change.

  **Describe is deliberately NOT routed.** `GET /workflows/{id}`, history export, the
  timeline, the stack, the awaitables, the per-execution logs, the event stream,
  `/diagnose`, the registered `/queries` listing, and the DLQ are specific-`exec_id`
  reads and must keep reporting the addressed row so an operator can inspect exactly
  the attempt that failed — pinned by a test.

  **Audit fidelity.** A routed cancel / terminate / pause / resume / signal now writes
  its **success** audit row keyed on the execution actually mutated, not the addressed
  id, so an auditor asking "who terminated attempt 3?" finds the row. The failure path
  keeps the addressed id (nothing was mutated), and the addressed id stays
  reconstructible either way because the `retry_of_exec_id` chain is durable.

  **Observability.** `POST /workflows/{id}/signal/{signal_name}` reports an additive
  `routed_execution_id` **only when** the addressed id differed from the attempt the
  signal landed on (`skip_serializing_if`), so a non-retried run's response is
  byte-for-byte unchanged. Registered in `management_api_response_fields()` and
  `docs/api-contract.json` for both the exec-id and by-id signal routes.

  **Docs.** New `docs/logical-handle.md` (the full contract: resolution rule, the
  no-row-gap proof, per-operation semantics, the describe carve-out, the race/re-drive
  rules, and the invariants), cross-linked from the signal-delivery section of
  `docs/management-api.md`.

  **Tests, TDD RED→GREEN.** New core suite
  `autumn-harvest/tests/integration/retry_chain_routing_tests.rs` (15 tests, real
  `Worker`-driven two-attempt chain fixture): cancel / terminate / signal / update /
  pause+resume routed to the live attempt, the same via the `WorkflowHandle` surface
  (`handle_cancel_*`, `handle_terminate_*`), `cancel_removes_a_queued_retrys_delayed_task`
  (AC2's "prevent a queued retry from starting" against a genuinely *delayed*
  `PENDING` task, using a 1-hour backoff so the retry has not started),
  `cancelled_chain_never_spawns_a_further_attempt`, keyed-signal dedupe on the routed
  attempt, whole-mailbox forwarding + re-arm, the worker-wiring guard
  (`the_worker_forwards_the_mailbox_when_it_schedules_a_retry`, which fails if the
  `worker.rs` call site is deleted), and the two resolver no-op/walk guards. New
  plugin HTTP suite `autumn-harvest-plugin/tests/retry_chain_routing_integration.rs`
  (9 tests): signal (+`routed_execution_id` present/omitted), cancel, terminate,
  pause+resume, `GET`/`POST` query, update, the paired update-**result** read, and the
  describe-unchanged guard. `typed_workflow_failure_tests` pins AC4's mixed-source
  guarantee (a routed `result_snapshot` must load `error_type`/`error_details`/
  `non_retryable` from the execution it was READ FROM, never the addressed id).
  RED was verified **behaviourally** by neutering `resolve_live_attempt` with an
  early return: 11/15 core tests fail, and the 4 that still pass are exactly the
  chain-independent controls (the fixture sanity check, the no-chain no-op guard, and
  the two mailbox-forwarding tests, which exercise the worker/helper rather than
  resolution). Both suites registered in `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt` and
  executed green against a real local Postgres 16.

  **Post-review hardening (Codex round 1, two P2s):** (1) **The update-result read now
  searches the chain, not just the live attempt.** An `update_id` is minted per
  admission and therefore lives on exactly *one* attempt, so resolving
  `GET /workflows/{id}/update/{update_id}/result` straight to the live attempt made a
  result that *had already resolved* on attempt *N* permanently inaccessible once *N*
  failed and *N+1* started — the durable `UpdateAdmitted`/`UpdateCompleted` pair stays
  on *N* while *N+1* replays an empty history, so the read 404'd forever. The route now
  walks the chain and returns the attempt whose history actually carries the admission,
  deepest first (the live attempt is the common case, and a workflow that never retried
  has a one-element chain — exactly the single history load this read always performed).
  The `wait=completed` admit path is unaffected: it already polls the attempt it
  admitted onto. The narrower known limitation stands and is re-scoped in the docs — an
  admitted-but-*unresolved* update still does not survive a retry, because nothing will
  ever run it. New `update_result_route_finds_a_result_left_on_an_earlier_attempt`
  (plugin suite, now 10 tests). (2) **A retry chain deeper than the walk bound now fails
  closed.** `RETRY_CHAIN_MAX_DEPTH` (256) is a defensive backstop, not an enforced
  invariant — `RetryPolicy` takes an arbitrary `u32` `max_attempts` and the builder's
  `max_workflow_attempts` ceiling is optional — so exhausting the walk previously
  `warn!`ed and returned the deepest row reached, which may itself be `FAILED` with a
  live successor beyond the bound: every routed signal / cancel / terminate / query /
  update / result would then silently target a stale attempt, the exact bug this
  contract exists to fix. `resolve_live_attempt` now returns `HarvestError::Config`
  (and logs `tracing::error!`) instead. The walk was refactored into a shared
  `walk_retry_chain` (returning every attempt in walk order) with `resolve_live_attempt`
  taking its last element and the new `retry_chain_ids` feeding fix (1) — zero extra row
  loads, since the walk already had to load each intermediate row to read its `state`.
  New `a_chain_deeper_than_the_walk_bound_fails_closed` (core suite, now 16 tests) seeds
  a chain of `RETRY_CHAIN_MAX_DEPTH + 2` links whose deepest attempt is genuinely
  `RUNNING`, so the pre-fix behaviour is falsified directly.

  **Inherited-lint heal (unrelated to #843, separate commit).** The CI runner's clippy
  moved to 1.98.0, which added `clippy::map_or_identity` and widened
  `clippy::missing_const_for_fn`; seven pre-existing violations in `timeout.rs` (3) and
  `det_check.rs` (4) — neither file touched by this PR — turned the shared `Lint` job red
  on every branch. Healed in place (`map_or(x, |d| d)` → `unwrap_or(x)`; four helpers
  made `const fn`), following the repo's existing inherited-lint-heal precedent. A second
  1.98 lint, `clippy::result_large_err`, then fired on nine more pre-existing sites —
  `api.rs` (`probe_committed_uws_replay`, `prepare_queue_pause_targets`,
  `parse_pause_request`, `prepare_activity_pause_targets`, `parse_activity_pause_request`,
  `prepare_activity_pause_targets_checked`), `ui.rs` (`find_schedule_row`), and, behind
  the `mcp` feature, `mcp_tools.rs` (`load_owned_execution`, `resolve_if_chained`) — none
  of them touched by this PR (verified against `origin/trunk-dev`). All nine are the
  plugin's pervasive `Result<T, axum::response::Response>` early-return idiom, and the
  128-byte `Err` is `axum::response::Response` itself, so the lint's suggested remedy
  (boxing) would mean deref churn at every `?` site in inherited code for no runtime
  benefit. Healed with a per-function `#[allow(clippy::result_large_err)]`, matching the
  three such allows that already exist in `api.rs` for exactly this idiom. The two
  `mcp_tools.rs` sites are only reachable under `--features mcp`, so they surface on the
  dedicated `Clippy autumn-harvest-plugin (mcp feature)` CI step rather than the default
  one — the full per-feature sweep is what caught them. A third 1.98 lint,
  `clippy::unused_async_trait_impl` (a new sibling of `clippy::unused_async`), fired on
  `ActivityContext::check_cancellation` in `context.rs` — also untouched by this PR — but
  only via the `autumn-harvest-cli` / `autumn-harvest-sqlite` steps, which build
  `autumn-harvest` with `default-features = false`: without `db` the body has no `.await`.
  That function already carried `#[cfg_attr(not(feature = "db"), allow(clippy::unused_async))]`
  for exactly this reason; because 1.98 introduced a *separately named* lint, the existing
  allow no longer covered it, so the `cfg_attr` was extended to name both. The lint's own
  suggestion (drop `async`, return `impl Future`) was rejected: it would change the
  signature of a public inherent method to silence a lint that is only reachable in a
  feature configuration where the `async` is genuinely vestigial. Fixing those three
  unblocked the `Lint` job far enough to reach its two docs-guard steps, which surfaced a
  fourth failure in `docs/rnd/sqlite-feasibility.md`: its `skip-locked` reach cell read 13
  modules where the tree has 15 (identical on `origin/trunk-dev`, so also inherited) and
  its derived `**Totals:**` line disagreed with the report's own inventory table — both
  corrected, and the one prose sentence that re-hardcoded the same count was rewritten to
  defer to the table, matching the policy the document already states for that figure
  ("kept current by CI, not this prose"). The same guard's migration count **is** this
  PR's own drift — `20260723000000_harvest_retry_chain_index` takes the live count 86 →
  87 — and was bumped accordingly.
- **R&D** (implemented): Time-travel replay debugger for recorded workflow histories — see issue #949. Gives an engineer the answer the existing replay surfaces stop short of: not *"does this history diverge?"* but ***"where exactly, and why?"***. Two entry points over one shared `ReplayTrace` type — the library `autumn_harvest::debugger` (behind a new `debugger` Cargo feature, which implies `testing`) and the local CLI `harvest debug`. **Read-only by construction (AC5): no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no engine-runtime change, no activity execution, no database access.** Zero core-engine edits were needed — every primitive the design required (`WorkflowContext::for_replay_canary_with_state`, `executor::drive_query_replay_async`, `drain_commands`, `take_nd_details`, `take_deferred_nd_error`, `replay_position`, and the `with_*` builders) was already `pub`.

  **Mechanism — prefix replay, blessed by AC2's own wording.** Step `k` is a *fresh* replay of `events[0..=k]`; "backward" is re-run-forward, exactly as the AC describes ("replay is deterministic, so 'backward' is re-run-forward"). The load-bearing insight is that a clean replay emits **zero** replay-significant commands — commands are only emitted at the live frontier — so a prefix replay yields precisely *"what does this code do next, given history so far"*, which is both the per-step frontier command batch and the ideal diff signal. Two supporting choices: **canary, not strict** replay (`for_replay_canary_with_state` sets `strict_replay` **and** `canary_mode`, so `strict_replay_no_match_is_divergence()` still catches a *mid-prefix* divergence while allowing frontier command emission — a prefix genuinely *is* an in-flight execution parked at its frontier); and **`drive_query_replay_async`** (issue #612) rather than `drive_workflow`, because the latter's 100 ms `SUSPENSION_TIMEOUT` would cost `N × 100 ms` (100 s for a 1k-event history) whereas the former detects suspension instantly via a per-poll command delta. Since that driver deliberately discards the handler's `Ok`/`Err`, non-determinism is read back through `ctx.take_nd_details()` / `take_deferred_nd_error()`.

  **AC1 — the snapshot.** `DebugStep` carries, after each consumed event: the event index and type, the pending `WorkflowCommand`s, the **open awaitables** (kind, name, id, and — as the AC explicitly requires — the `opened_at` **event index that opened them**), resolved **version-gate** values (`version:` markers) and **patch gates** (`patch:` markers, issue #687), recorded **side effects** and **markers** verbatim, the resolved payload, the signal name, and any recorded divergence. `AwaitableKind` is reused from `awaitables.rs` as the shared vocabulary, but the projection is debugger-owned: `awaitables::project_awaitables` requires timestamped `(DateTime<Utc>, WorkflowEvent)` rows that a `HistorySnapshot` does not carry, and its `Awaitable` has no `opened_at` index at all.

  **Handler-free vs handler-backed split.** Everything except pending commands derives from history alone in a single **O(N)** fold (`ReplayTrace::from_history`); only commands need registered workflow code (`ReplayDebugger::trace_snapshot` / `trace_json`). This split is what makes the CLI viable at all: the shipped `harvest` binary is statically linked and **cannot register an application's `#[workflow]` handlers** — the same constraint `harvest-replay` already states. So the CLI covers stepping, breakpoints and inspection plus the *two fixture histories* arm of AC3, while the library covers per-step commands and the *two code registrations* arm. Both produce the same `ReplayTrace`, so a session that starts in the CLI graduates to the library without reshaping anything; the capability split is documented as a table in the CLI module doc and in `docs/replay-debugger.md`.

  **AC2 — the driver.** `harvest debug replay <HISTORY>` with `--step N`, four breakpoint forms (`--break-at-event-type` / `--break-at-index` / `--break-at-activity` / `--break-at-signal`, declared mutually exclusive at the clap layer so a breakpoint never silently loses to another), `--max-steps N`, `--format text|json`, and `--tui` for an interactive stepper (`n`/`p`/`g`/`G` to move, `d` to jump to the next divergence — which requires a handler-backed trace, so in the handler-free CLI it reports that in the footer rather than sitting inert — `q` to quit; `--step`/`--break-*` seed the opening cursor; the terminal is restored even on error). JSON mode always emits the **whole** trace — silently emitting a focused partial document would be a trap for a `jq` pipeline.

  **AC3 — diff mode.** `diff_traces(left, right)` walks steps in order and reports the **first** difference only, because one root cause routinely produces dozens of downstream differences and reporting them all would bury the actionable one. `harvest debug diff <LEFT> <RIGHT>` exits **`1`** on divergence, mirroring `diff(1)`'s "differences found", so it drops straight into a CI pipeline. The **#614 boundary is stated in the module doc**, in `docs/replay-debugger.md`, and in the cross-tool tables of `docs/replay-verify.md` / `docs/replay-drift-gate.md`: #614 is a one-shot server-side verdict on one live run; this is the interactive local tool you reach for *after* it says "yes, diverging".

  **Display vs identity separation (a real bug caught by the corpus).** `CommandSnapshot` carries **both** a short, truncatable `summary` (for terminals) and an exact, never-truncated `payload: Option<Value>` (used for diffing). The first cut folded the input into the summary and truncated it, so the *"changed activity input"* corpus scenario reported its first divergence at step 3 instead of step 2 (the input difference was invisible until strict verification fired mid-history). Truncating into the compared field would silently hide a divergence deep in a large payload — on a divergence-finding tool, the worst possible failure mode.

  **History-fact diffing + per-run identity normalization (the second arm of AC3).** A handler-free trace emits *no* commands, so a command-only comparison could not see two **fixture histories** differing at all — `harvest debug diff` was structurally incapable of finding anything, a gap the new CLI tests caught. `diff_traces` now compares the history-derived facts first (via `DiffKind::HistoryFacts { field }`), ordered deliberately: history facts → commands → outcome (if the two *recordings* already differ, comparing "what did the code do next" across them is apples to oranges). Because two *independent recordings* of the same scenario necessarily differ on freshly-minted per-run values, the comparison **normalizes them out**: activity/child execution UUIDs, and the recorded values of the non-deterministic side-effect kinds (`Now`/`Uuid`/`Random`, issue #384) — normalized once, coherently, so the individual field checks cannot drift apart. Everything semantically meaningful is still compared, in two layers (see the Codex round 1 paragraph below): **curated projections** first, because they yield the legible field name the report prints (event type, signal name, awaitable kind/name/`opened_at`, version and patch gates, marker names and details, and the values of `Custom` side effects — application data, not engine identity), then **`event_facts`** as the exhaustive completeness backstop. This cannot hide a code-caused divergence — in the two-registrations arm both sides replay byte-identical events, so the normalized fields are equal by construction and the divergence surfaces through `commands`; in the two-histories arm a change that matters (renamed/reordered activity, different input, new marker, changed version gate) moves a field that *is* compared. `history_fact_diff` **exhaustively destructures** `DebugStep`, so adding a field without classifying it as history-derived or code-derived is a compile error rather than a silent false "clean".

  **Gates at a truncated frontier (documented semantic).** Since a step replays `events[0..=k]`, an intermediate step models an execution *parked at that truncated frontier* — so a `ctx.patched(...)` (#687) or `ctx.version(...)` gate reached there is, correctly, **newly** patched. A correctly-gated build therefore legitimately differs from an ungated one at intermediate steps while still replaying the *full* recorded history perfectly. The two questions need two checks, both documented and both asserted in the example: *"where do these builds first differ?"* → `diff_traces(...).divergence`; *"does this build replay this history cleanly?"* → no step has `divergence.is_some()`.

  **Cost, bounded honestly.** Building a full trace is `N` replays and therefore **O(N²)** — fine for the interactive histories this is for (tens to low hundreds of events), and deliberately not how the CI gates work (they replay each history once). `--max-steps` / `ReplayDebugger::max_steps` caps it, and `ReplayTrace::truncated` reports the cap so a partial view is never mistaken for a complete one. `DEFAULT_MAX_STEPS = 500`, `DEFAULT_STEP_TIMEOUT = 5s`.

  **AC4 — exported histories.** Input is the `HistorySnapshot` JSON round-trip format (`harvest history export`), so a production history is debugged on a laptop with zero database access. Payload-codec and offload-envelope fields **display as their envelopes** when no codec or store is configured, rather than erroring.

  **Success metric — met.** `divergence_corpus_identifies_the_first_divergent_step_in_every_scenario` runs a **13-scenario** corpus (≥10 required) spanning the `NonDeterminismKind` classes the issue names, and identifies the exact first divergent step index in **13/13**: reordered commands, inserted activity at the front, renamed activity mid-history, changed activity input, changed target queue, activity→timer, activity→child-workflow, dropped trailing activity, `SideEffectDrift` (inserted `ctx.new_uuid()`), inserted version gate, count-mismatch fan-out (2→3), signal-wait→activity, and a fan-out whose *second* slot's input changed. That last one is load-bearing: the corpus asserts the **command index** as well as the step index (the metric names the divergent *command*), and it is the one scenario whose expected command index is **not** 0 — so a stub hardcoding `command_index: 0` fails it.

  **AC6 — docs and example.** New `docs/replay-debugger.md`: the cross-tool comparison table (vs `replay-verify` / the replay-drift gate / #614), the two-arms capability table, and a six-step worked walkthrough that takes a new user from an exported history to an identified root cause — overview → breakpoint → interactive stepper → **diff old vs new build** (which pinpoints `fraud_check` inserted ahead of an already-recorded `charge_card` with no gate) → gate the change → confirm clean. Cross-linked from `docs/replay-verify.md` and `docs/replay-drift-gate.md`. Runnable companion `autumn-harvest/examples/replay_debugger.rs` (`required-features = ["debugger"]`) prints that exact walkthrough and carries four self-verifying tests, including the "ungated build does **not** replay cleanly" control that proves the clean-replay assertion measures something.

  **Tests.** 53 core tests in `autumn-harvest/tests/integration/debugger_tests.rs` (handler-free projection, `trace_snapshot`, breakpoints, diff, the 13-scenario corpus, the fixture-vs-fixture normalization contract, the three `DiffKind` variants the corpus cannot organically reach — `CommandCount` / `Outcome` / `Divergence` — and the robustness guards: a spinning workflow times out rather than hanging, a panicking workflow is contained, `max_steps: 0` clamps to one step, a redacted export is refused, and a **structural** AC5 guard that scans `debugger.rs`'s own source for any persistence symbol); 2 unit tests in `debugger.rs` — one pinning the `version:`/`patch:` marker prefixes against the engine's own `replay::{version,patch}_marker_name` builders, so a rename there cannot silently reclassify every gate as an ordinary marker; 8 clap-layer tests in `autumn-harvest-cli/src/lib.rs` (defaults, every flag, each breakpoint alone, and all three mutual-exclusion rejections); 43 black-box CLI tests in `autumn-harvest-cli/tests/integration/debug_cli.rs` (breakpoint/focus resolution, every `render_step_detail` section, `run_replay`/`run_diff` end to end, every error path's exit code, JSON-mode wholeness, the redaction warning, activity-breakpoint precision against a name prefix and against a queue name, plus a guard on the fixture itself so an id-reuse regression cannot silently weaken every open-awaitable assertion); 6 pure `StepperState` unit tests in `debug_tui.rs`; and 5 example tests. Registered in `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt` as one sorted `allos` row (`testing,debugger`), so it runs on every OS with no DB, plus a dedicated CI step for the example's tests.

  **Post-review hardening.** Three parallel review agents (replay-semantics, API/CLI design, and test-quality/AC-evidence) produced one **P1** and several P2s, all fixed: (1) **the debugger was strictly weaker than canary replay** — the canary/strict runners apply `ctx.history_has_unconsumed_events()` *after* the handler returns, and omitting that check meant a build that **dropped an activity** (or did nothing at all) replayed 100% "clean", the exact class the tool exists to catch; now gated on `ReachedTerminal`, using only already-`pub` API so AC5 still holds, with `a_build_that_completes_early_does_not_replay_cleanly` as the falsifying control. (2) **`command_payload` had a `_ => None` catch-all**, collapsing `Complete` / `Fail` / `RecordUpdateResult` / `CancelRaceLosers` / `RecordLog` onto equal snapshots — two genuinely different commands diffing as identical, on a divergence-finding tool; it is now exhaustive (no `_` arm), so an added `WorkflowCommand` variant is a compile error rather than a silently hidden divergence. (3) `record_deferred_nd` populates **both** nd slots, so the original lazy `.or_else()` chain never reached the informative message and **every `SideEffectDrift` reported `<unknown>`/`<unknown>`** — the headline case in the issue's own success metric. (4) Eight missing awaitable arms (`ExternalSignal*` / `ExternalCancel*` / `ActivityAwaitingExternal`) left external-workflow operations invisible in the open-awaitable column. (5) **AC1's signal waits were unimplemented** behind a misleadingly-named test; a `WaitForSignal` command now synthesizes an `AwaitableKind::Signal` — and, because that is *code-derived*, it is excluded from `history_fact_diff` so a code difference is never misreported as "the recorded histories differ". (6) The docs' export recipe handed the tool a **redacted** history (`harvest history export` defaults to `--payload-policy redacted`, rewriting payload fields in place), which fabricates a divergence at the first payload-bearing activity; fixed in the docs *and* enforced — `ReplayDebugger` refuses one (`DebugError::RedactedHistory`) and the CLI warns, mirroring the replay-drift gate's precedent. (7) A recorded divergence is **code**-derived, so it is now its own `DiffKind::Divergence` rather than being misfiled as `HistoryFacts { field: "divergence" }` — which would have told an operator "these are different recordings", a wrong and actively misleading diagnosis. (8) `DiffKind::TraceLength` gained a `capped` flag so diffing two traces built with different `--max-steps` is self-diagnosing instead of reporting a divergence that does not exist. (9) CLI ergonomics: `--tui` silently discarded `--step`/`--break-*` (they now seed the opening cursor), JSON mode swallowed a missed breakpoint's exit code, a capped trace rendered as a complete one, and the `d` key sat structurally inert in the handler-free CLI (it now says why). (10) Driving the built binary against a real fixture surfaced one more: `harvest debug diff` named the differing history field and then showed nothing about it — since the handler-free arm emits no commands, a fixture diff printed "the recorded histories differ (open_awaitables)" above two identical `<no pending commands>` lines. Both sides now render the **value** of the named field (`activity charge_card (opened at 3)` vs `activity fraud_check (opened at 3)`), which is the entire point of the CLI's primary diff path.

  **Post-review hardening, Codex round 1 (two P1s, both a *false clean* — the single worst failure mode for a divergence-finding tool).** (1) **A `CommandSnapshot` carried only a command's name and input**, so two builds that dispatched the *same* activity with *different scheduling options* compared **equal**. Codex reported it for `ScheduleExternalActivity` (a changed target queue or schedule-to-close deadline was invisible); verifying it against the real command enum showed the class was broader — `ScheduleActivity`'s per-call retry/start-to-close/schedule-to-start overrides and session pin, `RunLocalActivity`'s timeout and retry policy, `SpawnDetachedChildWorkflow`'s `ParentClosePolicy`, `SignalExternalWorkflow`'s idempotency key, and `ArmTimer`'s `for_await` were all dropped too. `command_payload` now carries **every semantic dispatch field**, and documents what it deliberately excludes and why (per-run ids, oneshot channels, `token`/`lock_seq`, and the retry-bookkeeping fields `already_scheduled` / `failed_attempts` / `last_error`, which are engine state rather than a dispatch decision). Note that exhaustiveness at the *variant* level — already enforced since the pre-PR review — is **not** sufficient: dropping a field *within* a matched variant produces exactly the same false clean, which is why the guard is now the field list, not the arm list. (2) **The fixture-vs-fixture diff missed semantic event fields**, because it compared a *curated* `resolved_payload` projection: a changed timer duration, a changed activity error, a changed child-workflow name — none moved a compared field, so two genuinely different recordings reported "no divergence" and exited `0`. Reproduced empirically before fixing (`harvest debug diff` on two histories differing only in `TimerStarted.duration_secs` → *"no divergence … agree across all 2 steps"*, exit 0). Fixed **structurally** rather than by extending the curated list, which would rot again the moment `WorkflowEvent` grows: `WorkflowEvent` **is** `Serialize` (it is the persisted wire type), so the new `DebugStep::event_facts` is the whole serialized event with only per-run identity normalized to `<per-run>` (top-level `data` keys that parse as a UUID, `timestamp`, and the recorded `value` of the non-deterministic `Now`/`Uuid`/`Random` side-effect kinds — normalization is deliberately confined to the *top level* of `data`, since business payloads nest under `input`/`output`/`payload`/`details` where a UUID is real data). It is therefore exhaustive by construction. It is checked **last**, after the curated projections, so the good diagnostics survive — `open_awaitables` still beats "the events differ" for a renamed activity — while the hole is closed; the same normalization keeps two independent recordings of one scenario diffing clean. The now-superseded `comparable_payload` helper was deleted, and the CLI renders `event_facts` per side so the operator sees *which part of the event moved*: `{"data":{"duration_secs":30,…}}` vs `{"data":{"duration_secs":60,…}}`. Plus two P2s: (3) a parked `ctx.mutex(k).acquire()` (issue #691) has no opening event — its waiter row lives in `harvest_mutex_waiters` and only the *grant* records `MutexGranted` — so, like a signal wait, it exists solely as a frontier `AcquireMutex` command; the awaitable synthesis now covers both, mapping command→kind exactly as `awaitables.rs` does, so a mutex-blocked run no longer displays as waiting on nothing (and, being code-derived, it is excluded from the history-fact comparison alongside `Signal`). (4) TUI setup rolled back incompletely: `enable_raw_mode()` succeeded and a subsequent `?` returned *past* the restore block, leaving the user's shell in raw mode — on a partially-supported terminal, a debugger that wrecks the shell it was launched from is worse than the bug being chased; each setup step now unwinds the ones before it. Regressions: a queue-only and a deadline-only external-activity change, and a start-to-close-only activity change (which additionally asserts the two summaries are *identical*, so the test is only meaningful while the payload is what carries the difference), a mutex park appearing among the open awaitables, and — at the CLI layer — an `event_facts` divergence rendering both normalized events.

  **Post-review hardening, Codex round 2 (three P1s, two P2s — plus one found by the regression written for them).** (1) **Sub-second timeouts collapsed through `as_secs()`** — the round-1 fix rendered `start_to_close` / `schedule_to_start` as whole seconds, so a local activity configured at 100 ms versus 900 ms produced *identical* snapshots and diffed clean. That is the round-1 false-clean class reintroduced by the round-1 fix, and it is not hypothetical: `execute_local_activity_raw_resolved` carries a full `Duration` precisely so "a subsecond OR sub-millisecond floor never truncates to `0`" (issue #620, itself a Codex finding). Durations now serialize at full precision via `Duration`'s own `Serialize` impl (`{secs, nanos}`). (2) **The prefix context dropped three snapshot replay inputs** — `parent_execution_id`, `execution_timeout` and `deadline_at` are execution-*row* columns that live in no `WorkflowEvent`, which is exactly why `HistorySnapshot` carries them; a workflow branching on `ctx.info().parent_execution_id` (#698), reading its deadline, or calling the deadline-sensitive `should_continue_as_new()` (#772) therefore emitted commands from defaults and **fabricated a divergence on a valid production export**. This is the same threading debt #772 paid down across eight rounds for the worker, replayer, export and query-hydration paths; the debugger is a new replay path and now threads them too, using only already-`pub` builders so AC5 still holds. (3) **Per-run normalization was value-based, not field-based** — "anything that parses as a UUID" also ate `ExternalSignalRequested { idempotency_key }`, a *caller-chosen* exactly-once key (#521) that is very commonly a UUID and is semantic: two histories differing only in it are genuinely different, and normalizing it reported them equal. Normalization now keys on a field-name allowlist derived mechanically from `WorkflowEvent`'s own declared types (a field qualifies exactly when its type is a UUID newtype), with the UUID parse retained *in addition* so `target`'s business-id form still compares verbatim. The allowlist is hand-written, so it is guarded by `engine_minted_id_fields_match_the_event_enum`, which re-derives the set from `event.rs` at test time and fails in **both** directions — a missing field is silently compared verbatim (noise), an extra one is silently normalized away (a false clean); verified falsifiable by deleting an entry. (4) **P2 — `ReplayDebugger::history_policy` was a dead setter**: stored, never read, so `should_continue_as_new()` always saw the default threshold and deadline fraction; now threaded via `with_history_policy`. (5) **P2 — `--tui` swallowed an unsatisfiable focus**: a missed breakpoint or out-of-range `--step` fell through to cursor `0` and exited `0` once the user quit, unlike the text and JSON paths — a breakpoint that reports a hit it never made is the one thing a breakpoint must never do. Both now error *before* the terminal enters raw mode (which is also what lets the regression run headless). (6) Writing the regression for (3) surfaced a **third instance of the same normalization gap, one layer up**: `awaitable_shapes` dropped the separate `id` field but kept the display `name`, and `ExternalSignalRequested` renders its name as `"{signal_name} -> {target}"` — so a per-run target exec id leaked back in and two independent recordings of one "signal a sibling" scenario diffed as different. Fixed by normalizing UUID-shaped tokens inside comparison labels; a business-id (`ExternalTarget::WorkflowId`) target contains no UUID and still compares verbatim. Regressions: a sub-second local-activity timeout change (asserting the two summaries are *identical*, so the payload is provably what carries it), a UUID-shaped `idempotency_key` change **and** its inverse control (engine-minted `signal_id`/`target` in the same event still diff clean, so the allowlist cannot be "fixed" by normalizing nothing), a workflow branching on `parent_execution_id`, and `--tui` rejecting both unsatisfiable focus forms.

  **Post-review hardening, Codex round 3 (two P1s — both false cleans again — and two P2s).** (1) **Two equally-capped traces reported as clean.** `diff_traces` only carried a `capped` flag on `DiffKind::TraceLength`, which fires on a *length* difference — so when both traces hit the same `max_steps` cap (500 by default) their step counts were equal, that check never ran, and a difference living past the cap was returned as `divergence: None`. `TraceDiff` also dropped both inputs' `truncated` flags, so a caller could not even tell. A CI gate reading `divergence.is_none()` was therefore treating an unexamined suffix as a pass. `TraceDiff` now carries `truncated`, and the verdict is `TraceDiff::is_clean()` — `divergence.is_none() && !truncated` — which is what callers must read. The CLI renders an explicit `INCONCLUSIVE` report (never the "no divergence" wording) and exits **`2`**, joining the CLI's existing "could not determine" gates (`WorkflowReachabilityGate`, `QueueCoverageGate`, `RestoreUndetermined`) so a script can distinguish it from `1` = "differences found" and `0` = "compared in full and agree". (2) **Two recordings of different workflow types reported as agreeing.** `diff_traces` compared only steps, and `workflow_name` is an execution-*row* column that appears in **no** `WorkflowEvent` — not even `WorkflowStarted`, which carries only `input` — so the round-1 `event_facts` backstop is structurally blind to it. Two histories of genuinely different workflows with similarly-shaped event arrays walked every step and exited `0`; reproduced end to end against the built binary (`onboarding` vs `checkout` → *"no divergence … agree across all 1 steps"*, exit 0). A new `DiffKind::WorkflowName { left, right }` is now checked **before** the step walk — the same "if the recordings are not of the same thing, comparing what the code did next is apples to oranges" principle as `step_diff_kind`'s history-facts-first ordering, one level up. `execution_id` is deliberately **not** compared alongside it (it differs on every pair of independent recordings, so comparing it would fabricate a divergence on every fixture diff — the same reason it is normalized out of `event_facts`), and that exclusion is pinned by its own test. (3) **P2 — a signal breakpoint could not match a multi-word name.** `WaitForSignal`'s summary *is* the signal name with no qualifier appended (unlike `ScheduleActivity`'s `"{name} -> {queue}"`), but the frontier match ran it through the whitespace-splitting `summary_names`, so `SignalName("order approved")` was unmatchable — at exactly the step a breakpoint exists for, since a waiting frontier has no `SignalReceived` yet to match instead. Now an exact comparison; the now-unused `summary_names` helper was deleted rather than left dead. (4) **P2 — `worker_id` was compared verbatim**, so two independent recordings diverged at the *first* `ActivityStarted`, burying every later semantic difference behind pure per-run noise. This is the round-2 allowlist's own derivation rule showing its seam: the rule was "a field qualifies when its type is a UUID newtype", but `worker_id` is `WorkerId`, a **`String`-backed** newtype whose *value* `WorkerRuntimeConfig::from` always mints as a fresh `Uuid::new_v4()` (there is no `WorkerConfig::with_worker_id`) — engine-minted by value, not by type. My round-2 doc comment asserting the opposite was simply wrong and is corrected. The dual guard already in place handles the remaining nuance for free: `WorkerRuntimeConfig::worker_id` is a `pub` field, so an embedder may set a stable label (`WorkerId::new("worker-eu-1")`), which does not parse as a UUID and therefore still compares verbatim — engine identity normalized, operator's choice preserved. The drift test's type list was renamed `ENGINE_MINTED_FIELD_TYPES` and gained `WorkerId`, with a comment recording that the type is a *proxy* for the real predicate and this is where the proxy needs an explicit entry. A full re-enumeration of every field type in the enum confirmed `worker_id` is the only such case (`TimerId` is the mirror image — `String`-backed but author-chosen, so correctly excluded). Regressions, each verified to fail against its own pre-fix code: equally-capped traces are inconclusive (plus an uncapped control, so the fix cannot have made every diff inconclusive), different workflow types diverge (plus a differing-`execution_id` control), a multi-word signal name matches a waiting frontier (plus a partial-name control, so the breakpoint stays precise), and a differing `worker_id` is *not* a divergence (plus an operator-label control, so adding it to the allowlist cannot have discarded a real difference — the round-2 `idempotency_key` mistake, one field over). At the CLI layer: a workflow-type diff exits non-zero and names both types, and a capped comparison renders `INCONCLUSIVE`.

  **CI portability fix.** `engine_minted_id_fields_match_the_event_enum` — the round-2 drift guard that re-derives the allowlist from `event.rs` at test time — scanned for the enum's closing brace with `find("\n}\n")`, which finds nothing on a checkout with CRLF line endings, so the test *panicked* on the Windows CI runner instead of asserting (3070 passed, 1 failed). The source is now normalized to LF immediately after reading, which fixes both the terminator scan and the per-line field scan on every OS. Verified by converting `event.rs` to CRLF in the working tree: the test passes with the fix and reproduces the exact Windows panic without it.

  **Post-review hardening, Codex round 4 (two P1s — a third and fourth false-clean shape — and one P2).** (1) **A build that never replayed successfully was certified as clean.** A step that timed out (a spinning workflow) or panicked reports `divergence: None` because the replay never *finished*, not because the build agreed — and the documented single-build check was a scan for `divergence.is_some()`, so both certified clean. Two builds failing the *same* way likewise compared equal at every field, so `diff_traces` returned no divergence: agreement between two non-answers. Fixed with the round-3 `TraceDiff::is_clean()` pattern applied one level down — `ReplayTrace::is_clean()` (`!truncated && no unsuccessful step && no divergent step`) is now the documented verdict, with `first_unsuccessful_step()` / `first_divergent_step()` reporting *which* reason applies, and `TraceDiff` gained `inconclusive_step` so a both-sides-failed comparison renders `INCONCLUSIVE` and exits **2** rather than `0`. The docs table, the example's three assertions, and the CLI all moved onto it. **The `NotReplayed` carve-out is load-bearing and nearly went the wrong way**: the first cut folded it in with timed-out/panicked, which broke the pre-existing round-3 control — a handler-free `ReplayTrace::from_history` projection is `NotReplayed` at every step, so AC3's compare-two-recordings mode (the CLI's *primary* diff path) would have exited `2` on every fixture diff. The two questions need opposite treatment and now have separate predicates: `is_clean()` on a single trace requires `replay_succeeded()` (a projection that ran no code has verified nothing), while `inconclusive_step` keys on `replay_failed()` only (a fixture-vs-fixture diff compares history-derived facts, which the two recordings determine completely, so it is genuinely conclusive). Both directions are pinned, including a named guard for the carve-out itself. (2) **The candidate build's payload caps were not applied during prefix replay.** `max_activity_input` / `max_signal_payload` / `max_workflow_input` and the #524 offload threshold live in no `WorkflowEvent` — the live worker supplies its own from `BuiltHarvest` — and the cap is consulted exactly at the `NoMatch` frontier, which is where *every* prefix step lands. Left at library defaults the debugger answered a question about a worker that does not exist, in both directions: a candidate that lowers a cap has an over-cap dispatch accepted here and rejected in production (false-GREEN), while a candidate configuring an offload threshold has a legitimate over-cap payload rejected here (false-RED, a fabricated early-return divergence on a valid export). This is the same threading debt rounds 2 and #798 paid down for `parent_execution_id` / `execution_timeout` / `deadline_at` / `history_policy`; `ReplayDebugger` gains `payload_caps()` and `payload_offload_threshold()` mirroring `WorkflowReplayer`'s, applied through already-`pub` `WorkflowContext` builders so AC5 still holds. `max_activity_result` is deliberately absent — the worker enforces it after an activity returns, never `WorkflowContext`, so it cannot affect a replay. (3) **P2 — event-less race-loser timers stayed open forever.** A signal-win of a signal-or-deadline race (#476), or a child-win of a child-or-deadline race (#779), tears its reserved deadline timer down through an **event-less** `CancelRaceLosers` row delete: no `TimerFired`, no `TimerCancelled` is ever recorded. Closing timers only on those two events left the loser in `open_awaitables` for every later step, rendering a resolved race as a run still waiting on a timer — the same bug `awaitables.rs` fixed for the history projection in #615. The accumulator now mirrors that cleanup and calls **the same** id parsers (promoted to `pub(crate)`), so a change to the reserved prefixes cannot drift the two projections apart; `close` returns the removed awaitable because a child terminal names only the `child_id` while its reserved timer encodes the workflow *name*. Regressions, each verified to fail against its own pre-fix code: a spinning and a panicking build are not clean (with a genuinely-clean control, so the tightening cannot have made every trace unclean), a handler-free projection is never clean, two identically-failing builds diff inconclusive (with a differently-failing control that must stay a real divergence, and a healthy-pair control), a signal-win and a child-win close their reserved timers (with two controls: an author's own `ctx.timer` and another signal's reserved arm must survive, and a late signal after a timer-win must not close an unrelated timer), and a lowered cap changes the replay outcome while an offload threshold exempts it. A self-review pass on the same commit closed two stragglers of the same class the round-4 fix itself left behind: the module-level doc still told readers to scan for `divergence.is_some()` — the exact hand-rolled check `is_clean()` replaces, so a reader following it would reintroduce the bug — and the CLI's `DiffKind::Divergence` arm labelled a side carrying no divergence as `replays cleanly` even when that side had **panicked**. The second is reachable because `step_diff_kind` compares `divergence` *before* `outcome`, so a crashed build that never got far enough to disagree with anything reaches that arm with `None` — describing it as clean in the very report a reviewer reads to decide is the worst possible wording on a divergence-finding tool. It now names the outcome instead (`no divergence observed, but the replay panicked (nothing was compared)`), pinned by `diff_render_never_calls_a_panicked_side_clean`, which drives two real registered builds to that exact shape and asserts the precondition (`left` divergence `None`, outcome `panicked`) so it cannot pass for the wrong reason. The `INCONCLUSIVE` wording was also corrected: it claimed a never-replayed step could trigger it, which the deliberate `NotReplayed` carve-out above rules out.

  **Codex round 5 — candidate configuration and per-run identity.** Six findings,
  all of the same two families the earlier rounds established: a *row column or
  build configuration that lives in no `WorkflowEvent`*, and *per-run identity
  compared verbatim*. Two P1s and four P2s, each fixed structurally and each
  proven falsifiable by reverting it in isolation.

  *Missing replay inputs (P1 ×2).* `ReplayDebugger` never registered the
  candidate's declarative `#[query]`/`#[update]` handlers, so a workflow body
  branching on `ctx.list_query_names()` ran every prefix against an **empty**
  registry and took the other branch — a divergence invented by the debugger on
  code nobody changed (false RED), or, for a candidate that added or removed a
  registration, a branch the promoted worker will take that replay never exercised
  (false GREEN). New `ReplayDebugger::queries` / `::updates` builders thread them
  through the executor's own `register_declarative_handlers`, which filters by
  workflow type off the context, so the debugger and the worker cannot drift and
  another workflow's same-named handler can never leak onto this one. Separately,
  a claim-check reference envelope (#524) was handed to the handler raw: new
  `ReplayDebugger::payload_offloader` inflates envelopes once at the snapshot
  boundary, so the display projection and every prefix replay share one inflated
  list. Optional by design — with no offloader configured an envelope displays as
  an envelope and is never an error, which is AC4's contract for an export
  debugged with no store to hand.

  *Per-run session identity (P2 ×2).* `ctx.create_session` (#606) mints a fresh
  `SessionId::new()` at the frontier, and that UUID reached the diff through
  **four** separate carriers: the `RecordMarker` command payload, the
  `ScheduleActivity.session_id` field, the reserved `__harvest_session_acquire` /
  `__harvest_session_release` activity's *input* (surfaced by the regression test,
  not by the review), and the recorded `MarkerSnapshot` in `history_fact_diff`.
  Each is now normalized to the shared `<per-run>` placeholder — discriminated by
  the **marker name** and the **reserved activity name**, never by "the value looks
  like a UUID", so an application marker or activity that legitimately carries a
  caller-chosen UUID still compares verbatim. Presence is preserved (`None` vs
  `Some` still differs), and `MarkerSnapshot::details` stays verbatim for *display*
  — the normalization lives on the comparison side, the same display/identity
  split as `CommandSnapshot`'s `summary` vs `payload`.

  *Breakpoint precision (P2).* `Breakpoint::ActivityName` tokenized the rendered
  command summary on `' ,()='`, so an activity named `"charge card"` was
  unmatchable at exactly the step the breakpoint is for — a dispatching frontier,
  where no `ActivityScheduled` event exists yet to match instead. Nothing restricts
  an activity name to one token. It now strips only the one known qualifier
  (`ScheduleActivity`'s `" -> {queue}"`), split from the right so a name that
  itself contains `" -> "` still resolves; `RunLocalActivity` and
  `ScheduleExternalActivity` summaries *are* the bare name. Sibling of the round-3
  signal-name fix, which only covered the signal path.

  *Terminal teardown (P2).* The TUI's normal-exit restore discarded
  `disable_raw_mode` / `LeaveAlternateScreen` / `show_cursor` failures, so a shell
  genuinely left in raw mode — the exact failure the panic hook and the setup
  rollback exist to prevent — exited `0` with no diagnostic. Every step is still
  attempted regardless of the previous one's outcome; the first failure is now
  reported as `CliError::DebugTerminal`, and the event loop's own error still wins
  (a teardown failure downstream of it is usually the same root cause).

  Tests: seven added to `debugger_tests.rs` (74 total) — a frontier session mint,
  two recordings differing only in their session marker (with an
  application-marker control proving the normalization is not itself a
  false-clean), a multi-word activity breakpoint plus a `" -> "`-containing name,
  a declarative-query branch with its empty-registry control, cross-workflow
  handler filtering, and offload inflation with its verbatim-envelope control.
- **R&D** (implemented): SQLite edge/local-first storage-trait feasibility report — see issue #966. Closes the one deliverable of the #966 spike that was never written. The spike's *code* half shipped and then some — the prototype (PR #1066) was productized into the `autumn-harvest-sqlite` companion crate (issue #1068, Phase 5.0; hardened in Phase 5.1) — but **Deliverable 1, the written storage-trait extraction report, did not exist**: `docs/rnd/` held only `wasm-activities-spike.md`, and `docs/sqlite-backend.md` is a *user guide* for the shipped crate, not the leadership decision doc the issue's success metric demands ("leadership can green-light or kill the direction **from the report alone**, without reading the spike code"). Resolved by the #543/#593/#609 reconciliation precedent: map the ACs onto the shipped prior art and close only the genuine gaps. **New `docs/rnd/sqlite-feasibility.md`**, framed honestly as a **retrospective decision record** (the report trails the productization it justifies — stated in the first paragraph rather than buried, and recorded as a process lesson: the written deliverable should gate the productization issue, not trail it).

  **Contents.** A one-page decision summary; a **coupling-mechanism table** — ten mechanisms, with reach measured live: `diesel` query layer 42 modules, `raw-sql` escape hatch 26, `row-lock` (blocking `.for_update()`) 15, `skip-locked` 13, `raw-pg-sql` (identified Postgres-only syntax) 18, `advisory-lock` (`pg_advisory_*`/`pg_try_advisory_*`) 9, `interval-sql` 8, `to_regclass` 6, `listen/notify` 4, `gen_random_uuid` 1 — plus the 83 Postgres-DDL migrations; the **exhaustive 43-row module-by-module inventory** (43 of the 93 core modules are coupled), every row classified **(a)** trivially trait-able **(8)** / **(b)** needs a semantic substitute **(17)** / **(c)** fundamentally Postgres-shaped, i.e. portable only by dropping a capability or reimplementing wholesale **(18)**; a costed sizing of the never-built `StorageBackend` seam and its **cost to the Postgres path**; the **test-suite portability** split (replay/event-schema → ported; single-execution lifecycle → ported with substitutes; multi-worker contention → *semantically void*, not merely hard; fleet/operational surfaces → out of model); the **go/no-go recommendation** (**go, as a separate companion crate — option ii — not a core trait**, which is what shipped) with its known capability losses; **hub-handoff scoping only** (edge `ExecutionId` shard semantics, `(workflow_name, workflow_id)` conflict rules for two disconnected nodes starting the same id, replay fidelity on ingest — with export-only archival named as the credible first cut); a paragraph on **other embedded backends** (libSQL/Turso as the strongest adjacent option, since it is file- and wire-compatible and could relax the single-writer constraint; DuckDB declined as an OLAP engine mismatched to high-frequency point writes; `sled` declined); and the **timebox** with the method note.

  **On the trait's cost to the Postgres path.** The report explicitly does **not** rest the rejection on performance. A coarse-grained generic seam (`<B: StorageBackend>`, the whole claim as one trait method) is monomorphised *and* keeps the fused claim CTE inside the Postgres impl, paying in viral type parameters rather than runtime — so the dispatch and query-decomposition objections are design-specific, not inherent, and the section says so with a two-design comparison rather than asserting the stronger claim. The costs that do carry are **code complexity** (an abstraction layer between the hardest bug class in this codebase — concurrency edges, lock ordering, claim-vs-scanner races — and the concrete SQL semantics every one of those fixes reasons about) and a **doubled test matrix** that is mostly meaningless skips, since the interesting suites (multi-worker contention, lock ordering, HA claim exclusivity) are not merely hard but *semantically void* against a single writer.

  **Load-bearing finding surfaced by the audit:** two modules (`store`, `concurrency`) reference `SKIP LOCKED` **only in comments** — they *consume* the claim invariant without issuing the SQL, so a `StorageBackend` trait derived mechanically from SQL call sites would have abstracted the invariant's *writers* and silently orphaned its *consumers* (compiles, passes unit tests, wrong under concurrency). That is the empirical reason the classification is a human judgement rather than a generated table.

  **Anti-rot enforcement (the TDD deliverable):** new no-DB guard suite `autumn-harvest/tests/integration/sqlite_feasibility_docs.rs` (**14 tests**) makes the report's "exhaustive … verifiable against a `grep`-level audit" claim **falsifiable** instead of aspirational. It re-derives the coupling inventory from `autumn-harvest/src/*.rs` at test runtime — never a hardcoded module list, which would rot identically to the prose — and asserts bidirectionally that every detected module is inventoried (failing with a **paste-ready table row** naming the new module and its mechanisms); that no row names a module that no longer exists or is no longer coupled; that every row carries an explicit (a)/(b)/(c) and names **exactly** the mechanisms grep finds for it (set equality, so a row can no more *over*-claim a mechanism — overstating the port — than under-claim one); that the per-mechanism counts, the (a)/(b)/(c) split, the 43/93 ratio and the migration count all match a live audit; that a module using raw SQL is **never** classified (a); that the cited cross-backend replay test exists; and that the zero-regression invariant is *structurally* true (core has no `rusqlite` and no `autumn-harvest-sqlite` dependency; the SQLite crate depends on core with `default-features = false`). Three further guards pin the suite's own machinery rather than the report: `markdown_section` is line-ending-agnostic and fence-aware, and the CI-step reader is bounded at the next `- name:` so a step key written *after* `run:` is still seen (YAML key order is not significant, so a guard that stopped at `run:` was evadable by reordering). Every guard is mutation-verified. Deliberately **not** guarded: the report's prose judgements (seam sizing, cost estimates, go/no-go reasoning) — those are argument, not fact, and freezing them would stop the document being revisable.

  **Detector design — precise, not generous.** An inventory padded with noise discredits the report as badly as one with holes, so every token was verified to produce zero Rust false positives before adoption. Rejected for that reason: bare `INTERVAL` (matches `DEFAULT_WORKER_POLL_INTERVAL`), bare `diesel` (matches the guardrail lint's own prose listing forbidden crates), bare `FOR UPDATE` (flags `mutex` for a doc comment reading "No `FOR UPDATE`" and for a unit test asserting `!expr.contains("FOR UPDATE")` — reporting a module as coupled because it documents that it is *not* — and cannot separate `FOR UPDATE OF t SKIP LOCKED` from a blocking lock), bare `LATERAL` (`queue` and `execution` both *document* it), bare `::` (every Rust path), `::uuid` (the re-exported `autumn_harvest::uuid`), `::interval` (`tokio::time::interval`), and blanket case-insensitive matching (would flag `diesel::sql_types::Text` as a Postgres cast). Four modules (`effective_config`, `guardrail`, `history_export`, `wasm_activities`) are false positives under a loose detector and are correctly excluded.

  **Closed rules vs open ones — the design lesson the review rounds produced.** `raw-pg-sql` *enumerates* Postgres-only syntax, and an enumeration of a dialect cannot terminate: four review rounds each found another construct it had missed (the blocking row lock; JSONB `#>>`/`LATERAL`/`~`; JSONB `@>`/`||` and `NOW()`; then every *lowercase* spelling of the casts already named). Each miss understated the port, always in the same direction, so **that count is documented as a lower bound**. `raw-sql` instead detects the *escape hatch* — any module reaching for `sql::<…>` or `sql_query` — and cannot miss a construct because it does not enumerate constructs. It is a weaker claim (raw SQL may be portable ANSI), so it is deliberately not evidence of coupling by itself; what it establishes is that such a module's portability **cannot be read off its Diesel usage**, which is exactly what class (a) asserts, and CI enforces the consequence. The split was then validated by the very next round: expanding the open rule more than doubled it (8 → 18 modules) and **changed not one classification**, because the closed rule had already caught all eighteen. The open rule keeps being wrong about *how much*; the closed rule has not been wrong about *which class* — and the class is the only thing a reader decides on. Two of the four misses were a third, distinct shape: not new constructs but the *same* construct spelled differently (`pg_advisory` does not substring-match `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock`; the cast list was UPPERCASE-only). Case and prefix are *bounded* dimensions, so those are closable exactly, and both are closed — the advisory prefix pair covers all ten Postgres advisory-lock functions, and casts are matched on cast *position* (`'::`, `)::`, neither valid Rust syntax) rather than by enumerating type names.

  **One literal AC gap closed:** Deliverable 2 words the first durability scenario as "one workflow with **two activities** and a retry", and the prototype only had the single-activity retry. New `two_activities_with_retry` puts the retry on the *first* activity, whose recovered output is the second's input, and asserts the value the second activity **received** (`(21*2)+1 == 43`, `double` twice, `increment` exactly once) — so a hand-off corrupted by the retry surfaces as a wrong input, not merely a wrong final answer. The report gains a scenario→test table so the "4/4" claim is checkable rather than asserted.

  **Docs + tests only — zero production code touched** (no core, no plugin, no `autumn-harvest-sqlite` source), so the "zero behavior/perf regression to the default Postgres build" invariant holds by construction; **no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no route/contract change, no replay/determinism impact.** Cross-links added from the SQLite crate README and `docs/sqlite-backend.md`. No CI manifest change was needed for the guard module — the pre-existing `allos autumn-harvest integration testing -` row runs the whole no-DB target on all three OSes, so it is wired by its `mod.rs` registration alone; a separate ungated `lint` step is what makes it also run on docs-only PRs, which CI's docs-only filter would otherwise skip entirely.
- **Tooling** — heal `trunk-dev` CI: two hand-rolled test INIT_SQL bundles were missing the issue #704 migration (issue #1074). **Test-code-only — no production code changed, no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration.**

  Issue #1074 tracks two named intermittent CI failures on `trunk-dev`
  (`nd_block_tests::nd_blocked_cycle_does_not_emit_signal_unhandled` and
  `integration_e2e::worker_completes_ten_child_fan_out_within_wall_clock_bound`).
  The first is already fixed (PR #1077) and confirmed passing in the most
  recent real CI run. The second is a documented timing-sensitive flake that
  issue #1074 explicitly scopes to "extend the existing #601 remediation if it
  re-flakes" — no new fix proposed there.

  Investigating the actual, currently-blocking `Test (ubuntu-latest)` failure
  on `trunk-dev` surfaced a **third, unrelated, fully deterministic regression**
  masking both named flakes behind a wall of ~40 failing tests, all sharing one
  distinct error: `column harvest_workflow_executions.history_bloat_warned_at
  does not exist`.

  **Root cause.** Issue #704 (PR landing migration
  `20260716000000_harvest_workflow_history_bloat_warn`, which adds
  `harvest_workflow_executions.history_bloat_warned_at`) updated the paved-path
  `full_migrations_sql()` bundle but missed **two of the four** allowlisted
  hand-rolled test `INIT_SQL`/`LEGACY_INIT_SQL` bundles
  (`autumn-harvest/tests/integration/migration_hygiene.rs`'s
  `ALLOWED_HANDROLLED_MIGRATION_INCLUDES`) that deliberately build their own
  subset of migrations instead of using the paved path:
  `autumn-harvest/tests/integration/integration_e2e.rs` (`INIT_SQL` — shared by
  `integration_e2e`, `chain_timeout_tests`, `child_timeout_tests`, and
  `dag_execution_timeout_tests`, all compiled into the same `integration` test
  binary — and `LEGACY_INIT_SQL`, used by the historical
  upgrade-path regression test) and
  `autumn-harvest-plugin/tests/timeline_integration.rs` (`INIT_SQL`). Because
  `WorkflowExecution::as_select()` selects the FULL row including every column
  defined in `schema.rs`, any full-row read-back against a database missing the
  new column fails immediately — which is exactly what every affected test
  does.

  **Fix.** Added the missing migration include to all three affected consts:
  `integration_e2e.rs`'s `INIT_SQL` gained
  `include_str!("../../migrations/20260716000000_harvest_workflow_history_bloat_warn/up.sql")`
  after the existing `20260715000000_harvest_queue_pause` include;
  `LEGACY_INIT_SQL` (which mixes `include_str!` for older migrations with raw
  hand-written `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS ...;` strings for
  newer single-column additions, matching its own established pattern) gained
  the matching `ALTER TABLE harvest_workflow_executions ADD COLUMN IF NOT
  EXISTS history_bloat_warned_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL;` line;
  `timeline_integration.rs`'s `INIT_SQL` gained the same migration include
  after its existing `20260710000002_harvest_workflow_continue_chain` include.
  The other two allowlisted hand-rolled bundles
  (`schedule_update_integration.rs`, `outbox_integration.rs`) are also stale
  but are compile-checked only — never executed in CI (documented via
  `ALLOWLIST_DEBT_REASON` in `ci_run_coverage.rs`) — so they are not currently
  causing any failure and were deliberately left untouched, out of scope.

  **Verification.** Since Docker/testcontainers is unavailable in the
  implementing sandbox, validation used a local Postgres 16 instance via the
  `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` escape hatch (honored by
  `setup_test_database_url_or_env()`/`setup_test_db()`, though not by every
  setup helper — e.g. `setup_test_database_url()` and
  `setup_blank_test_database_url()` always require Docker and could not be
  exercised locally). Against a **freshly migrated, genuinely isolated**
  database built from the fixed bundle (reconstructed via a script parsing the
  exact `include_str!`/literal sequence out of the Rust source and applying it
  with `psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`):

  - The full `chain_timeout_tests` module: **14/14 passed** (0 failures; 13 of
  these were on the CI failure list).
  - The full `integration_e2e::conflict_*` test cluster: **11/11 passed** (all
  11 were on the CI failure list).
  - `integration_e2e::drop_dag_runs_migration_copies_legacy_rows_to_workflow_executions`
  (a `setup_test_db()`-based test): passed.
  - `child_timeout_tests::child_completes_before_deadline_parent_gets_some`
  (representative of the 17 failing `child_timeout_tests`, run in complete
  isolation): passed. Running the whole `child_timeout_tests` module together
  against one persistent (non-ephemeral) local database reproduces spurious
  `UniqueViolation` failures from fixed-`workflow_id` collisions across

  CI gives each test its own throwaway container via testcontainers) and not
  a fix defect.
  - `timeline_integration.rs`'s reconstructed bundle applies cleanly to a fresh
  database (`history_bloat_warned_at` present, zero SQL errors); its
  `setup_database()` always requires Docker, so the compiled test target
  (verified to build cleanly for `autumn-harvest-plugin`) could not be
  executed locally.

  Two `dag_execution_timeout_tests` (`scheduler_tick_applies_fleet_wide_execution_timeout_ceiling_to_dag`,
  `scheduler_tick_buffered_drain_threads_dag_declared_execution_timeout`) still
  fail against the fixed bundle with an unrelated, pre-existing, fully
  deterministic error — `new row for relation "harvest_schedules" violates
  check constraint "harvest_schedules_kind_check"` — confirmed byte-identical
  to the error already present in the real CI log before this fix. This is a
  separate, out-of-scope bug (not a "loaded serial runner" timing flake, not
  caused by or related to the `history_bloat_warned_at` regression) and was
  deliberately left unfixed here.

  Gates run at the pinned CI toolchain (1.97.0): `cargo fmt --check` clean;
  `cargo clippy -p autumn-harvest --all-features --tests -- -D warnings` clean;
  `cargo clippy -p autumn-harvest-plugin --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean;
  `autumn-harvest-plugin`'s `timeline_integration` test target builds cleanly;
  all 9 `migration_hygiene` guard tests and all 13 `ci_run_coverage` guard
  tests pass unchanged (neither guard's allowlist/manifest was touched).

  **Follow-up: a real CI run on the fix above surfaced a second, genuine,
  test-only race.** `metrics_integration::history_bloat_counter_fires_even_when_the_same_decision_reaches_the_hard_cap`
  passed in the pre-fix baseline CI run but failed in the first real CI run
  after the fix above landed, with a NEW assertion failure:
  `history_bloat_warned_at must be stamped even when the SAME decision
  reaches the hard cap and terminally fails the execution`. This test is
  provably unrelated to the fix above (it builds its schema via the paved-path
  `full_migrations_sql()`, never the hand-rolled `INIT_SQL` consts touched
  here), so the intermittent failure was investigated on its own merits.

  **Root cause.** `fail_workflow_for_history_cap` (`worker.rs`) performs two
  SEPARATE, sequential commits within one decision cycle: state -> `FAILED`
  (via `move_workflow_to_dlq_for_history_cap`), then a trailing
  `history_bloat_warned_at` stamp (via `emit_history_bloat_warning_if_crossed`)
  — not one atomic transaction. The function's own extensive review-history
  comments document this ordering as a deliberate, narrow window (an
  at-least-once delivery tradeoff for the soft-threshold counter). The test's
  own comment already acknowledges `history_bloat_warned_at` becomes
  "still-eventually-true" and deliberately polls for `state == "FAILED"`
  instead (so a genuine regression — the mark never being set at all — times
  out clearly rather than looping on a condition that would never become
  true) — but then used that SAME pre-drain `wait_for_state` snapshot for the
  `history_bloat_warned_at` assertion, without accounting for the second
  commit possibly landing after the poll observed `FAILED`. Under CI load the
  gap between the two commits widens enough to make this reproducible.

  **Fix (first pass, since superseded).** The test already performs
  `worker.shutdown(); handle.await` immediately after `wait_for_state`
  returns. The first pass re-loaded the execution row right after that point
  instead of reusing the pre-drain `wait_for_state` snapshot, reasoning that
  `Worker::run`'s graceful-shutdown path (`drain_in_flight`) guarantees any
  in-flight decision cycle — including this trailing write — fully completes
  before `handle.await` resolves.

  **Hardening (automated Codex review on the PR).** That guarantee is not
  unconditional: `Worker::drain_in_flight` races the in-flight decision cycle
  against a **bounded** `shutdown_timeout` (hardcoded to `Duration::from_secs(2)`
  in this test file's `build_worker`) and returns *early* — logging only a
  `tracing::warn!` — if that timeout elapses first, meaning in-flight
  background work (including this test's trailing `history_bloat_warned_at`
  stamp) can still be running after `handle.await` unblocks. Under
  sufficient delay the identical race could therefore still manifest with the
  first-pass fix, just requiring a longer gap to trigger — exactly the "CI
  load" scenario under investigation. Verified independently by reading
  `drain_in_flight`'s source before acting on the review.

  **Fix (hardened).** Replaced the single point-in-time reload with a new
  `wait_for_history_bloat_warned` helper that polls the execution row with
  its **own** independent 15-second `tokio::time::timeout` (mirroring the
  existing `wait_for_nd_block`/`wait_for_state` pattern in this same file),
  entirely decoupled from the worker's internal 2-second drain deadline. This
  is robust to arbitrary delay in the trailing write up to the poll's own
  bound, while a genuine regression (the mark never being set at all) still
  fails clearly via the `.expect(...)` panic message rather than hanging.
  Test-only change, zero production code touched in either pass.

  **Verification.** Confirmed via GitHub Actions `rerun_failed_jobs` against
  the pre-fix commit that the failure is load-sensitive (not the baseline's
  one-off luck) before diagnosing; both passes were compile-checked
  (`cargo check -p autumn-harvest --features db --tests`, clean) and gated
  with `cargo fmt --check`/`rustfmt --check` (clean) and
  `cargo clippy -p autumn-harvest --all-features --tests -- -D warnings`
  (clean, after fixing an unrelated `doc_lazy_continuation` lint the new doc
  comment's rustfmt-wrapped `+` line-break tripped — CommonMark parses a
  leading `+ ` as a list marker) at the pinned CI toolchain. Docker/
