  testcontainers is unavailable in the implementing sandbox, so this specific
  test (which uses `setup_test_database_url()`, a Docker-only helper with no
  `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` escape hatch) could not be executed locally;
  the fix was validated by full production-code reading of
  `fail_workflow_for_history_cap`/`emit_history_bloat_warning_if_crossed`
  plus `Worker::run`'s shutdown/drain semantics, and confirmed by the real CI
  run this commit triggers.
- **Phase 3.x** (implemented): `ctx.race()`: follow-on durable command no longer nd-blocks when a loser is in-flight — see issue #1126. Fixed a `ctx.race()` (issue #600) replay bug where a durable command issued in the **same decision cycle** immediately after the race resolved — a plain activity, `ctx.mutex(k).acquire()` (issue #691), a timer, any positional `match_*` — would nd-block (issue #603) whenever a **losing activity branch was still in-flight** at resolution.

  **Root cause.** In the live resolving cycle, `HistoryMatcher::settle_terminal` consumes the winner branch's own `ActivityStarted`, but a losing branch that resolved as `ActivityInProgress` has its synthetic terminal (`ActivityFailed`, from the pending `CancelRaceLosers` bookkeeping command) appended **only at persist time** — invisible to this cycle's matcher. Its recorded `ActivityStarted` was therefore left unconsumed straddling the cursor, so the next positional `match_*` for the follow-on command diverged (`ActivityScheduleMismatch`) → nd-block → permanent wedge until a rollback. Later replays already worked (they take the `peek_u64_marker` branch, where the recorded winner marker + synthetic `ActivityFailed` reposition the cursor), so **only the live resolving cycle was broken**. Child-workflow races were unaffected (no separate started event to strand).

  **Fix (matcher-side only — append-only contract preserved).** New `HistoryMatcher::consume_race_loser_frontier(&[ActivityExecId], &[ExecutionId])`, called from `WorkflowContext::settle_race`'s **first winner-recording branch** (the `else` arm) after the loser id sets are collected and before the `CancelRaceLosers` push. It scans from the cursor, marks-consumed only the given losers' unconsumed `ActivityStarted` / `ActivityHeartbeat` (and, defensively — unreachable today, since a losing child's `ChildInProgress` already advances the cursor past its own `ChildWorkflowStarted`, per line above — a losing child's `ChildWorkflowStarted`), then advances the cursor past them. Scoped strictly to the resolving race's own loser ids, so it is safe under `futures::join!(race1, race2)` interleaving (a sibling race's events are untouched); no-op (early return) when there are no losers; never invoked on later replays (they take the `peek_u64_marker` branch). **No event mutation, no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no persist-ordering change, no migration** — histories recorded before the fix replay identically after it.

  **Behavior change.** The `ctx.race()`-then-`ctx.mutex(k).acquire()` (and race-then-any-durable-command) pattern in the **same** decision cycle now completes cleanly. This flips the `ctx.race()` interop **known limitation** documented on the `ctx.mutex` primitive (issue #691 / PR #1122) from a documented workaround to resolved behavior — the CLAUDE.md prose is updated accordingly.

  **Test evidence.**
  - **RED reproducer** (`context::tests::race_with_in_flight_activity_loser_does_not_wedge_a_follow_on_command`, no-DB): builds a history with a race, an in-flight loser `ActivityStarted`, and the winner's `ActivityCompleted`, resolves the race, then asserts the follow-on `match_activity("next_step")` returns `HistoryMatch::NoMatch` (fresh dispatch at the frontier) rather than diverging. Fails before the fix, passes after.
  - **Replay-neutrality fixtures** (`replayer_tests::replay_race_with_in_flight_loser_and_follow_on_activity_succeeds`, `..._race_ending_at_race_no_follow_on_succeeds`): a post-fix history with the follow-on and a pre-fix history ending at the race both `ReplaySucceeded` — proving histories recorded before the fix replay identically after it.
  - **DB end-to-end regression coverage** (`mutex_tests`, testcontainers/local-Postgres): a race with a fast winner + a genuinely in-flight slow loser (a shared-`AtomicBool` barrier makes the winner complete only after the loser's `ActivityStarted` is durably recorded) followed by (a) a plain activity and (b) `ctx.mutex(k).acquire()` + critical section. The oracle is the monotonic `harvest.workflow.nondeterministic_block` counter (a `RecordingMetrics` recorder): pre-fix each run **transiently** nd-blocks (counter ≥ 1) and only recovers once the loser eventually finishes — after which #603 clears `nd_blocked_at`, so a post-hoc column check alone cannot see the block; post-fix the follow-on lands cleanly and the counter stays `0`. Both tests assert `nd_block_count() == 0` and were confirmed to **fail** (`left: 1, right: 0`) with the fix reverted. This is the flagship flip of the #691 known limitation to regression coverage.
  - All 28 `race_` unit tests and 196 `replay::` matcher unit tests remain green.
- **Phase 3.53** (implemented): Open-awaitables diagnostic: why is this execution parked? — see issue #615. New read-only management route `GET /api/harvest/workflows/{id}/awaitables` (admin-gated, the eligibility endpoints' posture) answering "what is this run waiting on right now?" in one call — including the waits **no side table can see**: an awaited-but-unsent signal and an unresolved `ctx.await_condition` park, which exist only as parked commands inside the replayed coroutine. **Derivation:** the endpoint loads the recorded history once (`store::load_history_with_timestamps`), replays it read-only to the current suspension point via the #612 `drive_query_replay_async` machinery — with worker-fidelity context threading (`execution_timeout`/`deadline_at`/`parent_execution_id`/`workflow_name`/`workflow_id`/`context_headers` #481, declarative query/update handler registration, `registry.shared_state()`, `registry.history_policy()`) and real payload inflate/decode (offload #524 + runtime codecs #608, decoded plaintext feeding only the drive — the response is payload-free by construction) — then projects the drained pending-command buffer through the new pure, no-DB core module **`autumn-harvest/src/awaitables.rs`** (`project_awaitables`, `Awaitable{kind,name,id,since,deadline,local,external}`, `AwaitableKind`, `WaitSetInput`, `AwaitablesProjection`; re-used verbatim by the Vantage UI so the two can never disagree). **All six issue categories covered** — pending activities (regular/local/external-handoff), unfired durable timers, awaited-but-unfulfilled signals (by name), pending child workflows (name + child exec id), unresolved `await_condition` parks (inferred from a command-less non-transitioning suspension), and pending updates (`UpdateAdmitted` with no recorded terminal, minus any update resolved in the drained cycle) — plus two bonus kinds: parked mutex acquires (#691) and external-workflow await/signal/cancel operations (#757/#244/#492). Signal-or-deadline (#476) and child-or-deadline (#779) reserved race timers (`__signal_timeout:{seq}:{name}` / `__child_timeout:{seq}:{name}`) are **folded into their signal/child awaitable's `deadline`** rather than surfacing as internal timer rows (an orphan race arm degrades to a plain timer so nothing is silently dropped; duplicate same-name waiters — a `join!` of two `receive_signal_timeout("approval", …)` with distinct deadlines — are paired to their deadlines in command order via per-name FIFO queues so each open wait keeps its own deadline, rather than collapsing by name). Each awaitable carries `kind`, name/identifier, a `since` timestamp derived from its own recorded scheduling/arming event (falling back to the last-event suspension point for command-only waits), and a `deadline` where one applies — timer fire time, race deadline, external schedule-to-close (cleared on `ActivityExternalDeadlineExtended`, whose event carries no new value), and open activity awaitables enriched with the earliest of the task row's cross-retry `schedule_to_close_at` (#378) and the current attempt's `started_at + start_to_close`. **Degradation contract (a triage endpoint degrades, it never errors):** an unregistered handler (`handler_not_registered`), classic DAG (`classic_dag`), payload inflate/decode failure (`payload_decode_required`), replay timeout (`replay_timed_out`), contained handler panic (`replay_panicked`), a suspended drive carrying a deferred non-determinism error (`replay_diverged`), or a replay reaching `Poll::Ready` on a non-terminal row (`replay_reached_terminal`) falls back to a best-effort `wait_set = "history_only"` event-log scan with `wait_set_reason` naming why — activities/timers/children/updates/external awaits still report; awaited-unsent signals (except race-encoded ones) and condition parks are the documented blindness of that mode. In the fallback, the endpoint filters **dormant cancellable timer arms** (#768) — a `ctx.start_timer` arm records a `TimerStarted` but inserts no `harvest_timers` row and cannot fire until `await_fire()` — by threading the live unfired `harvest_timers` ids into the projection via `WaitSetInput::HistoryOnly { fire_eligible_timers }` (best-effort; a failed live-timer read passes `None` and reports every unclosed `TimerStarted` rather than failing the report), so an idle/debounce arm held while parked on a signal/activity is not misreported as a wait; the filter runs **inside** `project_history_only`, before the per-category cap, so a fire-eligible timer that sits beyond the cap position is never crowded out of the report by dormant arms ahead of it (issue #615 Codex P2). Fire-eligibility is unrepresentable in the replayed mode, which excludes dormant arms by construction (it matches only `ArmTimer { for_await: true }`). Duplicate same-type **child-or-deadline** waiters (#779) in the history-only fallback are paired to their reserved race deadlines via a **per-name FIFO** (`child_order` popping a per-name `VecDeque`), mirroring the replayed path so two concurrent `execute_child_workflow_timeout` waits on the same workflow type each keep their own deadline rather than collapsing to the last one (issue #615 Codex P2). Resolved races leave **no stale arms** in history-only mode: a signal-win/child-win tears its reserved deadline timer down via an event-less `CancelRaceLosers` row delete, so the history index closes the oldest open matching arm at the resolving `SignalReceived`/child terminal — selecting that arm by **recorded timer order** (`index.timer_order`), NOT by `TimerStarted` timestamp: two same-name race timers armed in one suspension are persisted in a single transaction and share a `DEFAULT NOW()` timestamp, so a timestamp tie-break (`min_by_key` over the arm's `since`) closes an arbitrary arm across the two `open_timer_arms` HashMap entries (HashMap iteration order is nondeterministic) and mispairs the surviving waiter's deadline; `timer_order` is the authoritative recorded order (insertion == command == increasing reserved seq) and is exactly what `project_history_only` walks to pair surviving arms with their deadlines, so the K-th race resolution FIFO-closes the K-th oldest reserved arm (issue #615 Codex P2). A timer-win's arm was already closed by its recorded `TimerFired`, making a late signal a no-op. Terminal executions return `200` with an EMPTY list, `wait_set = "terminal"`, and the state echoed; `SUSPENDED` is not a persisted state (the state CHECK constraint forbids it), so RUNNING/PAUSED coverage is the whole non-terminal surface. **Bounds:** first `category_cap` (50) entries per kind in recorded/command order, overflow surfaced via `truncated`/`truncated_kinds` (exactly-cap is not truncation; truncation is per-category). **Vantage UI:** the workflow-detail blocked-on panel is re-sourced from the same `build_awaitables_report` (admin-gated via `has_harvest_admin_access`, non-terminal runs only, best-effort with a history-only banner naming the reason), now rendering children, awaited-unsent signals, and condition parks. **CLI:** `harvest workflow awaitables <execution_id>`. **No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, zero writes** — proven by an integration test snapshotting the execution row, event count, and the task/timer/signal side tables before/after; shard-local read via `db_conn_for_execution` (O(1) from the exec id's embedded shard), no cross-shard fan-out; the pool connection is dropped before any payload fetch or user-code drive (the #612 pool-slot discipline, widened to offload I/O). Route registered across all five parallel registries (axum router, `management_api_routes()`, `management_api_response_fields()`, `docs/api-contract.json`, and `audit.rs` `CLASSIFIED_ROUTES` ReadOnly / `EXCLUDED_ROUTES` / `ALL_MUTATION_ROUTES` None) with pinned classification tests in both `audit.rs` and plugin `contract_regression.rs`, plus `security.rs::eris_unauthenticated_awaitables_is_blocked` (401). **Known approximations** (documented in the module docs, from the replay review): the #612 drive stops at the first command-emitting poll (a hand-rolled future that yields before awaiting could be absent), the Condition kind is an inference from a command-less, non-transitioning, **non-update-resolving** suspension (a drained `RecordUpdateResult` — an admitted update whose result is committing this cycle, its `UpdateCompleted` not yet persisted — is excluded from the inference so an in-flight update-result commit is not misread as a phantom `await_condition` park; pure-bookkeeping commands like `set_current_details` still precede a genuine cold park and are left alone; the deferred-ND check guards the divergence case), and an `ArmTimer { for_await: true }` deadline is anchored at its recorded ARM time while the true #768 deadline anchors at `await_fire`. **Success metric:** 10k-event projection measured at ~27 ms in debug builds (p95 < 1 s budget met with orders-of-magnitude headroom); 100% of the six categories covered by per-category tests. **Tests, TDD red→green→refactor + four-angle review (security / performance / replay-determinism / test-quality, all P1/P2 findings fixed):** 31 pure no-DB core tests in `tests/integration/awaitables_tests.rs` (falsifiable delta `unsent_signal_awaitable_is_named`, per-category coverage, race folds both modes, resolved-race regressions (including `history_only_resolved_signal_race_closes_oldest_arm_by_recorded_order` and `history_only_resolved_child_race_closes_oldest_arm_by_recorded_order` — two same-name waiters with tied `DEFAULT NOW()` arm timestamps and distinct deadlines, looped 1000× to defeat HashMap-seed nondeterminism, proving the resolving event FIFO-closes the K-th oldest arm and the survivor keeps its own deadline), synthetic command arms, truncation boundaries, `since`-provenance fixtures with trailing benign markers, 10k-event scale) + 3 inline module tests; 10 plugin DB/HTTP/UI tests in `autumn-harvest-plugin/tests/awaitables_integration.rs` (dual-mode `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL`/testcontainers, executed green against a real local Postgres 16; registered in `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt` for the Docker-backed Linux CI run) covering the falsifiable delta end-to-end, task-row deadline enrichment incl. earliest-of, child reporting, terminal echo, degrade reasons (`handler_not_registered`, `replay_reached_terminal`, `replay_panicked`, `replay_diverged`), zero-writes, stable error statuses (404/400), and the UI panel (signal + child rendering, terminal negative control); CLI mapping/coverage tests.
- **Phase 3.x** (implemented): Task-queue pause/resume: hold dispatch during a downstream outage — see issue #619. When a downstream dependency for a whole *class* of activities goes down (Stripe, SendGrid, the data warehouse), the operator's job-to-be-done is to **hold** the affected work, not fail it: freeze the queue, let the dependency recover, thaw, and have everything continue as if nothing happened. Before this, the closest primitives all did the wrong thing — the admission gate (#377/#618) halts new workflow *starts* while in-flight runs keep scheduling activities into the broken queue; the circuit breaker (#369) deliberately **fast-fails** dispatch, burning retry budget and pushing workflows down error branches; per-execution pause (#383/#609) holds *one* execution, useless when you know the queue but not the 50,000 executions behind it. **Gate the door, breaker the fast-fail, pause the hold.** New core module `queue_pause.rs` with the public surface `pause_queue`/`resume_queue`/`list_paused_queues`/`paused_queue_names`/`is_queue_paused`, the pure `validate_queue_name`/`queue_pause_suppresses_timeout`/`queue_pause_anti_join`, and the `PausedQueue`/`PauseOutcome`/`ResumeOutcome` records. **Enforcement is an anti-join, not a cache (the load-bearing design decision).** A pause is durable queue metadata enforced by a correlated `NOT EXISTS` conjunct on the claim path, exactly like the PAUSED-execution skip (#383) and the rate-limit gate (#332) — deliberately **not** an in-process cache like the admission gate's. AC1's "durable and re-applied before the worker pool begins claiming" is therefore true **by construction**: there is no boot window in which a held queue is briefly claimable, no refresh interval, no fleet-wide staleness, no global static, no fail-closed reasoning, and no write-through path that can diverge from the database. The cost is one primary-key probe per claim against a table bounded by the number of distinct queue names. Because the predicate is embedded verbatim in three separate SQL strings that do **not** share a table alias (the claim CTE and the oldest-pending-age scan are unaliased; the claimable-demand query uses `tq`), it is generated from one renderer `queue_pause_anti_join(outer_table)` with a drift-locked `const QUEUE_PAUSE_CLAIM_PREDICATE` for the allocation-free hot path — a paused queue a mirror query forgot about would report a phantom backlog and drive a false capacity alert during exactly the deliberate hold. **The outer column reference must be qualified**: inside the subquery an unqualified `queue_name` resolves against `harvest_queue_pauses` first, degenerating to `qp.queue_name = qp.queue_name` — always true, which would silently pause *every* queue the moment any one queue is paused. That was a real bug caught pre-commit and is now pinned by `anti_join_always_qualifies_the_outer_column`. **AC2/AC3 — hold, never fail.** The gate sits on the claim path only, so an already-`RUNNING` task finishes naturally (a pause holds *dispatch*, it does not abort in-flight work) and a held task simply stays `PENDING` — never `FAILED`, retried, or dead-lettered *because* the queue is paused. **AC4 — `schedule_to_start` suspended, `schedule_to_close` deliberately not.** The relative `schedule_to_start` timer is suspended for held tasks in **both** the scan predicate (`schedule_to_start_timeout_query` gains an unconditional queue carve-out) and the locked re-check inside `enforce_activity_timeout`, so neither a scan-vs-enforce race nor a pause landing mid-enforcement can time out held work. The **absolute** `schedule_to_close` deadline (#378) keeps ticking — issue #619 scopes crediting paused time back to an SLA deadline out explicitly, and that decision is pinned by its own test (`schedule_to_close_scan_does_not_exclude_paused_queues`). `Heartbeat`/`StartToClose` stay pause-blind (both apply only to `RUNNING` rows, mirroring the per-execution pause contract). **AC5 — the resume shift, the single most load-bearing query in the feature.** Without it, thawing a queue whose backlog waited past its `schedule_to_start` would immediately time out the *entire* held backlog — exactly the failure AC4/AC5 exist to prevent. `resume_queue` runs `scheduled_at += NOW() - GREATEST(scheduled_at, paused_at)` over the queue's **due** `PENDING` rows only: a task eligible *before* the pause is shifted by the full pause span (so 100 s of genuine pre-pause waiting is preserved), one that became eligible *mid-pause* collapses to `NOW()` (it was held from the instant it became due), and one *not yet due* (a retry backoff) is excluded entirely (it was never held, so its backoff must not be extended). The result is provably `<= NOW()` in every branch, so a thawed task is never pushed into the future — which would make it *un*claimable, the inverse of the intent. **AC9 — no new `WorkflowEvent` variant.** A pause writes nothing to `harvest_events`; replay of an execution that touched a paused queue is byte-identical to one that never paused. Pinned two ways: a source-level guard asserting `queue_pause.rs` never mentions `WorkflowEvent` or `harvest_events` outside its own doc prose, and a DB test that snapshots the raw event rows of an affected execution before the pause and compares them byte-for-byte after the resume. **Surfaces.** Migration `20260715000000_harvest_queue_pause` adds one table (`harvest_queue_pauses`, PK `queue_name`, plus `reason`/`paused_by`/`paused_at`/`scope_shard_id`). Three admin-gated management routes — `POST /admin/queues/{queue_name}/pause`, `POST /admin/queues/{queue_name}/resume`, `GET /admin/queues/paused` — registered across the axum router, all four plugin registries, `docs/api-contract.json`, and `autumn_harvest::audit` (`OP_QUEUE_PAUSE`/`OP_QUEUE_RESUME`/`TARGET_QUEUE`; the read route `ReadOnly` + `EXCLUDED_ROUTES`), with pins in **both** `audit.rs` and `contract_regression.rs` since the audit-side mutual cross-check stays green if a route is dropped from both lists. All three return `200 OK` (the hold is in effect the instant the row commits — there is no async application step, unlike `202`-returning `terminate`). Both mutations are **idempotent**: a repeat pause is a no-op that **preserves the original reason and operator** (a re-pause never rewrites the provenance of an existing hold), and resuming an unpaused queue is a success no-op so a retry after a lost response is safe. AC7's fleet-wide default is the absence of `shard_id`; supplying it scopes the hold to one shard, and the read endpoint merges per-shard rows into one entry with a `shards` array. **AC6 — audit + UI.** Both mutations write an audit row carrying the operator identity, operation, target queue, route, and source. The human-readable *reason* lives on the durable pause row (surfaced by the read API, the CLI, and the UI) rather than being duplicated into `error_summary`, which is failure-only across the entire codebase — this follows the #383 `OP_WORKFLOW_PAUSE` precedent exactly, and consistency with the sibling per-execution pause is what governs here. Because the pause row is deleted on resume, `ResumeOutcome` (and therefore the resume response, the CLI output, and the UI flash) **echoes back** `released_reason`/`released_paused_by` — the last moment the *why* is recoverable. The Vantage **Workers** page (the fleet page an operator lands on when investigating idle workers) grows a paused-queues banner listing each held queue with its reason, actor, `paused_at` and held-task count; per-shard rows are merged with held counts summed and the **earliest** `paused_at` winning (it is the one an operator reasons about), sorted by queue name so the banner is stable across refreshes. **Eligibility explainer coherence (#611).** `task_intrinsic_impediment_reasons` gained a `queue_paused` input that pushes `"queue_paused"` **first** — without it the explainer would report an *empty* (falsely "unimpeded") reason set for a held task during exactly the idle-worker triage it exists for. It is listed first because it is the operator's own deliberate action. **AC8 — gauge.** New `harvest.queue.paused` (`METRIC_QUEUE_PAUSED`, label `queue` only), `1` while a hold is in effect and `0` otherwise, sampled by `spawn_queue_pause_sampler` on the worker's poll interval across every shard of its `ShardedDbPool`. A read failure skips the whole tick so an outage never false-clears the gauge, and a queue that is no longer held is zero-filled rather than going stale. Wired through the three-touchpoint recipe (`telemetry.rs` const + no-op default + `metrics_rs_adapter` bridge) with the full anti-drift set: a dashboard panel in the "Queues & workers" row, the `harvest_queue_paused_too_long` alert rule (binary gauge → the **`for` duration is the threshold**, with a sharper `and harvest_queue_depth > 1000` variant so a hold on an idle queue stays quiet), a five-subsection runbook section, the ADR-0001 §7 catalogue, `docs/telemetry.md`, and the `dashboard_pack_docs`/`alert_pack_docs`/`metrics_coverage` registries. **CLI:** `harvest queue pause <q> --reason <why> [--shard-id N]` / `resume` / `list-paused` (aliases `list`, `status`); `--reason` is required at clap parse time (a hold with no stated cause is unauditable), and omitting `--shard-id` sends no field at all so the default stays fleet-wide. **Docs:** a `queue_paused` diagnosis in `docs/runbooks/triage-pending-tasks-idle-workers.md` calling out that a rising `harvest_queue_depth` while this gauge reads `1` is the hold working as designed — the single most common false capacity page during an outage freeze. **Tests, TDD red→green→refactor.** 7 pure unit tests in `queue_pause.rs` (incl. the const/renderer drift lock and the qualified-column regression guard) + 3 claim-query drift-lock tests in `queue.rs`; 20 tests in `tests/integration/queue_pause_tests.rs` (7 pure — claim + mirror queries carry the anti-join, the `schedule_to_start` scan excludes paused queues while the `schedule_to_close` scan pointedly does not, the timeout-suppression truth table, name validation, and the shift query never pushing `scheduled_at` past `NOW()`; 13 DB — hold-and-release, in-flight tasks not aborted, `schedule_to_start` suspended during and after, all three shift branches, idempotency, the read model, the gauge feed, and the two AC9 replay guards); 5 plugin HTTP tests in `queue_pause_integration.rs` (round trip with audit, idempotent resume, `400` validation, admin gate, and durability across a full API-state teardown — the "plugin restart" proxy, which passes with no re-application step precisely because the gate is a row); 2 no-DB admin-gate tests in `security.rs`; 4 UI banner tests; 14 CLI mapping/coverage tests; and the **success-metric** test `pause_holds_a_failing_backlog_and_every_task_succeeds_after_thaw` (`queue_pause_success_metric_tests.rs`), which drives a real worker through the whole story: downstream down → real attempts fail and burn retry budget (making the test falsifiable rather than trivially green on a queue that never ran anything) → operator pauses → hold across several poll cycles with **zero** further attempts claimed, zero `FAILED`, zero DLQ → downstream recovers → resume → **100%** of held workflows reach `COMPLETED` with an empty DLQ. All DB/HTTP suites were **executed** against a real local Postgres 16 (Docker is unavailable in the authoring sandbox), and all three suites are registered in `.github/ci/integration-suites.txt` for the Docker-backed Linux run. **Out of scope (per the issue):** per-execution pause (#609/#383), halting new workflow starts (#377/#618), fast-fail semantics (#369), schedule/cron pausing (#229), automatic health-driven pause, weighted multi-queue draining (#515), and crediting paused time back to `schedule_to_close` (#378) — this slice keeps the absolute SLA deadline ticking and suspends only the relative `schedule_to_start` timer. **Post-review hardening (three parallel review agents — correctness/concurrency, API surface/security, AC compliance — two findings reproduced empirically against Postgres 16).** (1) **P1, the enforcer's queue-pause re-check was not authoritative.** Its doc comment claimed parity with the execution-pause re-check, but that sibling works precisely because *both* sides lock the same execution row; `pause_queue` shares no row with `enforce_activity_timeout`, so the non-locking `is_queue_paused` read did not serialize — a reviewer reproduced a pause committing 38 ms into the enforcer's post-recheck write sequence and terminally `ScheduleToStart`-failing a task on the now-paused queue, violating AC2/AC3/AC4 during exactly the backing-up-backlog scenario the feature exists for. Fixed with a shared transaction-scoped advisory lock, `lock_queue_for_pause` (`pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(queue_name))`, mirroring the `concurrency_key`/`ctx.mutex` patterns), taken by `pause_queue`, `resume_queue`, and the enforcer before its re-check — and, in the enforcer, **only** on the `ScheduleToStart` path, so the far more common in-flight timeout paths never take it. Pinned by `a_pause_committed_after_the_scan_still_suppresses_the_timeout`, which holds the lock open across the enforcer's run. (2) **P2, a pause racing a resume returned 500 and left the queue live.** `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` does not lock the conflicting row, so a concurrent resume could delete it between the insert and the fallback `SELECT`, whose `get_result` then `?`-propagated `NotFound` — rolling the transaction back into an opaque 500 while the queue kept dispatching (reproduced). Collapsed to a single atomic `ON CONFLICT (queue_name) DO UPDATE SET queue_name = harvest_queue_pauses.queue_name RETURNING ..., (xmax = 0) AS newly_paused`: `DO UPDATE` takes the row lock, the no-op `SET` preserves the original provenance on a re-pause, and `xmax = 0` is the standard insert-vs-update discriminator. Pinned by `pause_racing_a_concurrent_resume_still_holds_the_queue`. (3) **P2, a partially-applied fleet-wide hold reported success.** If any shard succeeded the handler returned `200 {"ok": true}` with the detail buried in a `partial_failures` string — while writing its own audit row as `failed`. An operator would believe the hold was fleet-wide while the missed shards kept dispatching into the outage. Both mutations now return **`207 Multi-Status`** with `ok: false` and `status: "partial"`, reusing the read side's existing `complete`/`partial` vocabulary; a fully applied request keeps `200`/`ok: true`/`status: "complete"` and omits `partial_failures`. Re-issuing is safe (idempotent). (4) **P2, `queue_pause_target_pools` silently skipped router-known-but-poolless shards**, so mid a shard-add rollout a fleet-wide pause returned an *unqualified* success with no diagnostic at all — strictly worse than a partial failure. It now derives its target set from `shard_fanout::expected_shards` (the same helper the read path uses for exactly this reason) and reports an unreachable-but-known shard as a partial failure; naming such a shard explicitly is now a `503` rather than a misleading `400 "unknown shard_id"`. (5) **P2, rejected attempts were unaudited.** A malformed body, blank/oversized queue name, missing reason, or unroutable shard all returned without a trace — on a route whose whole purpose is a fleet-wide dispatch kill switch, the rejected-attempt trail is what an incident review needs. New `write_queue_pause_rejection_audit` writes a `STATUS_FAILED` row on every rejection path (symmetric with `fail_activity_now`'s malformed-id handling). (6) **P2, the operator `reason` bypassed the shared 500-char `truncate_operator_reason` cap** that every other durable operator reason on the router uses — it is stored, re-serialized on every read poll, and rendered into the Vantage Workers page, the very page an operator lands on during a queue-pause incident. Now capped at the API boundary. (7) **P3, the queue name was validated trimmed but stored untrimmed**, so `--queue "payments "` inserted a row matching no task and reported a successful hold (`newly_paused: true`, `held_task_count: 0`) on a queue that kept dispatching. `validate_queue_name` now *returns* the canonical trimmed name and every read and write uses it. Pinned by `a_padded_queue_name_still_holds_the_real_queue`, which asserts the *unpadded* queue is genuinely held. (8) **CI-breaking: `queue_pause_success_metric_tests.rs` was missing its `#![cfg(feature = "db")]` gate** while importing the `db`-gated `integration_e2e` helpers — an unresolved-import compile failure on all three OSes of the `--no-default-features` CI leg. Added. (9) The same suite was not hermetic on a shared `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` database (it scrubbed only `harvest_queue_pauses`), so a re-run inherited the previous run's `FAILED` rows and failed its own "zero tasks may transition to FAILED" assertion. It now scrubs every fixture it owns; CI's fresh testcontainer never needed this. (10) The `schedule_to_close`-keeps-ticking caveat was documented in code and the API contract but **absent from both operator runbooks**, which said a pause is "safe — nothing fails" — the one place an operator could lose work by trusting the runbook. Called out explicitly in both. **Coverage added for the gaps the AC audit named:** the AC7 multi-shard *write* path (a shard-scoped hold applies fully and reports its scope; a partially-applied fleet-wide hold is `207`; an unknown shard is `400` and audited), the AC4 locked-re-check race, the atomic-upsert race, name canonicalisation, rejected-attempt auditing, and the reason cap. **Clippy:** extracting the claim SQL into a shape-testable `const fn claim_task_query()` moved a 144-line string literal out of `claim_task`, which carried `#[allow(clippy::too_many_lines)]`; the allow moved with it.

  **Post-review hardening (Codex automated review, PR #1135) — three findings, all genuine, all fixed:**

  1. **P1 — a claim already in flight could beat the pause.** `claim_task` is a single autocommit statement, so under `READ COMMITTED` its whole CTE — including the pause anti-join — evaluates against **one snapshot taken at statement start**. A pause committing after that snapshot is invisible to it, so a claim already in flight when the operator paused still transitions its task to `RUNNING` and hands it to a worker that dispatches into the outage. The window is normally sub-millisecond but is unbounded in principle: the claim's rate-limit debit can block on a row lock held by a competing claim, and Postgres's `EvalPlanQual` re-check on unblock only re-evaluates conditions on the *locked row*, never a correlated subquery over another table. **Codex's literal suggestion — take the queue-scoped lock inside the claim path — was rejected**: it would serialize every claim for a queue against every other, defeating `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`'s parallel claiming for a feature that is inactive almost all of the time. Fixed instead with a post-claim authoritative re-check in a **fresh statement** (hence a fresh snapshot): new `queue_pause::release_claim_if_queue_paused`, one guarded `UPDATE` that returns the task to `PENDING` and **restores the `attempt`** the claim consumed (a hold must not burn retry budget — AC3), guarded on `state = 'RUNNING' AND worker_id = $2` so it can only ever undo *this* worker's own claim. Wired inside `claim_task` itself so the guarantee is a property of the primitive rather than of one caller; a released claim surfaces as `Ok(None)`, which both worker call sites already treat as "nothing to dispatch". Cost: one indexed primary-key probe per *successful* claim (never per empty poll). The contract becomes crisp: **a pause committed before the re-check's statement begins always wins**; one that commits after did not beat the claim, and AC2 explicitly allows an already-`RUNNING` task to finish naturally. The rate-limit token the claim debited is not refunded — the same safe-side, self-healing leak already documented for a lost claim in `claim_task` (it only ever under-dispatches). Tests: `a_pause_committed_mid_claim_still_holds_the_task` reproduces the race **deterministically end-to-end** by stalling the claim mid-statement on its rate-limit debit (the one part of the CTE that can block, since the candidate scan uses `SKIP LOCKED`) — hold the bucket row from another transaction, start the claim, commit the pause while it is parked, then release the bucket — plus `a_claim_that_beat_the_pause_is_released_with_its_attempt_restored`, the no-regression guard `an_ordinary_claim_is_not_released_when_the_queue_is_not_paused`, and a SQL-shape drift lock.

  2. **P2 — ABBA deadlock between the timeout enforcer and resume.** `enforce_activity_timeout` locked the execution row, then the task row, and only then took the queue advisory lock; `resume_queue` takes the advisory lock first and *then* row-locks every `PENDING` task on the queue via its `scheduled_at` shift. Reaching those locks concurrently, enforcement would hold a task row while waiting on the advisory lock and resume would hold the advisory lock while waiting on that task row — Postgres breaks the cycle by aborting one, failing either the timeout pass or the operator's resume request. Fixed by hoisting the `ScheduleToStart` queue-pause check to the **top** of the enforcement transaction, so both paths take advisory-then-rows; also cheaper, since a held task now bails before the row locks and the history load. The ordering convention is documented at both sites (matching the `harvest_external_tasks` task-row→execution-row note from issue #609). Test: `enforcer_takes_the_queue_lock_before_the_row_locks_no_abba` proves the ordering deterministically without provoking an actual deadlock — hold the advisory lock, start the enforcer so it blocks on it, then probe both row locks with `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` from a third connection and assert both are still free (mirrors the issue #779 `materializer_locks_execution_row_before_timers_no_abba` probe).

  3. **P2 — divergent per-shard pause provenance was silently discarded.** The list handler merged by queue name with `or_insert_with`, keeping whichever shard the fan-out reached first and dropping the others' reason/actor/scope while still listing every shard id. That state is produced by the feature's *own* idempotency rule: a re-pause deliberately preserves the **original** provenance, so a fleet-wide hold landing over a pre-existing shard-scoped hold leaves that shard telling a different story — and the `shard_id` parameter explicitly supports pausing one queue on two shards separately. Showing only one of them hands the operator a reason and scope that are not true for part of the fleet. Fixed with a pure, unit-tested `merge_paused_queue_rows`: the top-level summary is the **earliest** hold (a deterministic rule, and the same one the Vantage banner uses, so the two surfaces never disagree), `shards` carries each shard's own `{shard_id, reason, paused_by, paused_at, scope_shard_id, held_task_count}`, and `provenance_uniform` is a single field a script can gate on. Uniformity compares `(reason, paused_by, scope_shard_id)` and deliberately **not** `paused_at` — each shard stamps its own `NOW()`, so including it would report almost every healthy fleet-wide hold as divergent. `docs/api-contract.json` notes updated. Tests: 4 pure no-DB tests covering the uniform fleet-wide collapse, the divergent case (earliest-wins summary + per-shard preservation + `provenance_uniform: false`), distinct queues staying separate, and empty.

  **Post-review hardening, round 2 (Codex automated review of `26faefb`, PR #1135) — two findings, both genuine, both fixed:**

  4. **P2 — the pause response echoed the request's scope, not the effective one.** `pause_queue` is idempotent and deliberately preserves the **original** row on a re-pause, and the handler already echoed the preserved `reason`/`paused_by`/`paused_at` from that row — but it serialized `scope_shard_id` from the *request*. So re-pausing a hold scoped to shard 0 with a fleet-wide request (no `shard_id`) returned `newly_paused: false` and the original reason/actor/time alongside `scope_shard_id: null`, describing a hold that covers one shard as though it covered the fleet. That is precisely the mis-read that lets an operator believe an outage is contained when part of the fleet is still dispatching into it. The core is not at fault — `pause_queue`'s `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET queue_name = harvest_queue_pauses.queue_name RETURNING ... scope_shard_id` leaves the column untouched and returns the stored value, which its doc comment already documents as "the effective value (the original on a re-pause)". Fixed by serializing `effective.scope_shard_id` so the whole response describes one coherent row. `docs/api-contract.json`'s `idempotency` note now states the guarantee explicitly. The resume response was audited for the same class and carries no `scope_shard_id`, so it is unaffected. Test: `an_idempotent_repause_echoes_the_effective_scope_not_the_request` (RED-verified — it failed on exactly the `scope_shard_id` assertion before the fix).

  5. **P2 — the Vantage banner attributed a fleet-wide held total to one shard's story.** The finding is the UI-side twin of round 1's item 3: `merge_paused_queue_banner_rows` summed every shard's held tasks but labelled the total with only the earliest shard's reason and actor, giving an operator no indication that the displayed provenance applied to part of the fleet. Having just fixed the API to expose per-shard provenance and a `provenance_uniform` flag for exactly this supported case (two shards holding one queue with different reasons, whether via `shard_id` scoping or the idempotent re-pause), the banner had become the inconsistent surface — and it is the one an operator actually lands on during an idle-worker incident. Fixed by mirroring the API's merge rule exactly: the banner merge now takes `(shard_id, row)` pairs so the earliest-wins summary is tie-broken by shard id (deterministic, never fan-out-order dependent) and computes the same `provenance_uniform` over `(reason, paused_by, scope_shard_id)` — deliberately **not** `paused_at`, since each shard stamps its own `NOW()`. `PausedQueueBannerRow` gains `scope_shard_id` and `provenance_uniform`; the rendered banner gains a **Scope** column (`fleet-wide` or `shard N`) and, when a row's shards disagree, marks the reason and actor cells `(mixed across shards)` plus a summary count pointing at `GET /admin/queues/paused` for the per-shard detail. A uniform hold renders exactly as before apart from the new Scope column. Tests: `divergent_shard_provenance_is_flagged_and_visibly_marked` (asserts both the flag and the rendered marking) and `differing_paused_at_alone_does_not_flag_divergence` (the guard that keeps a healthy fleet-wide hold from being falsely marked, pinning the API/UI rule parity).

  **Post-review hardening, round 3 (Codex automated review of `4fabb85`, PR #1135) — two findings, both genuine, both fixed:**

  6. **P2 — a fleet-wide re-pause labelled a fleet-wide held total with one shard's story.** The mutation-response twin of round 1's item 3 (which fixed the *list* endpoint) and round 2's item 5 (which fixed the *Vantage banner*): with those two done, the pause **mutation** response had become the last surface still collapsing divergent provenance. `apply_pause_across_shards` summed `held_task_count` across every shard but kept only the **first successful** shard's `PauseOutcome` for the top-level `reason`/`paused_by`/`paused_at`/`scope_shard_id`. That state is produced by the feature's own idempotency rule — a re-pause preserves each shard's **original** provenance — so a fleet-wide request landing over pre-existing scoped holds legitimately leaves the shards disagreeing, and the response would then pair a fleet-wide total with shard 0's reason, actor, timestamp and scoped `scope_shard_id`, none of which are true for the rest of the fleet. Worse, "first successful" is fan-out-order dependent, so the same request could report different provenance on successive calls. Fixed by keeping every shard's outcome (`PauseApplication.per_shard: Vec<(i32, PauseOutcome)>`) and summarising with the pure, unit-tested `summarise_pause_provenance`: the top-level summary is the **earliest** hold tie-broken by shard id — the *same* rule `merge_paused_queue_rows` and the Vantage banner already use, so all three surfaces now agree by construction — `shards` carries each shard's own `{shard_id, newly_paused, reason, paused_by, paused_at, scope_shard_id, held_task_count}`, and `provenance_uniform` is a single field a script can gate on. Uniformity compares `(reason, paused_by, scope_shard_id)` and deliberately **not** `paused_at`, since each shard stamps its own `NOW()` — including it would flag almost every healthy fleet-wide hold as divergent. Both new fields registered in `management_api_response_fields()` and `docs/api-contract.json`. Tests: `pause_summary_is_earliest_and_keeps_every_shards_provenance` (RED-verified — reverting the summariser to first-success failed on the reason assertion, `left: "fleet-wide freeze"` vs `right: "shard-0 provider down"`), `pause_summary_is_uniform_when_only_paused_at_differs` (the guard pinning the `paused_at` exclusion), and `pause_summary_is_none_when_no_shard_applied`.

  7. **P2 — a fleet-wide resume permanently discarded every shard's released provenance but the first.** The same collapse on the resume path, and materially worse than item 6 because the resume **DELETES** the pause rows: whatever the response drops is gone for good, with no read endpoint left to recover it from. `apply_resume_across_shards` summed `released_task_count`, took the **max** `paused_duration_secs`, and kept the **first** released shard's `released_reason`/`released_paused_by` — so a fleet-wide resume over two independently-paused shards reported one incident's story next to another incident's duration, and silently destroyed the second. Fixed with the symmetric treatment: `ResumeApplication.per_shard: Vec<(i32, ResumeOutcome)>` plus a pure, unit-tested `summarise_resume_provenance` whose anchor is the **longest** hold (tie-broken by lowest shard id) — deliberately *not* "earliest", because `paused_duration_secs` already reports the longest hold, so anchoring the reason there makes the duration and the story it is paired with come from the same shard. `shards` carries every shard's own `{shard_id, newly_resumed, released_task_count, paused_duration_secs, released_reason, released_paused_by}` and `provenance_uniform` flags divergence over `(released_reason, released_paused_by)`; a shard that was never paused contributes null provenance and is ignored by the summary (so a mixed pause/no-op fleet resume is still reported uniform). Both new fields registered in `management_api_response_fields()` and `docs/api-contract.json`. Tests: `resume_summary_keeps_every_shards_released_provenance` (RED-verified — reverting to first-released failed with `left: Some("sendgrid down")` vs `right: Some("stripe outage")`), `resume_summary_ignores_shards_that_were_not_paused`, and `resume_summary_of_a_full_noop_is_uniform_and_empty`.

  **CI fix (first Docker-backed run of this branch) — `integration_e2e::INIT_SQL` was missing the queue-pause migration.** `Test (ubuntu-latest)` failed with 5 of ~93 suites red — `chain_timeout_tests` (3), `child_timeout_tests` (7), `integration_e2e` (52), `rate_limit_key` (1), `workflow_retry_tests` (2) — all with `Database("relation \"harvest_queue_pauses\" does not exist")` or the `Elapsed` timeout it causes downstream. Every `queue_pause_*` suite passed, which is what localised it: the failing suites are precisely the ones whose schema comes from `integration_e2e`'s hand-maintained `INIT_SQL` bundle (the other four reuse `crate::integration_e2e::setup_test_database_url_or_env`), and `claim_task`'s pause anti-join now references that table on **every** claim. This is the migration-drift class documented for #603/#1031/#1045: `INIT_SQL` is one of the four fixtures deliberately allowlisted off `full_migrations_sql()` (it omits the workflow-start-uniqueness migration on purpose), so it must be updated by hand. Fixed by adding `20260715000000_harvest_queue_pause` to the bundle. `LEGACY_INIT_SQL` is deliberately **not** updated — its test never claims (it exercises the historical start-path upgrade) and it passed; adding migrations there would defeat its purpose. **Why local runs missed it:** `setup_test_database_url_or_env` prefers `HARVEST_TEST_DATABASE_URL` and skips `INIT_SQL` entirely, so my pre-migrated shared local database always had the table; CI has no env URL and seeds a fresh testcontainer from the bundle alone. RED→GREEN was verified by reproducing CI's schema exactly — applying the pre-fix bundle's own bytes to a fresh database and running the real CI-failing test `integration_e2e::claim_task_returns_none_on_empty_queue`, which fails with the verbatim `relation "harvest_queue_pauses" does not exist` and passes against the post-fix bundle. **New guard so this cannot recur:** `init_sql_creates_every_table_the_claim_path_references` tokenises the live `queue::claim_task_query()` for `harvest_*` identifiers and asserts each appears in `INIT_SQL`. Deriving the table set from the real query means a future claim-path table is caught automatically with no second list to maintain, and it turns a ~13-minute Docker-only failure into a 0.18 s no-DB one (RED-verified: with the migration removed it fails naming exactly `["harvest_queue_pauses"]`).

  **Post-review hardening, round 5 (Codex automated review, three P2s on `cdbf0ad`).** (1) **A queue name carrying surrounding whitespace is now rejected, not trimmed.** `EnqueueParams` stores `queue_name` verbatim and the claim anti-join matches on exact equality, so `"payments "` and `"payments"` are two genuinely distinct, independently reachable queues — which makes *both* quieter options a lie: validating `name.trim()` while storing the raw string inserts a row matching no task (a reported hold on a queue that keeps dispatching), and the round-1 **trim** fix inserts a row for `"payments"`, silently holding a *different, valid* queue while the real one keeps dispatching, again reporting success. `validate_queue_name` now returns `HarvestError::Config` (a `400`) naming the problem, on both pause and resume. In the overwhelmingly common case a stray space is a copy-paste typo and the operator gets an actionable rejection instead of a false green; in the pathological case the queue really does carry whitespace it is not pausable through this API — an honest refusal, and strictly safer than a silent success against the wrong queue mid-incident. Normalising queue names at *creation* time is the alternative fix, but that reaches across every enqueue path and is out of scope. RED-verified: the new pure test `validate_queue_name_rejects_surrounding_whitespace` fails against the trim implementation, and the rewritten DB test `a_padded_queue_name_is_rejected_not_silently_retargeted` — which enqueues on **both** `q` and `"{q} "`, proves they are separate queues (holding `q` leaves the whitespace-named queue claimable), and asserts the padded form is refused without holding either — fails too. It replaces the round-1 test that asserted the trim behaviour.

  (2) **The operator's reason now reaches the durable audit row.** `harvest_queue_pauses` is its only other home and a resume `DELETE`s that row, so a post-incident review could see *who* paused a queue but never *why* — a hole in the AC6 audit contract. `harvest_audit_log` has no metadata/details column and adding one would touch all ~188 `NewAuditRecord` construction sites for a shared primitive (out of scope), so the reason is carried in the one free-text field the record already has, via the new pure `queue_pause_audit_context(reason, partial)`: labelled `reason: … | failures: …` so the two contributions stay distinguishable and `status` remains the outcome discriminator. `error_summary` is therefore non-`None` on a fully successful pause — deliberate, and the labelling keeps a context row from reading as a failure. On **resume** the same field records what was *released* (`resume_released_audit_reason`: `released hold by <actor>: <reason>`), since the resume deletes the only other copy. When independently-paused shards carried *different* holds it records **every** one of them rather than the longest plus a bare divergence marker — `released 2 holds (longest first); shards 0,2 by alice: stripe outage (held 900s); shard 1 by bob: pg failover (held 60s)` — because the per-shard array is written only to the transient HTTP response, so a marker alone would leave the other shards' *why* permanently unrecoverable. Holds are deduplicated by `(reason, operator)` (so the row grows with the number of distinct holds, not the shard count) and ordered longest-first, which keeps the row coherent with the response's top-level `released_reason`/`paused_duration_secs`; `ResumeProvenance::uniform()` is now *derived* from that grouping so the flag and the rendering cannot disagree. The #383 per-execution-pause precedent does **not** transfer: its pause metadata survives resume on the execution row, whereas this row is deleted. The reason is already bounded by `truncate_operator_reason` at the request boundary. Tests: `pause_audit_context_carries_the_reason_on_full_success`, `pause_audit_context_labels_reason_and_failures_separately`, `resume_audit_reason_records_the_released_hold`, `resume_audit_reason_preserves_every_released_hold`, `resume_audit_reason_renders_a_hold_with_no_operator`.

  (3) **Fleet-wide scope is now derived from real coverage, not stored intent.** A fleet-wide pause that only reached some shards persists `scope_shard_id = NULL` on the shards it reached and **no row at all** on the ones it missed, so the stored intent is byte-identical to a complete hold — while the missed shards keep dispatching into the very outage the operator is holding back. Both the list response and the Vantage banner rendered that as "fleet-wide" (and the one-row merge marked its provenance uniform). This is distinct from the round-3/round-4 provenance fixes: those handled *divergent stored rows*, this one handles *absent* rows. New shared pure classifier `queue_pause::classify_pause_coverage(holding_shards, scope_shard_ids, expected_shards) -> PauseCoverage` (`Fleet` / `PartialFleet` / `Shard`, with `label()` and `is_incomplete_fleet()`) lives in core beside `queue_pause_anti_join` and `queue_pause_suppresses_timeout` — the module that already owns the pure predicates the two surfaces must not drift on. It compares against the **expected** shard set (`shard_fanout::expected_shards`: every pool plus every shard the router knows about), not merely the inspected one, which is the safe direction — an unreachable shard may well still be dispatching, so it counts as expected-but-not-holding. `GET /admin/queues/paused` gains a nested `effective_scope` per entry (documented in the route description per the nested-field precedent; `scope_shard_id` is still reported verbatim as the recorded intent), and the banner's Scope cell renders the coverage label with a summary line telling the operator to re-issue a partially-applied pause. Tests: 2 pure core tests (`coverage_is_derived_from_shards_that_actually_hold_the_queue` covering all seven cases incl. the unreachable-shard safe side, `coverage_labels_are_distinct_and_flag_the_incomplete_case`), `effective_scope_reflects_real_coverage_not_stored_intent` (api), and `a_partially_applied_fleet_pause_is_not_rendered_as_fleet_wide` (ui, asserting both the label and the "still dispatching" banner text, plus that a complete hold is not marked partial), plus three DB/HTTP integration tests in `queue_pause_integration.rs` exercising the REAL fan-out the pure tests mock (`a_partially_applied_hold_reads_back_as_partial_fleet_not_fleet_wide` against a two-shard app whose shard 1 is unreachable, `a_complete_hold_reads_back_as_fleet_wide`, and `a_shard_scoped_hold_reads_back_as_shard_not_partial` -- the latter two proving the partial signal is not simply always-on, so an operator is never trained to ignore it) -- all RED-verified against an intent-only classifier.

  **Post-review hardening, round 6 (Codex automated review, one P1 + two P2s on `a2142de`).** (1) **P1 — a one-character typo in a queue-control body silently widened a scoped request to the whole fleet.** Serde ignores unknown fields by default, and `shard_id`'s *absence* is meaningful in this feature — it selects the fleet-wide default. So `{"shard": 1}` deserialized to `shard_id: None`, and on the **resume** route that released **every** shard's hold rather than the one named, returning `200` while dispatch resumed into exactly the outage the operator was riding out. The blast radius of a typo was the entire fleet, in the destructive direction. Fixed with `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` on both `PauseQueueRequest` and `ResumeQueueRequest`; because both bodies are parsed with `serde_json::from_slice` and the resulting error already flows through this route's audited `400` path, the fix is two attributes with no handler change and no `422`/`JsonRejection` detour (the `Result<Json<..>, JsonRejection>` treatment #771/#810 needed does not apply here). An empty resume body is still accepted — it never reaches the deserializer — so the fleet-wide default is unchanged. Tests: the pure `a_typo_in_a_queue_control_body_is_rejected_not_widened_to_fleet_wide` (the review's exact `{"shard": 1}` payload on both structs, plus every legitimate shape still parsing) and the end-to-end `a_typod_resume_field_is_rejected_and_the_hold_survives`, which holds a queue, sends the typo, and asserts the hold is **still in effect** afterwards, the rejection is audited, and the correctly-spelled `shard_id` release still succeeds so the guard is not over-broad. (2) **P2 — `queue_paused` lost its documented first position in the response an operator actually reads.** `task_intrinsic_impediment_reasons` pushes it first, but *both* eligibility merges collapse the per-task reason lists through a `HashSet` — destroying insertion order — and then call a plain `.sort()`, under which `concurrency_saturated` sorts **before** `queue_paused`. The helper's own doc comment and `docs/runbooks/harvest-alerts.md` both promise the operator sees the deliberate hold first, so the priority had to survive the merge rather than only the producer. Fixed with one shared pure `sort_reason_codes` (the hold leads, everything else alphabetical so the array stays stable across polls) called at **both** merge sites — the same single-source-of-truth shape as round 5's shared classifier, so the two sites cannot drift — plus a named `QUEUE_PAUSED_REASON_CODE` const so the producer and the comparator cannot disagree about the string. A response with no hold is byte-identical to today's alphabetical sort. Tests: the pure `queue_paused_stays_first_through_the_reason_code_merge` (priority, no-hold parity, idempotence, empty) and — because the review correctly noted a helper-level test still sits *before* the destructive merge — the DB/HTTP `test_queue_paused_leads_the_final_reason_codes_over_another_impediment`, which drives the real eligibility endpoint with a task that is **both** held and concurrency-saturated and asserts `reason_codes[0] == "queue_paused"` while the other impediment survives the reorder. (3) **P2 — `docs/api-contract.json` still documented the superseded trim behaviour**, telling clients that surrounding whitespace in the `queue_name` path parameter is "trimmed to the canonical name" when round 5 changed it to a `400` rejection. A generated client or an operator following the contract mid-outage would get an unexpected `400` and leave the queue dispatching. Both the pause and resume parameter descriptions now state that the name is matched exactly, that leading/trailing whitespace is rejected rather than trimmed, and why (queue names are stored verbatim at enqueue time, so `"payments "` and `"payments"` are genuinely distinct reachable queues). This was doc drift introduced by round 5's own behaviour change — the fix that made the behaviour honest left the contract describing the old one.

  **Post-review hardening, round 7 (three Codex P2 findings, all confirmed genuine):** (1) **The CLI exited `0` on a `207` partially-applied queue mutation.** `execute()` gates only on `!status.is_success()`, and `207 Multi-Status` *is* 2xx — so a fleet-wide pause that reached only some shards printed its `{"ok": false, "status": "partial"}` body and exited successfully. A scripted incident-response step (`harvest queue pause payments --reason … && …`) therefore proceeded believing the hold was in effect while the shards the request missed kept dispatching into exactly the outage the operator was riding out. Fixed with a body-level gate in the established `preflight_exit_code`/`shard_health_exit_code` shape: `queue_mutation_should_gate` (pause/resume only — `list-paused` is a read with no partial-application contract) plus `queue_mutation_exit_code`, which **fails closed** (a body carrying neither `ok: true` nor `status: "complete"` is not a response we can vouch for) and surfaces as the new `CliError::QueuePartialMutation { detail }` carrying the API's `partial_failures` summary at exit code `1`. Documented in the `harvest_queue_paused_backlog` runbook's Safe-actions list, including the re-issue-and-confirm step (`effective_scope` should read `fleet`, not `partial_fleet`). (2) **A `.` or `..` queue name silently retargeted the request at a different route.** `PATH_SEGMENT_ENCODE_SET` percent-encodes ` " # % < > ? \` { } /` but not `.`, and the WHATWG URL parser reqwest uses strips dot-segments **after** `ApiRequest.path` is assembled — verified empirically: `.` resolves `/admin/queues/{q}/pause` to `/admin/queues/pause` and `..` to `/admin/pause`. Percent-encoding cannot rescue the literal forms, so `checked_queue_segment` now rejects them up front with `CliError::QueueNameDotSegment`. The spec's percent-encoded spellings (`%2e`, `.%2e`, `%2e.`, `%2e%2e`, case-insensitively) are matched too as defense in depth — they are *already* neutralized one layer down, because the encode set encodes `%` so a queue literally named `%2e` reaches the URL as `%252e` and survives intact, and the guard should not silently depend on that staying true. A name that merely *contains* a dot (`orders.eu`) is unaffected: only a whole-segment `.`/`..` is a dot-segment. (3) **A failed pause-state lookup on the eligibility explainer was read as "no queues paused."** `evaluate_eligibility_for_shard` called `paused_queue_names(...).await.unwrap_or_default()`, so a database error produced an empty paused set — and this endpoint exists precisely to answer *"why is nothing being claimed from this queue?"* during an incident, so swallowing the error answered it with a confident, wrong "nothing is holding it". The sibling rate-limit read ~20 lines above in the same function already propagates via `.map_err(...)?`, making this an internal-consistency fix as well; it now propagates through `map_error` (the file's `HarvestError` → `AutumnError` mapping). Tests, TDD red→green: four pure CLI unit tests (`queue_mutation_exit_code` partial/complete/fail-closed, gate applies only to the mutating subcommands, exit code `1`) and three CLI request-mapping tests (pause and resume both reject every dot-segment spelling; `orders.eu` still maps cleanly) — all RED as compile errors against the not-yet-existing helpers; plus the DB/HTTP `a_failed_pause_lookup_surfaces_as_an_error_not_an_empty_paused_set`, which injects the fault by dropping `harvest_queue_pauses` (the lookup is a plain query with no `to_regclass` guard, so a missing table is a genuine error) and was confirmed RED against the pre-fix code returning `200 OK` with `"diagnosis": "no_online_workers"` for a queue whose hold state could not be determined.

  **Post-review hardening, round 8 (one Codex P2 — a sibling of the round-7 dot-segment finding, fixed route-wide):** `PATH_SEGMENT_ENCODE_SET` did not include `\`, but the URL parser reqwest uses treats `\` as a path separator for special (http/https) URLs — so a queue name like `payments\eu` split into extra path segments and both pause and resume silently landed on a different route. Verified empirically, and it is **worse than a missed route**: a backslash also re-enables `..` traversal *inside* what should be one opaque segment, so `payments\..\admin` resolved to `/admin/queues/admin/pause` — past the round-7 whole-segment dot-segment guard, which only rejects a name that IS `.`/`..`. Unlike the literal-dot case, **encoding is the correct fix here** (`%5C` is not collapsed, confirmed by the same probe), so a queue whose name genuinely carries a backslash stays pausable rather than being refused — enqueue stores queue names verbatim, so such a queue is genuinely reachable. Fixed at the encode set rather than with a queue-specific reject, which fixes **every** `path_segment` caller at once (workflow ids, keys, activity ids, calendar names, …) rather than one route; the const now carries a doc comment explaining why `/` and `\` are both present, why `%` is, and why the literal `.`/`..` forms are rejected instead of encoded. Tests: the pure `path_segment_encodes_both_path_separators` (both separators, the traversal case, and an untouched ordinary name) — RED-verified against the pre-fix set (`left: "payments\\eu"` vs `right: "payments%5Ceu"`) — plus route-level `queue_pause_percent_encodes_a_backslash_in_the_queue_name` and `queue_resume_percent_encodes_a_backslash_in_the_queue_name`. And because the character was a symptom of an unguarded *class*, the round also adds `every_printable_ascii_byte_survives_as_exactly_one_path_segment`, which walks every printable ASCII byte through `path_segment` plus real URL parsing and asserts it comes back as exactly one segment decoding to the original — currently zero offenders, and RED-verified to name the culprit precisely (`byte 0x5c ('\') encoded to "q\z" but parsed as "/admin/queues/q/z/pause"`), so the set cannot silently lose a separator-class character again. It covers *embedded* bytes only: a whole-segment `.`/`..` cannot be encoded away at all and stays on the round-7 rejection path, and control characters (including the tab/newline the parser silently strips) are already covered by `CONTROLS`. The sweep can only walk printable ASCII (a lone byte `>= 0x80` is not valid UTF-8 and so is not expressible as a queue name), so the reachable non-ASCII case is pinned separately by `non_ascii_queue_names_survive_as_exactly_one_path_segment` (accented Latin, CJK, Cyrillic, an emoji, and a combining sequence) — `utf8_percent_encode` encodes every non-ASCII byte regardless of the `AsciiSet`, so there is no separator hazard there, but that is a property of the encoding crate and is now asserted rather than assumed.

  **Post-review hardening, round 9 (two Codex P2 findings, both confirmed genuine and both in the same failure direction as the earlier rounds — the operator's hold reports success while dispatch keeps flowing, or the hold fails opaquely):** (1) **The resume-time `scheduled_at` shift charged the resume's own runtime to every held task.** `resume_shift_scheduled_at_query` measured the thaw with `NOW()`, which is `transaction_timestamp()` — frozen at transaction *start*, i.e. before `resume_queue` waits on the advisory lock, before the pause-row `DELETE`, and before the bulk `UPDATE` runs — yet the hold stays in force until that transaction **commits**. Every second the resume itself spends was therefore omitted from the credit, so any task whose `schedule_to_start` is shorter than the resume's runtime timed out the instant the queue thawed: precisely the AC3/AC4 promise ("never failed *solely because* of the pause") being broken by the thaw itself. The same frozen value also excluded rows that fell due *during* the transaction from the `scheduled_at <= NOW()` predicate. Verified empirically rather than assumed, because Postgres clock semantics decide the fix: `NOW()` held steady across a 2 s in-transaction wait while `clock_timestamp()` advanced by 2.01 s; and replaying the shift arithmetic showed a task with a genuine 100 s pre-pause wait reading as **103 s** after a resume that spent 3 s on the lock, versus **100 s** with the live clock. Fixed by using `clock_timestamp()` for both the credit and the due-ness predicate — volatile, so it is re-read per row at execution time, after the lock is held and as the scan progresses. It remains a deliberate **lower bound**: the true thaw instant is commit time, which no in-statement expression can know, so a row is under-credited by at most the remaining duration of the `UPDATE` — the *safe* direction, since over-crediting past commit would push `scheduled_at` into the future and make the task **un**claimable (the inverse of AC5). The `<= clock_timestamp()` result still holds in every branch, so the never-pushed-into-the-future invariant is preserved. (2) **A reason padded past the truncation cap turned an audited 400 into a 500 with the queue still dispatching.** The route validates the reason for non-emptiness and then bounds it with `truncate_operator_reason` (500 chars) before the core sees it, while the core independently re-rejects a whitespace-only reason — so validating the raw string and truncating a *different* one let the two disagree: 500+ leading spaces followed by real text passed the check (it trims to something), truncated to pure whitespace, and was then rejected by every shard, surfacing as `500 "queue pause failed: shard 0: invalid configuration: a queue pause requires a non-empty reason"` at exactly the moment the operator needed the hold. Fixed by normalizing (`trim`) in `parse_pause_request`, the same place the non-empty rule is enforced, so the value that was validated **is** the value that is stored — which makes the failure impossible *by construction* rather than by adding a second check: a trimmed non-empty string starts with a non-whitespace character, so every non-empty prefix of it still contains one. It also stops padding from evicting the operator's actual words from the 500-character budget (`490 spaces + "Stripe outage"` now stores `Stripe outage`). Scoped deliberately to this route rather than to the shared helper: an audit of all four `truncate_operator_reason` call sites found queue-pause is the only one that pairs truncation with a non-empty precondition (erase-payloads, legal-hold and force-fail all take an optional reason whose core path does not re-reject whitespace), so changing the shared helper would have altered three unrelated routes' stored values for no benefit here. Tests, both RED-verified: the pure `resume_shift_never_uses_the_frozen_transaction_clock` (forbids `NOW()`/`transaction_timestamp()`/`statement_timestamp()` and requires the live clock in *both* positions, since a frozen predicate silently skips rows that fall due mid-transaction) and the behavioural `resume_credits_the_time_the_resume_itself_spends_waiting`, which injects the delay the way production does — by holding the very advisory lock `resume_queue` takes — and first asserts the injected delay exceeds its own tolerance so a slow runner fails loudly rather than silently stopping falsifying anything (RED: `expected ~100s of genuine pre-pause wait preserved, got 102s`); plus the pure `trimming_before_truncation_can_never_yield_a_whitespace_only_reason` (which also asserts the pre-fix ordering *is* broken, so the guard cannot be vacuous) and `trimming_keeps_the_operator_words_inside_the_budget`, and the HTTP `a_reason_padded_past_the_cap_still_holds_the_queue`, which asserts the hold is genuinely in effect afterwards and that a truly blank reason is still the audited 400 (RED: the reviewer's predicted 500, verbatim).

  **Post-review hardening, round 10 (three P2s):** (1) **Credit tasks enqueued during the thaw.** `resume_queue`'s `scheduled_at` shift ran once, so a task enqueued after that statement's snapshot but before the transaction committed got no credit at all — even though it was genuinely held: the pause row's `DELETE` is uncommitted for the rest of the resume, so a concurrent claimer's snapshot still sees the hold and skips the queue. Uncredited, such a task thaws carrying its full apparent wait and the `schedule_to_start` scanner can kill it for time it spent held — the exact AC3/AC4 failure the shift exists to prevent. Fixed with a **narrowing second pass**, `resume_shift_late_arrivals_query`, run last (so it sees the freshest snapshot) and **disjoint** from the primary shift by `created_at` vs `transaction_timestamp()`: the primary pass gained `AND (created_at IS NULL OR created_at < transaction_timestamp())` and owns only the backlog that existed when the resume began, while the new pass owns everything enqueued during it (see the partition-totality note below for why the `IS NULL` arm is required rather than cosmetic). The partition is load-bearing — the primary pass's `+=` credit is *relative*, so applying it to a row twice would erase the pre-pause wait it exists to preserve, and it makes the summed `released_task_count` exact rather than double-counting. The frozen `transaction_timestamp()` is exactly "when this resume began", so the same property that made it *wrong* for the credit amount in round 9 makes it precisely *right* as the partition marker, with no extra bind or round trip. The late-arrivals pass is an **absolute** `SET scheduled_at = clock_timestamp()`, not the relative delta: a row created during the hold has no pre-pause wait to preserve (it was held from the moment it became due, so it accrues none), and an absolute assignment is idempotent under repetition — it can only move `scheduled_at` to a later instant that is still `<= clock_timestamp() <= commit time`, never into the future. **Irreducible residual, documented not eliminated:** this narrows the uncredited window from "the whole bulk `UPDATE`" to "this final, small statement", but a row committed after *its* snapshot and before commit is still held and still uncredited; the under-credit is bounded by that statement's remaining runtime (microseconds when there are no late arrivals) and is in the same safe direction as round 9's lower-bound credit. Closing it completely would mean serializing **enqueue** behind the queue's advisory lock — a queue-scoped serialization point on the hot enqueue path for every task on every queue, paused or not, which is the exact trade this module's design notes already reject for the claim path — so it is not worth paying for a sub-millisecond credit. (2) **State the `schedule_to_close` exception in the alert pack.** The `harvest_queue_paused_too_long` rule's `description` said a pause is safe because "nothing fails, retries, or dead-letters" — true of the relative `schedule_to_start` timer, which a pause suspends and credits back, but **not** of the absolute `schedule_to_close` deadline (issue #378), which keeps running during a hold. That is unsafe in the one alert an operator consults after the 1h/4h threshold, so the description now states the exception explicitly and tells the responder to check whether the held activities declare `schedule_to_close` and whether the remaining budget covers the outage — matching what the API contract and the runbook (`docs/runbooks/harvest-alerts.md#harvest_queue_paused_too_long`) already said. (3) **Surface pause-read failures in the Workers banner.** `load_paused_queues_from_shards` used `.ok()?`, so a shard whose connection or pause read failed contributed no rows. For *coverage classification* that is the safe reading (a not-holding shard makes the hold `partial_fleet`, i.e. possibly still dispatching) but for *presence* it is not: a hold that exists **only** on an unread shard vanished from the banner entirely, so an operator investigating idle workers saw a clean page and looked elsewhere while dispatch was in fact held. The loader now returns a `PausedQueueScan` carrying the failed shard ids alongside the merged rows, and `render_paused_queues_banner` renders a "Queue pause state incomplete" warning **first and even when there are zero rows** — naming the failed shards, saying a hold may be MISSING entirely, warning that a shown `Scope` can understate real coverage, and pointing at `GET /admin/queues/paused`. Same class as the round-7 eligibility fix, which propagated the failure rather than silently reporting "not paused". A healthy fleet page with nothing paused and every shard readable still renders nothing at all, byte-identical to before. **Partition totality (`created_at` is nullable):** `harvest_task_queue.created_at` was added by migration `20260619000000` as a *nullable* column, so a `PENDING` row enqueued before it has none — and in SQL a comparison against `NULL` yields `NULL`, not `false`. A bare `<` / `>=` split would therefore have left such a legacy row matching **neither** pass and credited by **neither**, silently regressing against the pre-partition query (which had no `created_at` predicate at all and shifted it). The primary pass's predicate is `(created_at IS NULL OR created_at < transaction_timestamp())` — a row with no `created_at` was certainly enqueued before this resume began — so the partition is provably total: every due `PENDING` row matches exactly one pass. Tests: the DB `resume_credits_a_task_enqueued_between_the_two_shift_passes`, which drives the two passes by hand with an enqueue interleaved between them (the window exists only *inside* `resume_queue`'s transaction, so no end-to-end call can produce it) and first asserts the primary pass genuinely missed the row so the second-pass assertion cannot be vacuous, then asserts the late arrival accrues ~0s while the pre-existing backlog keeps its genuine ~100s pre-pause wait and both passes report exactly one row; the DB `resume_credits_a_legacy_task_with_no_created_at` (a row with `created_at` nulled out is still credited its 600s hold, counted as released, and claimable); the pure `the_two_resume_passes_partition_on_created_at`, `late_arrivals_pass_is_absolute_and_bounded` and `the_partition_is_total_for_a_null_created_at`, plus the round-9 frozen-clock guard refined to judge the SET clause and the WHERE clause separately (so the partition predicate's one legitimate use of the frozen clock is allowed while the credit arithmetic still may not touch it); the alert-pack anti-drift guard `queue_pause_alert_states_the_schedule_to_close_exception`, which pins the exception in **both** the rule description and the runbook section so the two cannot drift apart; and for the banner the pure `unreadable_shard_warns_even_with_no_visible_holds` and `unreadable_shard_warning_composes_with_a_visible_hold` (which also pins the ordering: "we do not know" outranks the partial-coverage detail it may itself explain) plus the end-to-end `ui_workers_warns_when_a_shards_pause_state_is_unreadable`, which renders the real Workers page against a two-shard pool with one unreachable shard and nothing paused on the reachable one — the exact silent-clean-page case — and asserts the warning appears while no hold is claimed.

  **Post-review hardening, round 11 (three P2s — two fixed, one confirmed-narrow and documented rather than redesigned):** (1) **Stamp the pause time after acquiring the queue lock.** The pause row's `paused_at` came from the column's `DEFAULT NOW()`, i.e. `transaction_timestamp()`, frozen at transaction *start* — before `pause_queue` waits on the queue's advisory lock. So a pause that queued behind a concurrent claim or resume recorded a `paused_at` earlier than the instant the hold actually took effect.
