  cut views. A Verus proof (`formal/verus/src/scan_skip.rs`) shows that the
  skip query returns the first unconsumed entry. The Verus mirror guard now
  drops loop clauses (`invariant`, `invariant_except_break`, `ensures` and
  `decreases`) in a loop header, so a proof can cover a loop.

  No migration, no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, and no `harvest_events` change.
- **Engine** (implemented): Group commit across executions in one decision partition — see issue #2256. `group_commit::GroupCommit` lets an owner commit the decisions of several executions of one decision partition in one Postgres transaction. [`DESIGN-2256.md`](design/DESIGN-2256.md) section 1 is the design note. ADR 0009 decision 14 records it.

  - One lane per shard and partition, with `width` slots (default 4). A
    decision commits alone at once while a slot is free. A batch forms only
    when decisions wait, so group commit engages only under queue depth.
  - A batch holds decisions of one tenure, one per execution, up to
    `max_batch` (default 32). It fences once and holds the owner row
    `FOR KEY SHARE` until it commits. An acquisition waits for the whole
    batch. A renewal does not.
  - Each stage of a batch of two or more runs in a savepoint. A failing stage
    rolls back alone. A fence error in a stage rolls the batch back.
  - No result goes out before the batch commits. A batch of one sends no
    savepoint.
  - A batch runs on a task of its own, so a leader whose caller leaves does
    not cancel it. After a failed stage, the batch probes the transaction,
    so an aborted transaction never reports `Ok`.
  - The worker persist paths do not use the lane yet. Issue #2318 tracks the
    wiring.

  **No migration. No new `WorkflowEvent` variant. No replay impact.**

  Tests:

  - `group_commit_db_tests.rs` has ten tests. A failing decision rolls back
    alone. No result goes out before the commit. A stale batch commits
    nothing. The fence holds the owner row for the whole batch. A lone
    decision sends no savepoint. One execution never shares a batch. A
    caller that leaves before its batch never runs. A batch survives its
    leader's caller leaving. A fence error from a stage rolls the batch back.
    A failed checkout fails the batch.
  - `dst::group`: a seeded simulator with three nemeses, seven invariants
    and six mutants. Each mutant fails on its own invariant. The design
    passes at widths 1, 2 and 4.
  - `formal/verus/src/group_commit.rs`: the plan rules and the result rule.
  - `group_commit_props.rs`: the planner against the Verus spec model.
  - `benches/group_commit_bench.rs`: throughput at depth and p50 at one
    writer. Paired bursts give 1.16x at 16 writers and 1.33x at 64 writers.
    At one writer, the p50 is 0.998 of the lane with grouping off. See
    [`performance-group-commit.md`](performance-group-commit.md).
- **Perf** (implemented): the external, timer and child matcher scans are no longer quadratic — see issue #2338. Three `HistoryMatcher` scans walked history one event at a time on each call, so a fan-out replay cost O(N²):

  - `scan_ahead_for_external_signal_terminals` walked to the end of history
    before every `match_*` call while an external signal, cancel or await was
    stashed.
  - The fire scan of `match_timer_strict` stepped over the later timer starts
    and the consumed fires.
  - The terminal scan of `match_child_workflow` stepped over every later child
    start.

  All three now read the scan index of issue #2330 (`activity_scan_index.rs`).
  The index keeps the external terminals in one skip list, and the fires and
  child terminals per id. The timer scan runs through the activity scan code,
  because the rules of the two scans agree on every event class. The
  ski-rental rule of #2330 applies, so a sequential history builds no index.

  At N=1000, `fanout_extsig` costs 80% fewer instructions,
  `timers` 79% fewer and `children` 68% fewer. See
  `docs/performance-match-activity-fanout.md` and `docs/design/DESIGN-2338.md`.
  The local activity scan and the external signal, cancel and await scans are
  linear already. A scaling test guards all of them.

  Replay semantics do not change. The differential property test of #2330 now
  runs copies of the old external, timer and child scans as its oracle.

  No migration, no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, and no `harvest_events` change.
- **Fix** (implemented): Calendar tests the schedule's local date — see issue #2332. A calendar skip policy tested the UTC date of a fire time. A `CronInTimezone` schedule outside about UTC±5h then met the wrong day. A Mon–Fri 08:00 `Asia/Tokyo` schedule with `weekends-off` lost its Monday fire.

  `calendar::schedule_local_date` now returns the date in the schedule's timezone. Other schedules keep the UTC date. These paths use it: firing preview, backfill planning, the scheduler tick (pre-check and dispatch loop), and both overdue-schedule resolvers (one now delegates to the other).

  The shift helper is now one function. A shifted local time inside a DST gap moves forward to the first valid time on the same local day. It used to fall back to the UTC time and could land a day late.

  Upgrade note: a timezone schedule with a calendar can skip or shift different days than before. The new days match the local calendar. No migration is needed. See `docs/upgrading/0.8.0.md` section 1.14.

  Tests: Tokyo and Los Angeles weekday previews, a local-day holiday, a local-day shift, backfill, the pure overdue resolver, a DST-gap shift, and the helper fallbacks.
- **Perf** (implemented): the external stash no longer costs O(N²) — see issue #2346. The external stash of `HistoryMatcher` had three quadratic paths:

  - Before each `match_*` call, the external stash scan visited each unconsumed
    external terminal at or after the cursor. A terminal that matches no stash
    entry stays unconsumed, so each later call visited it again. A plain loop of
    an activity and an external signal therefore replayed in O(N²).
  - A terminal found its stash entry with a linear search. A fan-out of P
    external calls, and a plain loop of external signals, then cost O(P²)
    compares. The drift check searched the stash once for each event.
  - A match removed its entry with `Vec::remove`, so a P-wide fan-out moved
    O(P²) bytes.

  The fix:

  - Only a new stash entry can make a terminal match. Each request helper now
    notes the key of its entry. A scan reads the terminals of the new keys,
    through a per-key index of the external terminals. It reads every terminal
    only outside the range of the last scan with work, after a rewind or a
    restore. The external scan no longer walks the history.
  - `ExternalStash` keeps the entries in push order, with a map from each id to
    its first entry. A terminal finds its entry in O(1) in a fan-out. A remove
    from the front costs O(1).
  - `match_external_cancel` and `match_external_await` now call
    `stash_transparent_external_event`, as the drain does.

  At N=2000, the new `external_stash_profile` bench costs 96% fewer
  instructions for `loop`, 92% fewer for `loop_seq` and 93% fewer for `fanout`.
  All three shapes now grow about 1.95 times per doubling.
  See `docs/performance-match-activity-fanout.md` and
  `docs/design/DESIGN-2346.md`.

  Tests: the scaling test gains four `ExternalLoop` shapes, six
  `ExternalFanOut` shapes, `ExternalPairs` and a fan-out after a middle remove.
  It now counts stash probes and runs the drift check. The old code fails it
  for the first eleven. A proptest compares `ExternalStash` with a
  plain `VecDeque` search. The differential test gains a rewind, a forward skip
  and a bare `prepare_match`, and edge tests cover each terminal kind, a rewind
  and a restore.

  Replay semantics do not change. The differential property test compares the
  new scan with a copy of the old walk.

  No migration, no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, and no `harvest_events` change.
- **Phase trace export perf** (implemented): return Chrome trace events without a serde round trip (PR #2279). `trace_export::export_chrome_trace` returned `json!(events)`. On a `Vec<Value>`, that macro serializes the finished tree into a second, deep copy. It now returns `Value::Array(events)`, which moves the vector. The output is identical. No event, migration or append-only change.

  Evidence: the new `dag_tooling_profile` harness lints, profiles and exports a
  2,000-task layered DAG. Total instructions fall from 56.63M to 36.92M
  (-34.8%), and allocated blocks from 79,009 to 51,008 (-35.4%). See
  `docs/performance-chrome-trace-export.md`.
- **Phase replay perf** (implemented): hash replay event positions without SipHash (PR #2303). `HistoryMatcher::is_consumed` runs once per scanned event, and it probed three sets of event positions with the default `SipHash`. Those sets now use `EventIndexHasher`, a multiplicative hasher in `replay.rs`. An event position is not data that an attacker chooses, and no code iterates the sets, so behavior is unchanged. No event, migration or append-only change.

  Evidence: the new `match_activity_profile` callgrind harness replays a
  fan-out through `HistoryMatcher::match_activity`. At N=1000, instructions
  fall 61.6% for `fanout` and 56.4% for `fanout_rev`. A sequential history
  moves +0.2%. The scan stayed quadratic until issue #2330. See
  `docs/performance-match-activity-fanout.md`.
- **Phase** (implemented): Queue age gauge seeks the oldest rows (Ledger, issue #2339). `queue::oldest_pending_ages` no longer reads every eligible pending row. For each queue it reads the oldest 32 rows through `idx_harvest_tq_coverage_sample`, runs the claim gates over them, and keeps the result when it is provably exact. A queue that cannot be settled from the window reads the whole queue, as before. The result is the same as the old aggregate. There is no migration, no new index and no change to the gate text, which one macro now shares.

  Measured on a skewed backlog with `pg_stat_statements`: the age statement took
  89.5% to 98.6% of all buffers in a poll tick. Its buffers fell by 88.8%, 98.6%
  and 99.5% at 20,000, 100,000 and 300,000 pending rows. WAL bytes and statement
  count did not change. The harness, baseline and plans are in
  `docs/perf-artifacts/queue-age-gauge/`. The write-up is
  `docs/performance-queue-age-gauge.md`. The test
  `age_gauge_matches_the_reference_query` compares the new query with the old
  query on edge cases.
- **Phase** (implemented): Assay #16: the Postgres 12 floor at the engine layer. Assay ledger #16 tried to run the engine's database suites on PG 12.22, PG 14.24 and PG 16.15. The verdict is undetermined: the PG 16 control passed 79.0% of in-scope tests against a registered 90% validity line, so no arm was graded. The report names a per-test re-charter. See `docs/assays/0016-postgres-12-engine-paths.md`.

  No engine change: no `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no public API change.
- **Chore** (implemented): land the Dependabot bumps that needed code: Rust 1.99.1, syn 3, aes 0.9 with aes-gcm 0.11. Four Dependabot PRs could not pass CI alone. This change lands them together with the code each one needs.

  - **Rust 1.99.1** (#2233). The worker image moved to `rust:1.99.1-bookworm`.
    `docs/audits/worker-image-contract.py` requires the build image, the
    Dockerfile's `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` and `rust-toolchain.toml` to name one
    release. The pin, the env var and the docs that quote it now say 1.99.1.
    `harvest-verify` matches validated `rustc` releases on major and minor, so
    its validated set does not change.
  - **syn 3** (#2238). syn 3 stores raw pointer mutability as
    `PointerMutability` and drops the negative-impl slot from
    `ItemImpl::trait_`. `harvest-verify` now matches `PointerMutability::Mut`
    and reads the trait path from the two-field tuple. The existing
    `*mut`/`*const` field test covers the pointer rule.
  - **aes 0.9.2 and aes-gcm 0.11.1** (#2088, #2239). They must move together.
    With only one bumped, the `zeroize` features on `aes`, `ghash` and
    `polyval` apply to copies that `aes-gcm` does not use. `cargo tree` now
    shows `aes-gcm 0.11.1` on `aes 0.9.2` and `ghash 0.6.0`, with `zeroize`
    on. The codec and the owner disk cache move from the deprecated
    `AeadInPlace` to `AeadInOut`. The key is passed as a reference to its
    array, so no unzeroized copy is made. A nonce or tag of the wrong length
    is an error, never a panic.

  - **zstd advisories.** cargo-deny began failing on RUSTSEC-2026-0391,
    -0395 to -0406 and -0410 in `zstd` 0.13 and `zstd-safe` 7. The only path
    to them is wasmtime's `cache` feature, and no wasmtime release uses the
    patched `zstd` 0.14. Harvest never reads wasmtime's on-disk cache, so
    `wasmtime` now takes its default features minus `cache`, and `zstd`
    leaves the lockfile.

  The stored format does not change: a nonce, the ciphertext and a 16-byte
  tag, as before. The existing codec round-trip, tamper and wrong-key tests
  pass unchanged.

  No migration. No `WorkflowEvent` change.
- **Perf** (implemented): the signal wait is no longer quadratic — see issue #2349. `HistoryMatcher::match_signal` had two quadratic paths:

  - A wait found its stashed signal with a linear name compare. Waits in
    reverse order of N stashed signals cost O(N²) compares. The push handler
    claim, the non-blocking receive and the signal race searched the stash
    the same way.
  - Each wait walked from the cursor and crossed every unclaimed sibling
    command. The cursor then went back to the first one. N waits beside N
    unclaimed commands cost O(N²) steps.

  The fix:

  - `SignalStash` keeps the stashed signals in push order. A stash that grows
    past 16 slots also keeps a queue for each name. A search then walks one
    queue, in push order, as the old search did. A smaller stash scans its
    slots, at about the old cost. A push or a cut compacts the stash when its
    empty slots outnumber its entries. A cut and a restore keep the order and the
    cost of the old deque.
  - The race scan searched the stash at each consumed event. A stash entry
    names its own event, so only a consumed signal of the same name needs a
    search now.
  - `signal_scan_step` holds the rule of the old walk for one event. A wait
    that is not a race branch leaves the walk by the rule of #2330 and
    continues on the scan index. It visits each unconsumed barrier and
    runs the same step on it. A race branch keeps the walk, because it must
    stop at its own settle marker.

  At N=2000, the new `signal_wait_profile` bench costs 84% fewer
  instructions for `rev` and 93% fewer for `after_fanout`. Both now grow
  about 2 times per doubling. The `fwd` shape costs 0.4% more, and a loop
  that stashes one signal at a time costs 1.0% to 1.2% more. See
  `docs/performance-match-activity-fanout.md` and
  `docs/design/DESIGN-2349.md`.

  Tests: the scaling test gains eight signal shapes and counts the stash
  compares. The old code fails it for seven of them. The differential test
  runs copies of the old signal wait, push handler claim, non-blocking
  receive, signal race and pure signal reads as its oracle. A proptest
  compares `SignalStash` with a plain `VecDeque`, with and without the name
  map. Edge tests cover a deadline timer, an unexpected event, a predicate,
  a cut and a race branch, on the walk and on the index.

  Replay semantics do not change. No migration, no new `WorkflowEvent`
  variant, and no `harvest_events` change.
- **Benches** (implemented): deterministic profiles for the 0.8.0 fork, owner and agent paths. No `*_profile.rs` harness measured the new 0.8.0 paths of the fenced decision owner, the non-destructive fork or the durable agent. Nine harnesses now do. Each runs under `valgrind --tool=callgrind`, needs no database, asserts its outcome and has a page with its baseline numbers and reproduce steps.

  | Harness | Path | Page |
  |---|---|---|
  | `fork_resolve_profile` (new shapes `hold`, `scope`, `override`, `miss`) | `fork::resolve_activity`, `settle_holds` (issue #2000) | `docs/performance-fork-resolve-shapes.md` |
  | `fork_validate_profile` | `reset::resolve_reset_point`, `fork::validate_fork` (issue #2000) | `docs/performance-fork-validate.md` |
  | `owner_kernels_profile` | partition hash, claim mask, `plan_batch`, `LeaseWrite::done` (issues #2249, #2256) | `docs/performance-owner-kernels.md` |
  | `owner_disk_cache_profile` | `OwnerDiskCache` store, load, entity row (issue #2258) | `docs/performance-owner-disk-cache.md` |
  | `entity_sql_profile` | `entity_sql::run` (issue #2260) | `docs/performance-entity-sql.md` |
  | `entity_snapshot_replay_profile` | entity snapshot replay (issue #2259) | `docs/performance-entity-snapshot-replay.md` |
  | `agent_model_turn_profile` | `AgentHarness::model_turn` (issues #1973, #2264) | `docs/performance-agent-model-turn.md` |
  | `agent_loop_replay_profile` | `agent_loop` replay (issue #1973) | `docs/performance-agent-loop-replay.md` |
  | `durable_agent_replay_profile` | durable `agent` replay (issue #2263) | `docs/performance-durable-agent-replay.md` |

  The `serve` shape of `fork_resolve_profile` keeps its workload, so the
  numbers in `docs/performance-fork-scheduled-occurrence.md` still apply. Its
  check is stricter: an activity counts as served only when its record
  completes it.

  Three findings stand out. None is fixed here.

  - A fork of a race whose timer won holds every loser. `source_race_winner`
    scans the source once per sibling, so `settle_holds` is cubic in the
    batch width. At K=800 it runs 9.71 billion instructions for one decision.
  - The delta form of a model turn hashes the whole held prefix again on
    every turn (`harness.rs:433`). A run of T turns is then O(T²), and the
    check is 82.9% of the profile at T=200.
  - The `agent_loop` replay serializes the whole request twice per tool
    round, so it is quadratic in the rounds.

  CI compiles and lints the six core harnesses in the `clippy-core` job. The
  agent crate harnesses were already in its `--all-targets` clippy run.

  No production code change, no migration, no route change and no
  `harvest_events` change.
- **Phase** (implemented): Queue depth gauge counts up to a cap (Ledger, issue #2356). The `harvest.queue.depth` sampler no longer counts every eligible pending row. `queue::bounded_queue_depths` counts each queue up to `telemetry::QUEUE_DEPTH_CAP` (10,000). Statistics in `pg_class` pick one of two ways to count. The walk runs a `LATERAL` subquery per queue that walks `idx_harvest_tq_coverage_sample` in key order and stops at the cap. The pass counts every eligible row once and caps the count. The walk runs when its worst-case heap visits stay below one pass over the table. So a run costs no more than the smaller of the two, and an empty visibility map costs what the exact count costs. The count runs with sorts off. The sampler sums the shards with `add_bounded_depth` and caps the sum again. Below 10,000 the gauge is exact. A value of 10,000 means 10,000 or more. `queue::queue_depths` stays exact. There is no migration, no new index and no new write.

  **Behaviour change.** An alert that needs a depth above 10,000 can no longer
  fire. The starter rule `harvest_queue_backlog_growth` keys on growth, and a
  gauge at the cap shows none. While the gauge holds at the cap for the whole
  window, the rule now fires on the level, on a queue that is not paused. So a
  deep backlog that drains or holds steady fires too. promtool cases in
  `docs/alerts/starter-pack-v0.1.0.backlog-growth.test.yml` test the rule in the
  `lint` job. The plugin scrape endpoint now exports `harvest_queue_paused`,
  which `docs/telemetry.md` already listed. For an exact count, scrape
  `harvest_queue_backlog` from `GET /admin/queues/scaling?format=prometheus`.
  Autoscaling reads that metric, so it does not change. The load shedder reads
  the age, not the depth, so it does not change either.

  `docs/design/DESIGN-2356.md` records the options and the decision. Tests:
  `bounded_depths_match_the_exact_count_up_to_the_cap` compares the bounded and
  exact counts at ten caps, each cap in one transaction.
  `bounded_depth_scan_stops_at_the_cap` checks that each queue scan walks the
  index and reads at most the cap, with no visibility map and with future rows.
  `bounded_depth_counts_in_one_pass_until_a_vacuum` checks the pass with an empty
  map and the walk after a vacuum.
  `queue_depth_gauge_caps_the_sum_of_the_shards` runs a worker on two shards of
  6,000 rows each and expects 10,000. `queue_depth_alerts_sit_below_the_gauge_cap`
  keeps the starter thresholds within reach of the gauge.
  `formal/verus/src/depth_cap.rs` proves that the shard fold equals the capped
  total. The measurement is in `docs/performance-queue-depth-gauge.md`.
- **Change** (implemented): perf(replay): the recorded-update lookup is no longer quadratic.. `HistoryMatcher::match_update` scanned the whole history for each update. It now builds an index of update results once the scans have walked as many events as the history holds. Behavior is unchanged: the first result wins and a cut view still hides its tail. Measured with `benches/update_lookup_profile.rs` under callgrind: 32.19M to 9.11M instructions at 1000 updates (-71.7%), 415.4M to 35.1M at 4000 (-91.5%). The cost is now linear in the history.
- **Tooling** (implemented): Ledger profile for every SQL query — see issue #2364. Every function that sends SQL to Postgres or SQLite now has a Ledger profile. The catalog lives in `docs/ledger/`, with one TOML file for each source file, so two PRs conflict on it only when they change queries in the same source file. A profile records the query's `driver` (`per_task`, `per_tick`, `per_request`, `setup` or `test_support`), its `backend`, its `kind` (`read`, `write`, `ddl`), the `tables` that it touches, and the Ledger page that measures it, or `unmeasured`.

  The first catalog holds 953 profiles in 96 files across `autumn-harvest`,
  `autumn-harvest-plugin`, `autumn-harvest-sqlite`, `autumn-harvest-cli` and
  `autumn-harvest-agent`. About one in ten names a measured Ledger page. The
  rest are `unmeasured`, which makes the measurement gap countable for the
  first time.

  `docs/audits/ledger-profiles.py` gates the catalog in CI's `lint` job. It
  scans the shipped `src/` trees for query sites outside `#[cfg(test)]`, and it
  fails on a query with no profile, on a stale profile, and on a profile whose
  `backend`, `kind` or `tables` omit what the scan detects. `--scaffold` prints
  a stub for each missing profile. `--self-test` covers the lexer forms that it
  must get right.

  No engine change: no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no schema
  change and no public API change.
- **Tooling** (implemented): Ledger census: the access path of every per-task query — see issue #2366. A new census plans each SQL statement that the DB suites send, and maps it to its Ledger profile. A Diesel instrumentation hook in the integration test binary records each statement and its call stack when `HARVEST_LEDGER_CENSUS` names a file. `docs/audits/ledger-census.py` maps the stack to a profile and runs `EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN)` with `enable_seqscan = off` on a migrated database. Bool and string bind values replace their parameters, as in a custom plan, so a partial index such as `WHERE NOT consumed` applies.

  The first pass covers the `per_task` Postgres profiles. The census reached 144
  of the 175, and each one now has a `plan` field that links its page under
  `docs/ledger/plans/`. One statement has no usable index:
  `signal::forward_signals_to_retry_attempt` scans all of `harvest_signals` on
  each workflow retry (issue #2367).

  `ledger-profiles.py` accepts the new optional `plan` field and checks that its
  page names the function. CI runs the census self-test in the `lint` job.

  No engine change: no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no schema
  change and no public API change.
- **Scheduler** (implemented): Runtime DAG schedule overrides — see issue #2385, epic #2384. A DAG schedule came only from code. The scheduler converged each `harvest_schedules` row to the code value on every tick, so an operator could change a schedule only by a restart or a deploy. `PATCH /dags/{dag_name}` could only pause.

  `PATCH /dags/{dag_name}` now also sets an operator override:
  `schedule_expr`, `timezone`, `catchup`, `max_active_runs`, `jitter_secs`,
  `overlap_policy` and `buffer_all_max`. Each field is tri-state: absent keeps
  the stored override, `null` returns to code, a value sets it.
  `clear_override: true` returns every field to code. The override wins over
  code, survives a restart and applies to every replica.

  The scheduler loads the overrides of each shard once per pass and applies
  them to the DAG catalog and to the lowered workflow schedules before
  registration. The reconciler converges to the effective value with no other
  change. `ensure_dag_schedule` applies the override too, so an API path never
  undoes it. A pass that cannot read the overrides skips its shard.

  See [`docs/operations/schedule-overrides.md`](operations/schedule-overrides.md).

  **Migration.** `20261028195301_harvest_schedule_overrides` adds the table
  `harvest_schedule_overrides`. No existing table changes, no `WorkflowEvent`
  variant, no replay impact. Each worker role needs `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`
  and `DELETE` on it, and the startup preflight checks them.

  **API.** Non-breaking for a request that sends `paused` alone. The request
  body now rejects an unknown field and an empty body with 400. `paused` is
  optional.

  **Tests.** `schedule_override_db_tests` (override wins and survives a rebuilt
  catalog, a converged row is not rewritten, clear and per-field revert, invalid
  override writes nothing, an unreadable override skips the pass, the API path
  agrees with the tick, an unscheduled DAG gets a schedule) and
  `harvest_api_patch_dag_sets_and_clears_a_schedule_override`.
- **Performance** (implemented): the retention candidate scan uses its index again — see issue #2395. The retention janitor selects terminal executions in six states, `TERMINATED` included. Its partial index, `idx_harvest_we_retention_scan`, listed only five. Postgres uses a partial index only when the query predicate implies the index predicate, so each retention tick read the whole of `harvest_workflow_executions`, on every shard.

  Migration `20261029034500_harvest_retention_candidates_index` builds
  `idx_harvest_we_retention_candidates` with all six states and drops the old
  index. `MIGRATED` stays out, because a sealed row is not purgeable.

  **Upgrade.** A plain `CREATE INDEX` takes `SHARE` on
  `harvest_workflow_executions` and blocks state changes until the build ends.
  On a large deployment, build the new index `CONCURRENTLY` first, then drop the
  old one `CONCURRENTLY`. The migration header and the upgrade guide row give
  both statements.

  `retention_candidate_scan_index_tests` gates the plan. It fails when either
  variant of the candidate scan cannot use the new index.

  `retention::candidate_scan_sql` is now public, so the gate can plan the exact
  text the janitor runs. No new `WorkflowEvent` variant and no replay impact.
- **Tooling** (implemented): Ledger census batch 2: the per-tick profiles — see issue #2396. The Ledger census now plans the `per_tick` Postgres profiles, the background loops, scanners and sweepers. 172 of them link a plan page under `docs/ledger/plans/`. The suites did not reach 23.

  `docs/audits/ledger-census.py` now guesses the type of each parameter from
  its recorded bind value. When a generic plan fails on `($3)[2]` or
  `unnest($1)`, it plans again with casts. It keeps the guessed types once per
  statement, and it drops them for a bulk write with more than 64 parameters.

  The pass found one real defect. The retention candidate scan lists six
  terminal states, but `idx_harvest_we_retention_scan` covers only five. So
  the scan cannot use its index and reads all of `harvest_workflow_executions`
  on each tick (issue #2395). The same PR fixes it. See
  `issue-2395-retention-candidates-index.md`.

  One driver is corrected. `audit_export::pending_and_lag` backs an admin
  read, so its driver is `per_request`.

  The census itself changes no engine code: no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no

- **Tooling** (implemented): Ledger census batch 3: the per-request profiles — see issue #2402. The Ledger census now plans the `per_request` Postgres profiles, the queries behind API calls and operator reads. 153 of them link a plan page under `docs/ledger/plans/`. The suites did not reach 173. Most of those are in `autumn-harvest-plugin`, whose tests run in separate binaries that the census hook does not cover yet.

- **Fix** (implemented): Durable workspace snapshots (agent workspace store) — see PR #2431. `DirWorkspaceBlobs::put` now syncs the scratch file before the rename. It then syncs the folder and its parent. Until one put has synced every ancestor of the folder, each put syncs them all, so a retry after a failed first put still makes the new root durable. An ancestor above the root that denies the open is skipped. A sync error fails the put. Before, a crash after a committed tool call could lose the snapshot that the history names. Replay does not rerun a completed tool call, so the workspace was lost for good.

  Tests: `a_put_syncs_the_file_before_the_rename_and_the_folder_after_it`, `a_put_syncs_the_parent_of_each_folder_that_it_creates` and `a_search_only_ancestor_does_not_fail_the_put`, `a_retry_after_a_failed_first_put_syncs_the_ancestors`, `a_put_into_an_existing_folder_still_syncs_the_folder_and_its_parent`. On Windows the rename is not durable, because a directory cannot be opened there for a sync.
- **Fix** (implemented): two claim loops no longer slow activity dispatch — see issue #2418. Found when the 0.8.0 benchmark ran beside a v0.7.0 control on one box. The activity dispatch p50 at 8 starts per second was 12.6 to 14.0 ms on v0.7.0 and 66 to 67 ms on trunk-dev. A bisect over the 210 commits since v0.7.0 named #2106, which made two claim loops the default. With `HARVEST_BENCH_CLAIM_LOOPS=1` the p50 was 13.6 ms again.

  **Cause.** One loop polls back to back, about every 3 ms. A workflow task also takes about 3 ms, so the next poll finds the activity that it committed. Two loops drain the workflow backlog in parallel and both go empty before those commits. The leader then idles. A NOTIFY is nearly always queued, so it sleeps the 50 to 75 ms settle of `notify::settle_delay`, and nothing cuts that sleep short. Each activity committed in it waits for its end.

  **Fix.** A workflow permit now wakes the leader on release through `Worker::decision_done`. The task has committed the tasks that it schedules, so this wake does not settle. It also cuts a running settle short. The NOTIFY of a cut settle can name a row that is not claimable yet, so the cut settle owes one poll at its original end (`Worker::owed_poll`). The single-pool and the multi-shard leader both take the wake. On the same box, two loops now give a p50 of 8.1 ms and a p99 of 14.1 ms, against 66.3 ms and 91.4 ms before.

  **Tests.** `a_local_decision_end_wakes_the_idle_wait_without_a_settle`, `a_local_decision_end_cuts_the_settle_short_and_owes_a_poll` and `a_released_workflow_permit_wakes_the_leader`, all on paused time. `a_released_permit_does_not_cut_the_settle_delay_short` still holds: only a workflow task that ends cuts the settle. No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no replay impact.
- **Fix** (implemented): a NOTIFY polls before it settles — see issue #2422. After a NOTIFY, the idle leader slept `notify::settle_delay` (50 to 75 ms) before its first poll. The settle gives a row that a host clock stamped ahead of the database `NOW()` time to become claimable. A row that the database clock stamped is claimable at once, and it waited the whole settle too. The #2418 fix showed it: the bench's signal round-trip p50 rose from 44 to 68 ms. Before #2418, the leader was nearly always in a settle that an earlier NOTIFY had started. The poll at its end took the signal's task early, so the old p50 sat below the 50 ms floor.

  **Fix.** A NOTIFY now ends the idle wait at once, so the leader polls first. It sets `Worker::settle_pending`. The next idle wait comes only after an empty poll, and it runs the settle in place of a wait (`Worker::settle_if_pending`). The loop then polls again, so a host-clock row still gets its margin. The single-pool and the multi-shard leader both work this way. A local decision end still cuts the settle short (#2418).

  **Measurement.** One shard, same box, with the #2418 fix in both columns:

  | workers per shard | signal p50 before | signal p50 after | dispatch p50 before | dispatch p50 after |
  |--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
  | 1 | 68.0 ms | 13.4 ms | 8.1 ms | 7.6 ms |
  | 4 | 55.8 ms | 24.8 ms | 7.1 ms | 7.5 ms |

  The cost is extra polls. With four workers on one shard, the index scans on `harvest_task_queue` rose 28% in the dispatch scenario and 47% in the signal scenario. The settle jitter no longer spreads the first poll of each worker after one NOTIFY. `SKIP LOCKED` keeps those polls correct, and the claim seek keeps each one cheap.

  **Tests.** `a_notify_polls_before_it_settles`. `a_released_permit_does_not_cut_the_settle_delay_short` and `a_local_decision_end_cuts_the_settle_short_and_owes_a_poll` now drive the poll-first sequence. No new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no migration, no replay impact.
- **Tooling** (implemented): Ledger census batch 4: the setup profiles — see issue #2414. The Ledger census now plans the `setup` Postgres profiles, the queries that run at startup, in migrations and in partition layout changes. 63 of them link a plan page under `docs/ledger/plans/`. The suites did not reach 62.

  No setup statement is a defect. The ones with no usable index read the system
  catalog, rewrite all of `harvest_events` during a layout change on purpose, or
  sync the small completion-trigger registry at startup.

  The census itself changes no engine code: no new `WorkflowEvent` variant, no
  migration and no schema change.
- **Scheduler** (implemented): Runtime overrides for code-declared workflow schedules — see issue #2386, epic #2384. `PATCH /admin/schedules/{id}` edited a schedule row in place (issue #771). For a schedule declared with `WorkerBuilder::workflow_schedule`, the next scheduler tick converged the row back to its code value. The edit lasted about one tick, and the API still returned 200.

  `PATCH /admin/schedules/{id}` on a code-declared schedule now writes an
  operator override instead. The override wins over code, survives a restart and
  applies on every tick. Each field that the request sets becomes part of the
  override. The new `clear_override: true` returns the schedule to its code
  value, and the new `reason` is stored with the override. A schedule made with
  `POST /admin/schedules/workflow` keeps the #771 row edit and gets no override.

  The API tells the two apart with the code catalog of its process, the same
  test that `DELETE /admin/schedules` uses.

  See [`docs/operations/schedule-overrides.md`](operations/schedule-overrides.md).

  **Behaviour change.** On a code-declared schedule, `input` now returns 400.
  Before, it returned 200 and the next tick reverted it. `clear_override` and
  `reason` return 400 on a schedule made through the API.

  **Migration.** `20261029023935_harvest_schedule_overrides_workflow` lets
  `harvest_schedule_overrides.kind` hold `workflow`, and adds the column
  `workflow_fields JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'`. No other table changes, no
  `WorkflowEvent` variant, no replay impact. The grants of #2385 cover it.

  **Tests.** `workflow_schedule_override_db_tests` (the patched cadence holds for
  three ticks, the override survives new code, clear restores code, a second
  patch merges, an invalid patch or a live fire claim writes nothing, an
  unreadable override skips the pass) and the `schedule_update_integration`
  override tests.
- **Engine** (implemented): Runtime SLA and execution-timeout overrides per workflow type — see issue #2387, epic #2384. `WorkflowInfo::sla`, `WorkflowInfo::execution_timeout` and their `DagInfo` counterparts were static, so a change needed a restart.

  The new `PATCH /admin/workflow-types/{workflow_name}/run-defaults` sets an
  operator override of `sla_secs` and `execution_timeout_secs` for one type. A
  DAG uses its own name. The override wins over code for every new run and
  survives a restart. `GET` on the same route shows the code value, the
  override and the effective value. Each field is tri-state, and
  `clear_override` returns the type to its code values. A duration must be
  from 1 second to 100 years, so a start can always add it to its start time.

  Every start path reads the override from an in-process cache, so a start
  sends no extra query. The cache reloads once it is older than 5 seconds. The
  start clamps still hold: an SLA above the effective timeout is clamped to it.

  By default a change applies to new runs only. `recompute_in_flight: true` also
  moves the SLA deadline of each non-terminal run of the type that has not
  breached, on every shard. The hard `deadline_at` never moves.

  See [`docs/operations/run-default-overrides.md`](operations/run-default-overrides.md).

  **Migration.** `20261029050916_harvest_run_default_overrides` adds one small
  table on the default shard. **Grants:** `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`
  on `harvest_run_default_overrides`; `GET /admin/preflight` checks them. No
  `WorkflowEvent` variant, no replay impact.

  **Tests.** `run_defaults_integration` (a new start takes the override, the
  opt-in recompute moves only in-flight runs and the breach scanner fires on
  the new deadline, clear restores code, a timeout override clamps the SLA, bad
  requests are refused and audited) and `run_defaults_db_tests` (a warm cache
  sends no query, another process sees a change within one TTL).
- **Operations** (implemented): See and change runtime overrides from the CLI and Vantage — see issue #2388, epic #2384. The overrides of #2385, #2386 and #2387 were visible only one route at a time. An operator could not tell which parameters were overridden.

  - `GET /admin/overrides` lists every stored override. It reads the schedule
    overrides from every shard pool, and the run-default overrides from the
    default shard. Each entry names its actor, reason and time. A shard that
    cannot be read is named in `unavailable_shards`.
  - `GET /admin/config` gains `overrides`, the count of each kind.
  - The CLI gains `harvest dags set-schedule <dag>` (`--interval`, `--cron`,
    `--manual`, `--timezone`, `--catchup`, `--max-active-runs`,
    `--jitter-secs`, `--overlap-policy`, `--buffer-all-max`, `--reason`),
    `harvest dags clear-override <dag>` and `harvest overrides list`. Each
    command sends one request. `dags` is now an alias of `dag`.
  - The Vantage DAG page shows each schedule field as declared in code, as
    overridden and as effective. A field with an override has a marker. A DAG
    with no override shows none.

  See [`docs/operations/schedule-overrides.md`](operations/schedule-overrides.md).

  No migration, no `WorkflowEvent` variant, no replay impact.

  **Tests.** `run_defaults_integration` (the list names actor, reason and time,
  the config counts match, and the route is admin-only), `ui_integration` (the
  DAG page shows the code value and the override, and no marker without an
  override), and the CLI `request_mapping` and `contract_coverage` suites.
- **Scheduler** (implemented): Schedule overrides follow their DAG to a new shard — see issue #2389, epic #2384. A DAG schedule override lives on the shard that owns the DAG. A shard routing change moved the schedule row to its new owner, but the override stayed behind. The new owner then reconciled the row to the code value.

  Now the old shard's scheduler pass finds each override that it holds for
  another shard. It copies the row to the new owner, then deletes its own copy.
  The copy commits first, so a failure at either step leaves the override on at
  least one shard, and the next tick retries. An override that the new owner
  already holds wins. Two shards on one pool share one table, so nothing moves
  between them. No migration and no configuration change.
- **SQLite** (implemented): Runtime overrides of schedules — see issue #2390, epic #2384. The SQLite backend could not override a schedule at runtime. An app that upserts its schedules on every open reset each one to its code value.

  `SqliteRuntime` gains `set_schedule_override`, `clear_schedule_override`
  and `schedule_override`. An override is stored in the new
  `harvest_schedule_overrides` table. It wins over the code value of
  `upsert_schedule` and survives a reopen with new code, as on Postgres
  (#2386). Both backends merge a `WorkflowSchedulePatch` with the same rules.
  That type now lives in `autumn_harvest::schedule_patch`, which builds without
  the `db` feature. `autumn_harvest::scheduler::WorkflowSchedulePatch` still
  names it.

  The backend can override the cadence, `max_active_runs`, and the `skip` and
  `allow_all` overlap policies. Any other field returns
  `SqliteError::Unsupported` with the field name, and writes nothing.
  `ScheduleSummary` gains `max_active_runs`.

  SQLite has no DAGs, so the DAG override of #2385 has no SQLite form.

  **Schema.** `harvest_schedules.code_json` (nullable, added on open) and the
  `harvest_schedule_overrides` table. A row from before this change gets its
  code value on its next upsert.

  **Tests.** `schedule_override_fixture.rs` holds four cases: an override wins
  over code, it survives a restart with new code, a clear restores the code
  value, and a refused override writes nothing. `schedule_overrides` runs them
  on SQLite, and `schedule_override_parity_tests` runs them on Postgres. The
  SQLite suite also checks that each unsupported field is refused by name.

  See [`docs/operations/schedule-overrides.md`](operations/schedule-overrides.md#sqlite).
- **Tooling** (implemented): Ledger census batch 5: the plugin test suites — see issue #2425. The Ledger census now runs in the plugin's test suites too. The census hook moved out of the core test binary into a `ledger-census` cargo feature, so any test binary can link it. `docs/ledger/README.md` gives the commands.

  729 Postgres profiles now link a plan page under `docs/ledger/plans/`, up from
  552. Most of the new ones are `per_request` profiles of the admin API, the UI
  and the status endpoints, which only the plugin's tests reach.

  The census found a correctness bug, fixed here, and four scans worth an index
  decision (issue #2424). More dead-letter and signal readers were added to
  issues #2401 and #2367.
- **Fixed** (implemented): Schedule budget updates touched every schedule — see issue #2423. Trigger-now and backfill reserve a `max_runs` slot with a conditional `UPDATE`. Its budget guard was a raw SQL fragment with a bare `OR`, and `AND` binds tighter than `OR`. So the `id` guard covered one branch only, and the statement also matched every capped schedule under its cap on that shard.

  - Trigger-now and backfill reservation incremented `runs_started` on those
    schedules too.
  - Backfill release cleared `exhausted_at` on those schedules. That resurrected
    schedules that `end_at` had exhausted.

  Schedules with no `max_runs` were not affected. Each guard is now
  parenthesized, and the statements touch the target schedule only. Check
  `runs_started` and `exhausted_at` on capped schedules in a shard that ran a
  trigger-now or a backfill. A schedule may have exhausted early, or resumed
  after its `end_at`.
- **Engine** (implemented): Held claims no longer send the claim to the full scan — see issue #2420. **Claim order does not change.** The claim picks the same row as before. Only its cost changes under contention.

  **The problem.** The seek window of issue #1971 reads 32 rows per queue
  head with a plain read. A peer claim holds its row lock until it commits,
  so the window still returns that row. With 32 or more claims in flight on
  one head, every window row can be locked. The claim then ran the full scan
  of the backlog. At 100K pending rows it read 106,467 buffers and 2,259 temp
  blocks, against 263 with no held claim. A slow claim keeps more claims in
  flight, so the cost fed itself.

  **The fix.** `queue::claim_task_query` has a deep window between the window
  and the full scan:

  - It runs only when the window found no candidate and a guarded window row
    passes every claim gate. So peers hold that row. A head that a gate
    blocks never starts it.
  - It reads up to `queue::CLAIM_DEEP_SEEK_WINDOW` (256) rows from each held
    queue head only.
  - The window guard runs on the window plus the deep rows. Each head is
    still a prefix in claim order, so the guard stays exact.
  - It counts the running rows for its own concurrency keys, so a capped key
    stays capped.
  - The full scan runs only when a bound remains. A held head that the deep
    window reads to its end needs no full scan.

  No migration. No new bind. No new `WorkflowEvent` variant. The fence, kind,
  owner and fair splices reach the new scans.

  **Evidence.** `held_claims_on_one_head_keep_the_claim_off_the_full_scan`
  holds K claim transactions open on one queue. At 100K pending rows, K = 32
  reads 1,727 buffers and K = 64 reads 1,772, with no full scan and no
  spill. The cost is the same at 10K.
  `a_claim_behind_held_rows_takes_the_next_row_in_order` checks the order
  inside and past the deep window.
  `the_deep_window_keeps_the_bound_of_a_full_head_it_does_not_read` and
  `a_fully_held_short_head_skips_the_full_scan` cover the deep bounds.
  Shape tests pin the new CTEs and the splice counts. With 256 or more held
  claims on one head, the claim falls back to the full scan, as before. `docs/performance.md` § "Held claims" has the
  table.
- **Performance** (implemented): Scaling signals, canary status and shard rebalance use an index — see issue #2424. The Ledger census of the plugin suites found four statements that read a whole table. Each one now reads an index.

  - **Scaling signals.** `queue::queue_task_counts` counted every task row,
    finished rows included. An autoscaler polls it on every shard. It now reads
    `PENDING` and `RUNNING` rows only, through the existing
    `idx_harvest_tq_live_created`. The counts do not change. A queue with only
    finished tasks no longer gets an all-zero row from the task side. It still
    gets a row when a healthy, active worker lists it.
  - **Canary status.** `GET /admin/canary` read each execution row to find the
    canary runs. The statement moves to `canary::CANARY_ROWS_SQL`. It names the
    canary prefix as a literal, so a partial index can serve it. The new index
    `idx_harvest_we_canary_completed` holds canary runs only, newest first. The
    read stops after its row cap.
  - **Shard rebalance.** The quiescence check and the cutover read every
    `harvest_cross_shard_children` row to find the children of one parent. The
    timer copy and the timer delete read every `harvest_timers` row. The new
    indexes `idx_harvest_cross_shard_children_parent` and
    `idx_harvest_timers_exec` serve them. The timer index also serves each
    `ON DELETE CASCADE` from an execution, which retention triggers.

  Migration `20261030015439_harvest_census_scan_indexes` builds the three
  indexes. Migration `20260901130054` left out the parent index on purpose. Since
  then, the rebalance check and the PII erasure added lookups by parent.

  **Upgrade.** A plain `CREATE INDEX` takes `SHARE` on its table and blocks
  writes until the build ends. On a large deployment, build the three indexes
  `CONCURRENTLY` first. The header of the migration's `up.sql` gives the
  statements.

  `census_scan_index_tests` gates each plan with `enable_seqscan` off and a
  generic plan. It also checks the counts of each live state, and that the canary
  read matches the prefix only, newest first, under its cap. No new
  `WorkflowEvent` variant and no replay impact.
- **Tooling** (implemented): Ledger census batch 6: the SQLite profiles — see issue #2429. The Ledger census now covers SQLite. The `ledger-census` feature registers a SQLite auto-extension, so every connection that a test opens records its statements. `ledger-census.py plan-sqlite` plans them with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on the schema that the census recorded. It needs no database.

  103 of the 109 SQLite profiles now link a plan page under `docs/ledger/plans/`.
  Five of the rest send only DDL or pragmas, so they have nothing to plan. No
  test reaches `OwnerDiskCache::purge_entity`.
- **Fixed** (implemented): A resolved race scanned the whole SQLite task table — see issue #2429. `ctx.race()` cancels each losing activity. On SQLite, that `UPDATE` matched the task by `activity_id` alone, and no index covers that column. The task table keeps the rows of finished runs, so each cancel read every task in the file. The statement now names the run too, so `idx_harvest_tasks_exec` finds the row.
- **Fixed** (implemented): Each SQLite timer arm read every timer — see issue #2429. Each timer arm takes the next `arm_seq` from `MAX(arm_seq)` over all timers. Fired timers stay until retention purges their run, and no index covered the column, so each arm read the whole table. The base schema now builds `idx_harvest_timers_arm_seq`, so the read is one index step. An existing file gets the index on its next open.

  The other SQLite scans are by design: a startup reclaim, a one-time
  back-fill, the small schedule and writer-lock tables, a test fixture, and the
  read-only SQL that an operator runs over one entity.
- **Fix** (implemented): wasmtime 48.0.8 for three new RustSec advisories — see issue #2434. **Security fix.** The daily advisory scan failed on `wasmtime` 48.0.7. It affects the optional `wasm-activities` sandbox feature.

  - RUSTSEC-2026-0422: a typed function with `i31` or `nullref` arguments can
    panic, because the type check is too weak.
  - RUSTSEC-2026-0423: host-created struct types with supertypes can cause a
    type confusion between engines.
  - RUSTSEC-2026-0424: a transfer of borrowed resources between components
    does not check memory use.

  The changes:

  - `Cargo.lock` moves the `wasmtime` 48.0.x family to 48.0.8, with its
    `cranelift` crates at 0.135.8. The resolver also re-points a few
    dependency edges inside the allowed semver ranges: `windows-sys`,
    `itertools` and `getrandom`.
  - The manifest floor in `autumn-harvest` moves from 48.0.7 to 48.0.8. A
    downstream consumer reads the manifest, not this lockfile, so only the
    floor keeps it off a vulnerable release.

  **Checks.** `cargo deny check advisories` failed with the three ids before
  the change. It reports `advisories ok` after the change.

  **No migration. No new `WorkflowEvent` variant. No public API change.** The
  `wasm-activities` feature still needs Rust 1.95, as `wasmtime` 48 does.
- **Phase 4** (next): production hardening -- sharding, observability, metrics, dashboard (Vantage UI — Workers tab shipped in issue #142; DLQ, schedules, and DAG visualization pages remain); Step 5 of issue #256 (remove classic DAG executor, drop `harvest_dag_runs`). Note: the cancellation primitive and `Saga` both ship; their interaction semantics, idempotency contract, and replay-determinism contract are documented in `docs/saga.md` and locked in by three integration tests in `tests/saga_tests.rs` (issue #238).
